narrate.summary: This paper develops a scalable method for choosing sensor locations for tsunami early warning. It addresses a Bayesian optimal experimental design problem for a linear time-invariant model of seafloor motion and tsunami observations, seeking to reduce uncertainty through a D-optimal criterion. The method reformulates the problem in the data space, then uses greedy sensor selection with Schur-complement updates rather than repeatedly factoring large matrices. A distributed, pipelined implementation overlaps file input with accelerator computations. In the Cascadia Subduction Zone application, it selected 175 sensors from 600 candidates for a parameter field with more than one billion degrees of freedom.
narrate.key_results: The proposed design method selected 175 sensors from 600 candidate locations in about 1.5 hours on 16 NVIDIA A100 graphics processing units, after the necessary model and data-space matrix preparation. It achieved near-ideal weak and strong scaling over a 256-fold increase in processors; at the largest strong-scaling tests, reported efficiency was 94% on Perlmutter and 89% on Frontier. The pipelined implementation was about 3.5 times faster than a non-pipelined, single-buffered implementation. Compared with 10,000 random configurations, the selected design scored 13.83 standard deviations above their mean and 9.92 standard deviations above the best-scoring random configuration; some random configurations performed worse than the uniform configuration.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a design method for discrete choice experiments used to study preferences, including healthcare preferences. The method uses simulated annealing to construct Bayesian D-optimal partial profile designs for multinomial logit models with main effects and interactions, while keeping a specified number of attributes constant in each choice set. To address uncertainty about which interactions belong in the model, it combines criteria for a main-effects model and an interaction-effects model. In simulations, the method produced more efficient designs than the two-stage coordinate-exchange approach under the tested conditions. A healthcare case study also found that the robust design gave more accurate estimates than the original and main-effects designs.
narrate.key_results: Across 144 simulated settings, the two-stage coordinate-exchange designs had an average relative Bayesian D-efficiency of 92.60% compared with the simulated annealing designs, and were less efficient in every setting; the comparison allowed the annealing method the same runtime as the coordinate-exchange method. In 10 model and prior scenarios, the robust design averaged 96.25% efficiency relative to the scenario-specific benchmark. In the healthcare case study, the robust design reached 89.70% efficiency relative to the true-model design, compared with 78.64% for the original design and 75.89% for the main-effects design. In 500 simulated datasets with 300 participants, the robust design’s expected mean square error was 0.0370, close to 0.0361 for the true-model design and below 0.0528 for the original design and 0.0714 for the main-effects design.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Synthetic Designed Experiments for Representational Sufficiency (SDRS), a method for diagnosing and correcting failures in vision models using controllable synthetic images. It treats the model as a system to investigate and uses designed combinations of scene factors, rather than random image generation, to probe model behavior. The method uses analysis of variance on task loss to identify missing coverage of factor levels and unwanted dependence on nuisance factors. It then prescribes varied synthetic examples for coverage gaps and matched counterfactual examples for nuisance-factor dependence. Three controlled experiments report improved task performance over models trained without synthetic corrections and show that the audit can detect factor entanglement in a generator.
narrate.key_results: In the dSprites shape-classification experiment, targeted synthetic data trained with task loss alone improved held-out accuracy from 0.499 to 0.790, using 3,000 synthetic images; the full SDRS objective reached 0.751. Random synthetic data and domain randomization reached 0.824 and 0.851, respectively, using balanced-distribution samples as oracle references. In procedural-scene segmentation, held-out mean intersection over union improved from 0.948 to 0.998 with SDRS and to 0.9995 with task-loss-only training on the same diagnosed data; random sampling and domain randomization reached 1.000. narrate.summary: This paper develops a cost-aware design for estimating a treatment effect in a multivariate linear front-door causal model with unobserved confounding. Measurements are collected in stages: baseline covariates and treatment are observed first, then the mediator and response may be measured at additional cost. The authors derive an efficient influence function and use it to construct sampling probabilities that allocate measurements according to their contribution to estimation precision and their cost. The design minimizes asymptotic variance within a specified class of augmented estimators and also yields a back-door design. Simulations and applications report lower variance than a full-measurement strategy at the same total budget.
narrate.key_results: Across the four dataset configurations in the applications, the optimized design’s reported relative efficiency values were 0.7662, 0.6802, 0.8987, and 0.9470 compared with full measurement; these correspond to variance reductions of about 23.4%, 32.0%, 10.1%, and 5.3%. The corresponding required sample-size increases were 135%, 154%, 115%, and 109% to match the total cost of full measurement. In simulations, theoretical asymptotic mean squared error tracked empirical error even at modest sample sizes, and the optimized design outperformed full measurement at matched budgets. Under the paper’s tested mild quadratic departure from linearity, the optimized design also had smaller mean squared error, although the authors expect its advantage to diminish with stronger departures.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify linearity as the strongest restriction and expect efficiency gains to diminish as nonlinearity becomes more pronounced. Their sampling schemes follow the causal order, and their main theory assumes a front-door structure; they also state that characterization of efficient observed-data influence functions beyond the chosen augmentation class remains open.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The optimal policy depends on model coefficients and error-distribution quantities that must be estimated before or during design, so errors in these inputs may lead to poorly allocated measurements. The empirical evaluation is limited to a small set of biological, medical, and industrial datasets and comparisons chiefly against full measurement, rather than prospective studies or a broad range of competing allocation methods.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying designs that do not follow the causal order, including sequential updates to sampling probabilities. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test plug-in designs prospectively and assess how uncertainty in estimated model inputs affects realized costs and effect estimates. It could also adapt the optimization to operational constraints such as minimum measurement rates, fixed batch sizes, or measurement capacities, and compare it with other cost-aware design strategies.

narrate.summary: SEED-SET is a sequential design method for testing the ethical alignment of autonomous systems under limited evaluation budgets. It models measurable system outcomes separately from stakeholder judgments, using variational Gaussian processes for the scenario-to-outcome and outcome-to-utility mappings. Its acquisition rule combines information gain about both models with preference for scenarios predicted to have higher utility. The method uses pairwise judgments from a large language model as a proxy for stakeholder feedback and is tested in power-grid resource allocation, drone fire rescue, and urban routing, as well as on a travel-mode dataset. The authors report that it finds more highly preferred test scenarios and explores high-dimensional spaces more broadly than the compared methods.
narrate.key_results: Across the reported applications, SEED-SET achieved higher preference scores than random sampling, a single preference model, and the version-space active-learning baselines; the paper also reports better performance than the tested Bayesian optimization with preference exploration variants in the power-grid comparison. The abstract reports up to 2 times as many optimal test candidates as baselines and a 1.25 times improvement in coverage of high-dimensional search spaces. The main experiments plot results through 100 iterations and use five random seeds per experiment. On the travel-mode dataset, generated samples matched the real data most closely for travel time, income, and party size, while wait time showed substantial variation.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that sparse variational models can handle tens of thousands of observations, but scaling to hundreds of thousands or more remains challenging. They also note that the current stationary kernel may be restrictive, that the method requires the full set of objective metrics to be known in advance, and that language-model judgments may be sensitive to prompts and context.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main preference evaluations rely on language-model proxies and handcrafted preference scores, so they do not establish that the selected scenarios align with actual stakeholders’ values in deployment. The evidence also comes from a small set of selected applications and five-seed simulation studies; the travel-mode analysis does not validate ethical judgments against a broad sample of real stakeholder preferences.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest stochastic variational inference to scale to much larger datasets, and nonstationary kernels or deep Gaussian processes to address limitations of stationary kernels. They also identify extending the framework to multi-agent settings and real-time applications as future work, and recommend ongoing alignment checks or fine-tuning for language-model evaluators.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could replace or calibrate the language-model proxy with direct, diverse stakeholder judgments and test whether the resulting designs remain useful under changing or conflicting preferences. Applying the method to real system trials with practical constraints on operating conditions, safety, and experiment costs would help assess its value beyond the paper’s simulations and travel dataset.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an empirical Bayes (EB) framework for using results from related studies to design a new experiment. It assumes that study-specific treatment effects come from a shared distribution, which is estimated from earlier study results using either a Gaussian model or a nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE). The estimated distribution is then used to choose a design that maximizes expected value for a specified goal, including estimating treatment effects, improving welfare during the experiment, or informing a later policy decision. The authors apply the approach to stratified randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with examples from oncology drug trials and Project STAR. They show theoretically that the chosen design approaches the design that would be selected if the true cross-study distribution were known, and demonstrate that prior evidence can change treatment allocation across groups.
narrate.key_results: For the oncology overall-survival example, the data include 821 subgroup estimates from 87 studies, with the analyzed overall-survival prior drawing on 64 studies. Under the stated equal-share, equal-cost design, the no-information allocation assigns treatment probabilities of 0.250 to both groups; the joint Gaussian EB and joint NPMLE designs shift these to 0.229 and 0.271, and 0.231 and 0.269, respectively. In Project STAR, 79 schools and 5,772 students provide historical information; for the policy-choice objective, the probability for the second stratum rises from 0.149 without prior information to 0.331–0.341 under joint EB designs, while the fourth-stratum probability falls from 0.317 to 0.265–0.271. Under the paper’s regularity conditions, regret falls at the inverse-square-root rate in the number of prior studies for Gaussian EB, while the NPMLE rate is slower and includes logarithmic factors; under additional smoothness and curvature conditions, the rates improve to the inverse-number-of-studies rate, with logarithmic factors for the NPMLE.

key_equations.name: Empirical Bayes design rule

key_equations.name: Oracle regret bound

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify exchangeability across studies as a maintained assumption and note that their main analysis uses harmonized study-level parameters for clarity, although many real studies report only partial or differently defined effects. They also note that nonparametric prior estimation is computationally harder than Gaussian estimation, and that the oncology application requires consequential choices about which studies and estimates can be pooled.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The examples do not prospectively run the proposed designs, so the reported allocation changes are design calculations rather than evidence that they improve outcomes in a new trial. In the oncology example, harmonizing diverse subgroup definitions and selecting one estimate when studies report multiple related results may alter the estimated prior, while the design comparisons do not quantify that sensitivity.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to conditional exchangeability using study characteristics, developing sequential designs that update the prior as new evidence arrives, and constructing inference procedures that account for uncertainty in the estimated prior and resulting design choice.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate robust designs that remain useful when historical studies are only partly comparable, and incorporate practical constraints such as minimum subgroup sample sizes or limits on assignment changes. Prospective validation in real experiments, along with accessible implementation software, would help establish how well the proposed allocations work in practice.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a sequential experimental design method for reconstructing an unknown function with a Gaussian process (GP). It addresses two weaknesses of variance-based selection: expected information gain (EIG) does not use measured values when model settings are fixed, and it tends to select points near domain boundaries. A geometric equalizer corrects the boundary preference, while a reconstruction warp uses variation in the acquisition model's posterior mean to focus measurements where finer resolution may be needed. Both corrections change acquisition only; the prediction model remains unchanged. Across synthetic and real-data benchmarks, the equalizer improves reconstruction, and the warp can add further gains when the posterior mean captures local function variation.
narrate.key_results: The study evaluated 16 synthetic benchmarks and two real-data benchmarks, using 10 seeds and up to 200 acquisition rounds. On bounded domains, the geometric equalizer achieved 8–14% area reduction (AR) relative to farthest-point sampling (FPS) across tested dimensions and acquisition lengthscales; plain EIG sometimes performed worse than a fixed Sobol design. At 200 rounds, adding the reconstruction warp matched or improved on the equalizer alone on all 18 benchmarks; on Gramacy–Lee, the combined method reached 44.5% AR, 37.1 percentage points above the equalizer alone. The equalizer was two to three orders of magnitude cheaper per round to evaluate than negative integrated posterior variance (NIPV) and expected predictive information gain (EPIG), which require numerical integration at each round.

key_equations.explanation: The corrected acquisition score alpha at location x is the geometric equalizer g multiplied by the posterior variance s_T squared after applying the reconstruction warp; the equalizer depends on acquisition lengthscale ell_a and design size N.

narrate.limitations_stated: The design-density derivation assumes a local first-order approximation of the function, which may fail when local curvature is large. Early in acquisition, an inaccurate posterior mean may make unexplored regions appear flat; the uniform density component provides a minimum sampling rate but does not improve the gradient estimate. The main experiments use a fixed acquisition kernel and pool-based selection, and the transport construction is constrained by coordinate ordering.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-data evaluations use fitted surrogate functions as reference targets rather than demonstrating a sequential campaign in a physical laboratory, so operational gains and measurement costs in real experiments remain uncertain. The benchmark study covers a limited set of functions and domains, and its results may not transfer to irregular feasible regions or experiments with constraints and costs that affect which runs can be performed.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify joint adaptation of acquisition-model hyperparameters and gradient-based acquisition optimization as open extensions. They also suggest more expressive or rotation-invariant transport maps, and leave open whether separating geometric correction from observation-dependent allocation is useful for optimization objectives.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective validation in physical experiments, including the cost and feasibility constraints that affect actual run selection. Further studies could test the method on irregular or constrained design spaces and examine whether its gains persist when measurement noise and the reconstruction objective differ from the benchmark setup.

narrate.summary: The paper designs randomized experiments to compare two predetermined matching plans on the same finite population, without assuming a model for outcomes or agent behavior. Its main method, the Alternating Path Randomized Design, first separates the pairs on which the plans disagree into alternating paths and cycles, then randomizes sequentially along those components to keep assignments feasible. The method estimates the average treatment effect with a Horvitz–Thompson estimator and provides a finite-population central limit theorem for inference. For many-to-one matching, the paper adds graph-based procedures to find feasible path and cycle decompositions that respect capacity constraints. The authors show that the method can reduce variance as the population grows and derive an asymptotically optimal conditional randomization probability for long components.
narrate.key_results: For long paths and cycles, the worst-case variance per edge is minimized as the conditional randomization probability approaches the square root of 2 minus 1, approximately 0.4142. The theoretical variance of the proposed estimator decreases at rate 1/N, while the naive design that switches between the complete treatment and control matchings has worst-case variance that does not vanish as the population grows. In the controlled numerical comparison, using sizes from 10 to 50 and 500 randomizations per size, the proposed design’s true variance fell from 0.8983 to 0.1848; the naive design’s true variance remained around 3.1. In the dataset-based demonstration, 5000 randomizations gave a normality-test statistic of 0.9999 and a p-value of 0.2817, and the empirically best probability at size 50 was approximately 0.417; the estimated variance upper bound closely tracked the true variance.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation uses a constructed, grouped matching environment based on employment records rather than a field experiment that randomizes actual workers and jobs. narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the design in live matching operations and study implementation constraints such as limited availability, varying capacities, or restrictions on which assignments can be randomized. narrate.summary: This paper develops a design-based method for estimating causal effects when experimental participants do not always take the treatments assigned to them. For lag-1 panel effects, HT average biases ranged from -0.0051 to -0.0008 and coverage from 0.928 to 0.956; the multivariate 2SLS comparison had biases from 0.1306 to 0.1968 and coverage from 0.798 to 0.815. narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for constructing optimal experimental designs for regression models, with its main focus on E-optimality, which maximizes the smallest eigenvalue of the information matrix. The authors represent designs as probability measures and use Wasserstein geometry to move design points toward improved designs. Because the E-optimality objective can be nonsmooth, they choose feasible ascent directions by projecting candidate directions onto the design region's tangent cones and solving a convex semidefinite program. They prove that the resulting continuous flow has an exact objective-increase identity and that every limit point is stationary. Numerical examples on second-order response surface models and a logistic regression model show near-optimal E-design values and greater reliability than particle swarm optimization in several higher-dimensional comparisons.
narrate.key_results: The computational comparisons used 100 equally weighted design points; particle swarm optimization used a swarm of 100, a 1,000-iteration budget, and 100 independent runs. For the second-order model with two factors, CWSA reached the reported theoretical E-optimal values of 0.200 on the cube and 0.100 on the ball, while the best particle swarm results were 0.199 and 0.099. With five factors on the ball, CWSA reached 0.027, the theoretical value, while the best particle swarm result was 0.025; on the cube, CWSA reached 0.192 against a theoretical value of 0.200, while the best, mean, and worst particle swarm values were 0.167, 0.153, and 0.062. For the seven-dimensional logistic regression model, CWSA reached 0.154, exceeding the best of 100 particle swarm runs at 0.153; the particle swarm mean and worst values were 0.152 and 0.150.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a design-based method for estimating quantile treatment effects in randomized experiments. It studies rerandomization, which accepts assignments only when treatment and control groups meet a specified covariate-balance rule, and compares it with complete randomization. The authors derive the estimator’s asymptotic distribution for a finite population, allowing the covariates and potential outcomes to be fixed rather than drawn from a model. The distribution combines a normal component with a truncated normal component, and the paper uses this result to construct conservative confidence intervals. Theoretical results and simulations show that rerandomization can improve estimation efficiency when the covariates predict the outcome indicators at the target quantiles.
narrate.key_results: The theory gives a percentage reduction in asymptotic variance of (1 minus the truncated-normal variance) times the squared correlation measure for the quantile estimator and covariates. In the linear simulations, rerandomization reduced variance by about 12.4% to 45.2% relative to complete randomization; the simulations used 10 covariates, 1,000 units, 10,000 assignments, and an acceptance probability of 0.001. In nonlinear simulations with 1,000 units, reductions ranged from about 12.4% to 46.9%; for an imbalanced allocation, some confidence-interval coverage rates fell below 95%, while the reported rerandomization coverage rates at 2,000 units were at least 95.3%. In simulations using covariates from the Infant Health and Development Program, variance reductions ranged from about 11.6% to 28.9%, and rerandomization generally produced shorter confidence intervals than complete randomization.

key_equations.explanation: An assignment is accepted when the Mahalanobis distance M, calculated from the covariate mean difference tauhat_x and covariate covariance matrix S_xx, does not exceed threshold a_n.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors require regularity conditions, including local smoothness near the target quantiles, a sufficiently slow decline in the assignment-acceptance probability, and that covariates do not perfectly predict the relevant outcome indicators. They also report that, in the nonlinear simulations with an imbalanced allocation and 1,000 units, some confidence-interval coverage rates were below the nominal 95% level; increasing the sample size to 2,000 improved coverage.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The efficiency improvement depends on how strongly the covariates predict the outcome indicators at the chosen quantile, so balancing covariate means may offer little benefit when that relationship is weak. The paper does not assess the operational cost of obtaining an acceptance probability as low as 0.001, and its real-data-based exercise uses simulated potential outcomes rather than observed treatment effects from a real trial.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying regression-adjusted quantile treatment effect estimators under rerandomization in the finite-population framework. They identify deriving their asymptotic distributions and establishing inferential guarantees as needed work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare alternative balance criteria and practical constraints, such as limited assignment attempts or restrictions on treatment allocation. Testing the method in real randomized experiments and examining sequential or adaptive use would help establish its practical value beyond the simulated settings.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for sequential Bayesian optimal experimental design in inverse problems governed by partial differential equations, where the unknown is a spatially varying random field. It learns a policy using policy-gradient reinforcement learning so that new designs can be selected from the experiment history without repeatedly optimizing designs online. The method combines parameter and state dimension reduction with a latent attention neural operator that approximates both the physical solution and its sensitivities. It evaluates designs using a Laplace-based D-optimality criterion and can use prior samples as substitutes for maximum a posteriori estimates when computing rewards. In simulated contaminant tracking, the learned sensor-placement policy generally beat random placements and moved sensors upstream toward more informative measurements.
narrate.key_results: The latent attention neural operator had average test errors of 2.13% for the solution and 2.42% for the reduced Jacobian, while its D-optimality estimates had a relative root mean square error of 1.29% against the finite element reference. For eigenvalue evaluation, the surrogate took 0.14 seconds compared with 13.46 seconds using the finite element method, which the authors report as about 100 times faster. Using prior samples in place of maximum a posteriori estimates gave a 0.44% relative root mean square error and a 0.99 correlation with the standard calculation. In tests on five parameter samples, the learned policy outperformed more than 97% of 200 random placements for each sample; the reported win rates ranged from 97.5% to 98.0%.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Neural Optimal Design of Experiments (NODE), a method for choosing measurement locations while training a neural reconstruction model for inverse problems. It directly optimizes a fixed number of continuous sensor locations instead of selecting weighted points from a dense candidate grid, and jointly trains the locations and reconstruction network. The objective targets accurate parameter or image recovery, and the method also supports sequential selection of additional measurements using data already collected. The authors test it on an exponential-growth model, handwritten-digit images, and simulated sparse-view X-ray computed tomography. They report that NODE recovers the analytically optimal endpoint pattern in the benchmark and improves on the tested fixed-design baselines in image reconstruction and classification.
narrate.key_results: For the exponential-growth benchmark, NODE was tested with sensor budgets from 2 to 200 and drove the locations toward the two interval endpoints; the theoretical large-budget split is about 41.42% at one endpoint and 58.58% at the other. On the Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology (MNIST) dataset, tests used budgets from 1 to 100 pixels and a test set of 10,000 images; NODE gave lower reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracy than random and highest-variance fixed designs, although the paper does not report a single numerical improvement figure. In computed tomography (CT), the authors optimized designs with 10 and 45 projection angles and report better-looking filtered backprojection reconstructions than with uniformly spaced angles. The adaptive CT demonstration added measurements in increments of 5 angles and showed reconstruction improvement across successive stages for three test images; these experiments used simulated measurements rather than measurements acquired from patients.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the reconstruction-network architecture depends on the sensor budget, so studying different budgets requires retraining. They also note that their interpolation strategy is not specific to optimal design and that NODE, like existing single-level learning-based methods discussed in the paper, does not directly address D-optimality.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence comes from simulated or public benchmark data, not from a deployed measurement system, so practical constraints such as sensor access, acquisition time, and patient or process variability are not validated. The adaptive CT evidence is visual and limited to three test images, while the MNIST and CT comparisons do not provide a common quantitative measure of improvement or an evaluation under distribution shift.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using autoencoders to learn a lower-dimensional output representation and potentially reuse training across sensor budgets. They also propose interpolation methods tailored to discrete design spaces, including mollifier-based approaches, and extensions toward D-optimal design using generative models to represent posterior distributions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the chosen locations under physical acquisition constraints and on real experimental or clinical measurements, with prespecified quantitative performance and cost measures. It would also be useful to test robustness to changes in noise and data distributions, and to assess whether one trained model can support a range of measurement budgets without full retraining.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an optimal experimental design method for choosing which magnetic resonance imaging frequencies to measure when estimating cardiovascular model parameters directly from undersampled frequency-space data. It targets parameter estimation in a simulated flow model, including an aortic model governed by the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with Windkessel outlet conditions. The authors calculate how predicted measurements change with each parameter, use those sensitivities to form a Fisher information matrix, and select frequency masks using average-variance or uncertainty-volume criteria. They construct masks with greedy and restricted exchange algorithms and compare them with circular and pseudo-random Gaussian masks. In the analytical and aortic simulations, the optimized masks generally yield more accurate parameter estimates than the conventional masks, including at high undersampling.
narrate.key_results: In the aortic study, the authors tested masks with budgets of 5, 10, 25, and 50 frequencies per two-dimensional slice, corresponding to acceleration factors of approximately 211, 106, 42, and 21. Optimized masks generally had lower estimation error than circular and pseudo-random Gaussian masks, with the clearest advantage at low budgets; the authors report that 5-point masks can outperform conventional 50-point masks and reduce acquisition time by more than 10 times in the flow-encoding directions. The aortic estimates were evaluated over 50 independent noise realizations, while the analytical case used 30; both used a signal-to-noise ratio of 15. For the aortic case with three parameters and a 50-point budget, the greedy algorithm took 4 minutes 34 seconds, compared with 2 hours 18 minutes for the exchange algorithm; for low budgets, exchange sometimes produced better estimates.

The authors also note that the exchange algorithm may become impractical as the number of parameters or data resolution grows, and that the design may depend on the parameter values used to calculate sensitivities.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses one simulated aortic geometry and one analytical example, so performance across different patients, geometries, and acquisition systems is not established. The aortic design also restricts masks to a two-dimensional pattern stacked through the third dimension, applies the same mask to all velocity directions, and optimizes only the three Windkessel resistances rather than the inflow parameter.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose evaluating more advanced or efficient optimization methods, including initializing exchange from a greedy design, stochastic methods, or continuous relaxations. They also plan to test real magnetic resonance data with coil sensitivities and to incorporate parameter uncertainty and uncertainty in the measurement sensitivities; they identify other criteria, including a criterion focused on a specified parameter combination, as options to investigate.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the masks across multiple simulated subjects and real acquisitions, with explicit scanner and sampling-trajectory constraints, to establish whether the reported benefits transfer to practical protocols. Sequential designs that update the mask as parameter estimates improve, and prospective validation against independently acquired reference measurements, would also assess practical value.

narrate.summary: This review and practical guide studies rerandomization in two-group randomized experiments that aim to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE). Rerandomization repeatedly assigns treatment until the groups satisfy a prespecified covariate-balance rule, most often one based on Mahalanobis distance. The authors review theoretical results and give guidance on choosing balance rules, conducting inference, handling missing data, and addressing computational demands. They also compare rerandomization with complete randomization (CR) in simulations for difference-in-means, linear-adjusted, and doubly robust estimators. The simulations suggest that rerandomization can improve finite-sample precision and make estimates from different analysis choices more similar, especially in smaller samples and when covariates predict outcomes well.
narrate.key_results: The main simulations used sample sizes from 100 to 1,000 in increments of 100, 10 covariates, and an acceptance proportion of 0.01; the authors generated 1,000 assignments under each design for each simulated dataset. Compared with CR, rerandomization improved precision for adjusted estimators in finite samples, especially for the doubly robust estimator at smaller sample sizes, while gains generally moved toward no difference as sample size increased. Across the 10-covariate linear and nonlinear scenarios, rerandomized designs were at least as powerful as CR, and adjusted estimators generally had nominal coverage; the difference-in-means estimator showed some overcoverage or undercoverage in particular linear scenarios. In the 100-covariate extension, the authors report instability, low power, and coverage problems for adjusted estimators at small sample sizes, although rerandomization improved some precision and coherence measures; the paper does not report a single numerical percentage for the size of these gains.

narrate.summary: This theory paper studies how maximum-entropy sampling (MESP) and binary D-optimality (0/1 D-Opt) can be represented in terms of one another. MESP selects a fixed-size subset of variables to maximize the determinant of a covariance submatrix, while 0/1 D-Opt selects design points to maximize the determinant of an information matrix. The authors define four mappings between the two problem types and use them to transfer upper bounds and analyze branch-and-bound (B&B) subproblems. Their results show that transferred bounds can match known bounds or improve their computation, and that the most effective bounds can depend on the matrix structure. Numerical experiments demonstrate particularly strong performance for some bounds on instances constructed from D-optimality problems.
narrate.key_results: For simulated pure 0/1 D-Opt instances built from random matrices with 120 candidate rows and 40 or 60 columns, the MESP-induced NLP-Id and BQP bounds generally performed best, while linx and NLP-Di were among the weakest. In experiments with 100 candidate rows and 50 initial columns, changing the multiplicity of the greatest eigenvalue changed the relative performance of bounds; observed gaps decreased as that multiplicity increased, though the authors give no explanation. On a real-data-derived covariance matrix with 2,000 rows and rank 949, the D-induced natural bound was faster to compute than the equivalent NLP-Id bound, with larger speed improvements when the greatest eigenvalue had higher multiplicity. The paper also proves that transferring bounds from 0/1 D-Opt subproblems to MESP preserves the corresponding B&B subproblems, whereas for the reverse direction the two branching approaches need not yield the same subproblems; the authors establish that one approach has no larger natural bound on the child problems they analyze.

narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for making two-group A/B experiments more reliable when outcomes are skewed or heavy-tailed and group sizes are unequal. It studies Welch’s t-test, with the objective of keeping false-positive probabilities close to their nominal levels and balanced between the two tails. The authors derive how outcome moments and the treatment-to-control allocation affect the test statistic, then use those results to calculate minimum sample sizes. For experiments below those thresholds, they propose correcting p-values with an Edgeworth expansion that uses estimated skewness and kurtosis. Simulations and platform data show that the thresholds track observed error behavior and that the correction can improve tail error control at smaller sample sizes.
narrate.key_results: For simulated lognormal data with allocation ratio 5, nominal significance level 0.05, and tail tolerance 0.01, the first- and second-order minimum sample sizes were 8,712 and 5,986; the second-order threshold was more precise and less conservative. For publish-count data, the corresponding thresholds were 51,094 and 35,042, while for live-duration data they were 15,022 and 9,361. In the reported repeated experiments, the corrected p-value generally brought both tail deviations within the 0.01 tolerance at sample sizes where the ordinary t-test still showed notable bias. Under more extreme allocations and a tolerance of 0.03, the predicted and observed minimum sample sizes were 31,422 and about 31,500 for publish count, and 50,347 and 51,300 for live duration.

narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for estimating the average treatment effect (ATE) in finite populations when treatment assignments are made sequentially and can depend on past assignments and outcomes. It studies inverse propensity weighted (IPW) and augmented inverse propensity weighted (AIPW) estimators without assuming a probabilistic model for the outcomes. The analysis establishes central limit theorems under two forms of design stability: one requiring assignment probabilities to converge, and a weaker form requiring averages of inverse assignment probabilities to converge. The authors also construct conservative variance estimators and confidence intervals, with conditions under which those intervals have asymptotically exact coverage. Applications to Wei’s adaptive coin design and Efron’s biased coin design illustrate the results; simulations generally show shorter intervals for the AIPW estimator.
narrate.key_results: The theory establishes asymptotic normality for both estimators under strong or weak design stability, with explicit asymptotic variances. Wei’s adaptive coin design is shown to be strongly stable with limiting treatment probability one half; Efron’s biased coin design is weakly stable, and the simulations use its bias parameter set to 0.7. For Wei’s design, coverage and interval-length simulations use 5,000 units and 20,000 replications; the authors report that AIPW intervals are substantially shorter than IPW intervals across the examined outcome settings. In the Wei-design diagnostics at 10,000 units, variance ratios for AIPW are 0.9046 for additive outcomes, 0.9885 for non-additive outcomes, and 1.0090 for log-additive outcomes, compared with 0.8600, 0.8553, and 1.0140 for IPW, respectively. The paper reports negligible Monte Carlo bias overall and generally improved variance-ratio agreement at the larger sample size.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the asymptotic variances contain cross-moment terms that cannot generally be estimated because both potential outcomes are not observed for the same unit; their proposed variance estimates are therefore conservative. Under weak design stability, consistent variance estimation also requires an additional condition beyond weak stability itself. Exact asymptotic coverage requires specified forms of treatment-effect homogeneity.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The results rely on bounded outcomes and assignment probabilities bounded away from zero and one, which may not hold in experiments with rare treatment allocation or highly variable outcomes. The simulations cover two allocation mechanisms and a small set of outcome structures; they do not establish finite-sample performance for the wider range of adaptive designs and practical constraints encountered in experiments.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to covariate-adaptive designs and using it for inference in adaptive designs aimed at optimal allocation. They also identify further investigation of stability in more general designs, especially when assignment probabilities depend on unknown outcome features.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could assess the methods under practical constraints such as minimum group sizes, restricted or delayed randomization, and covariate balance requirements. Sequential confidence procedures and validation in real experiments would also help establish how the proposed intervals perform when monitoring and operational decisions occur before the experiment ends.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces A2D2E, an accumulated aggregated D-optimal design estimator for estimating main effects of individual inputs in black-box prediction models. It targets the same population main effect as Accumulated Local Effects (ALE), while seeking more precise local slope estimates and reducing sensitivity to out of distribution evaluations. For each observed input, the method evaluates the model at the vertices of a small hypercube and uses those results to estimate local slopes, which it aggregates within bins and accumulates into effect curves. The method does not require a differentiable predictor and has a closed-form estimator. Theory and simulations show consistency with the ALE target and favorable performance, especially when inputs are correlated.
narrate.key_results: Across additive simulations using several predictive models and dependence settings, A2D2E generally performed better than ALE-based alternatives, with its advantage most evident under high feature correlation; in one high-dependence setting, its ORMSE was 0.0907, compared with 0.1220 for ALE and 0.1985 for DALE. In a sensitivity experiment with 100 independent replications, A2D2E had an ORMSE of 3.14 at one bin, versus 79.97 for ALE and 3.15 for DALE, and it had the lowest reported error at each tested bin count. Under independent inputs, partial dependence often performed best, while A2D2E remained competitive. For one input variable with four inputs and 500 observations, A2D2E took 0.241 seconds, compared with 0.028 seconds for ALE; when estimating all four effects with vertex caching, the times were 0.132 seconds for A2D2E and 0.112 seconds for ALE. Real-data examples used the Auto and Iris datasets, but the authors describe these examples as illustrative rather than accuracy comparisons.

key_equations.name: Local hypercube design
key_equations.explanation: S_i is the local set of evaluation points, x_i is observation i’s input vector, δ sets the design width, s is a vector of coordinate-wise signs, and p is the number of input variables; the equation places evaluations at the vertices of a hypercube centered on x_i.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the D-optimal design relies on local linearity and homoscedastic error assumptions, and that its variance optimality need not hold under model misspecification. They also note that A2D2E requires exponentially many model evaluations in the number of inputs for a single effect, and that ALE can be a cheaper competitive option when out of distribution sensitivity is absent.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The hypercube vertices can still fall outside the feasible combinations of inputs in a constrained engineering process, even when they are close to an observed point. The method also requires choosing the bin count and local width, and the paper’s simulations do not establish performance across a broad range of real experimental constraints or response surfaces.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose a principled way to choose among partial dependence, ALE, and A2D2E using observable features such as dependence strength and a model’s sensitivity to out of distribution evaluations. They also identify generalized optimal design criteria for nonlinear local models or heteroscedastic errors as a direction for future research.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could adapt the local design to engineering constraints, such as allowable factor combinations, discrete settings, or safety limits, and compare its performance on real designed experiments. It would also be useful to investigate sequential selection of evaluation points and to validate estimated effects against independently measured process responses.

narrate.summary: The paper develops sliced space-filling designs for mixture experiments that also have process variables, with the goal of spreading runs across the mixture region in both the complete design and each process-level slice. It treats the design points as representative points of a target distribution, usually the uniform distribution over the mixture region. The construction uses an energy-distance decomposition to link the quality of the complete design and its slices, and gives one-shot and sequential optimization algorithms. The authors prove distributional convergence under stated conditions and show that the algorithms converge to stationary solutions. In their numerical examples, the proposed energy-distance methods generally provide better space-filling and prediction performance than the compared existing methods.
narrate.key_results: In uniformity comparisons repeated 50 times, the hybrid energy-distance one-shot method generally performed best, with its sequential version also substantially better than the compared existing methods on the reported criteria; the coset decomposition method had better minimum separation in one standard-simplex comparison. In prediction tests using 15 runs in each of three slices and a test set of 1,000 points, the energy-distance methods substantially outperformed the existing methods across three simulated response models, with the two hybrid-criterion methods performing best. In the drug-combination example, the design used seven dose levels and a test set of 1,400 points; the proposed methods performed better than other methods when dose was treated as continuous, while the compared energy-distance designs had broadly similar performance with the qualitative-level Gaussian process models. The paper reports these findings in figures rather than giving exact numerical error values in the text.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose combining their energy-distance decomposition with marginal coupled and double coupled design approaches to address growth in the number of process-level combinations. They also propose developing metrics and algorithms that improve uniformity in low-dimensional projections.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could benchmark computation time and sensitivity to starting points and sample approximation size, alongside design quality, across larger constrained mixture regions. Validation in physical mixture experiments and testing how well the sequential designs support real early-stopping decisions would also clarify their practical performance.

narrate.summary: The paper develops optimal-design results for multivariate crossover trials, in which several responses are measured for each subject in each period. It assumes fixed effects for periods, subjects, direct treatment effects, and first-order carryover effects; responses are uncorrelated with one another, while measurements within each response may be correlated and have response-specific variance structures. The authors derive the information matrix for direct treatment effects and use its eigenvalues to assess estimation of estimable treatment contrasts. They show that a type I orthogonal array of strength 2 is A-optimal, D-optimal, and E-optimal for binary designs when the number of periods equals the number of treatments and is at least 3. A numerical illustration finds that the cited 3-by-3 gene-profile design has low efficiency relative to the orthogonal-array benchmark under the examined covariance settings.
narrate.key_results: For binary designs with p = t ≥ 3 and n = lambda t(t − 1), the type I orthogonal array of strength 2 is proved A-optimal, D-optimal, and E-optimal for direct effects in the multivariate model. The result allows each response to have its own within-response covariance matrix and variance, while assuming that distinct responses are uncorrelated. In the illustration, the 3-by-3 design assigns sequences ACB, BAC, and CBA to 6 subjects each; for the examined bivariate setup, its reported A-, D-, and E-efficiencies are at most 0.0278, 5.9537 times 10 to the power of negative 7, and 0.0278, respectively. The comparison is with the optimal orthogonal-array design, and the authors conclude that it would have been substantially more efficient for that example.

narrate.limitations_stated: The results are established for the fixed-effect model with responses uncorrelated between themselves; within-response correlation and heteroscedastic variances are allowed. The main optimality theorem applies to binary designs with p = t ≥ 3, and the authors note that more complicated covariance structures can make it difficult to identify exact theoretical optimal designs.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The optimality theorem is restricted to a particular run size and design class, so it does not establish optimality for arbitrary numbers of subjects, unequal numbers of periods and treatments, or nonbinary allocations. The assumptions exclude correlation between different responses, and the numerical illustration compares one cited design with the orthogonal-array benchmark rather than validating performance across a broad set of real trials.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying multivariate mixed-effects models with random subject effects, including settings with within-response correlation. They also propose investigating A-, D-, and E-optimality when observations have within-response correlation but responses remain uncorrelated, where the dispersion structure may make exact theoretical results difficult.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could assess designs under correlations between different responses and under practical constraints such as limited treatment sequences, unequal subject allocation, or dropout. It could also compare the theoretical designs in prospective or retrospective clinical experiments and examine sequential design updates as data accrue.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the factorial-design optimal transport test (FDOTT), a method for testing relationships among probability distributions observed across factorial-design groups. It extends the analysis-of-variance idea of testing linear effects to discrete distributions on metric spaces, using optimal transport (OT) to quantify differences between distributions. The method tests general linear hypotheses, including main effects and interactions, by comparing empirical distributions with pairwise OT-based distances. The authors derive large-sample distributions for the test statistic and study plug-in, bootstrap, and permutation approaches for obtaining critical values. They report good performance in simulations and illustrate the method with cellular biophysics and fingerprint data.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical results provide limiting distributions under null hypotheses and alternatives; under the null, the test statistic has a limit expressed through OT applied to Gaussian sampling variation. Simulations used equal sample sizes of 50, 100, and 500 in hypothesis-testing comparisons, with 250 repetitions and 1,000 draws from limiting distributions; the authors report that FDOTT and the barycenter method had stronger power than rank-based and distance-based competitors when distributions shared a mean but had different covariances, while the rank-based method had higher power in some Poisson-distribution comparisons. In the three-factor microtubule analysis, the cell-line main effect had p-value 0.028, while the vimentin and actin effects had p-values 0.856 and 0.125; the tested interactions were not significant, with reported p-values from 0.614 to 1.000. In the fingerprint analysis, the overall comparison, interaction, and main effects had p-values below 0.001; the real-versus-synthetic whorl comparison was not significant, with p-value 0.666, whereas the other reported pairwise comparisons were significant.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that extending the theory to continuous domains is considerably more challenging, because convergence of the positive and negative parts of signed empirical measures is not assured. Their permutation procedure is presented for the one-way layout, and extending it to higher-way layouts or obtaining an exact permutation procedure remains open. They also note that the cost must identify distinct measures for the test to identify differences.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method tests distributional effects but does not provide a procedure for choosing or randomizing a physical experiment’s treatment runs, so it is not a design-generation method for quality engineers. Its real-data demonstrations depend on histogram construction, discretization, and the selected cost matrix, and the paper does not report sensitivity analyses for those choices. Computational and inferential performance may also be difficult to transfer to settings with much larger support spaces or factorial layouts beyond those examined.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating computationally advantageous alternatives such as debiased Sinkhorn divergences and sliced Wasserstein distances. They also identify extensions of permutation procedures to higher-way layouts, exact permutation testing, and combining their method with approaches that treat the observed data themselves as random probability measures as future research directions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the test in randomized, constrained industrial experiments, including blocking, missing runs, and unequal allocation, and to establish practical guidance for selecting bins and cost matrices. Further work could also develop sequential monitoring or adaptive allocation procedures and validate error rates and computational needs in prospective real-world experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops Locally Optimal Restricted Designs (LORDs) for phase I/II dose-finding studies that assess both efficacy and toxicity. For illustration, it uses a four-parameter continuation-ratio (CR) model and seeks precise estimation of dose-response parameters or target doses while restricting assignments to doses judged acceptably safe or within a therapeutic window. The authors use particle swarm optimization (PSO) to search for dose locations and allocation proportions on either a continuous dose range or a prespecified discrete set. They examine four hypothetical dose-response scenarios and compare the resulting designs with a random walk rule. In those scenarios, the designs generally offer a stronger balance of estimation efficiency and expected successes, though the authors emphasize that the findings assume the model and its true parameter values are known.
narrate.key_results: The study considered four scenarios and a discrete set of nine doses; the continuous-design solutions used between two and four support doses across the reported examples. On the authors’ combined performance score, the best LORD scored 0.91 versus 0.48 for the random walk rule in Scenario A, 0.86 versus 0.34 in Scenario B, 0.84 versus 0.32 in Scenario C, and 0.99 versus 0.97 in Scenario D. For Scenario C, extending the dose range produced a 5.36-fold increase in overall-model D-efficiency and a 27.86-fold increase in target-dose c-efficiency relative to the original discrete design. The paper reports no numerical trial sample size or finite-sample run-size comparison; its efficiency calculations use information-based, asymptotic criteria.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that LORDs depend on a chosen statistical model, which may be misspecified, and on true model parameters that are unknown at the start of a study. Their comparison is idealized: it assumes the CR model is plausible, the true parameter values are known, and asymptotic assumptions apply. They also note that they did not solve the problem of optimally choosing the prespecified dose set.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluations use four constructed dose-response scenarios rather than observed trial data, so practical performance under real clinical conditions is not demonstrated. The designs are specified as allocation proportions, but the paper does not show how to convert those proportions into integer patient assignments for a particular sample size or account for operational constraints such as cohorting. The PSO search is stochastic, and the paper does not report repeated-search variability or a comparison of computational reliability across settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify adaptive LORDs as important future work, including how to choose an initial design, stage sample sizes, and rules for interim analyses when parameters cannot be estimated. They also propose further work on selecting and refining the prespecified dose set, and mention alternative response models and designs for discriminating among candidate models. They suggest comparing LORDs with other phase I/II designs, including BOIN12 and U-BOIN.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate LORDs through finite-sample simulation and real-trial case studies, with parameter uncertainty and model misspecification built into the evaluation. It could also develop methods for translating optimal proportions into feasible integer allocations under cohort, safety-monitoring, and dose-availability constraints, then validate those implementations prospectively.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a model-free method for expanding a Latin hypercube sampling design used in simulation and computer experiments. Its goal is to add samples while retaining one-dimensional bin coverage and good space-filling properties. The method regrids the parameter space, selects empty bins, and places a new Latin hypercube design within those regions before combining it with the initial design. The authors also define the LHS degree to measure how much of the one-dimensional bin coverage is retained. Their examples show that expansion quality depends on the added sample count, and that optional optimization can improve discrepancy.
narrate.key_results: In one example, an initial design with 20 samples in 2 dimensions was expanded by 18 samples; the reported centered discrepancy decreased from 1.0 × 10^-3 without optimization to 4.7 × 10^-4 with discrepancy optimization, and the expanded design had an LHS degree of 1. In another example, for an initial design with 20 samples, adding 12 samples gave a degree of 1, while adding 8 gave 0.9107; the authors report that increasing the addition from 8 to 9 raised the degree from about 0.91 to about 0.98. Across initial sizes of 10, 100, and 1000 samples and dimensions of 2, 4, and 8, the degree was largely independent of dimension and followed a similar trend with the ratio of added to initial samples, with perfect designs at additions that were multiples of the initial size. Compared with repeated one-at-a-time expansion, the direct expansion had a higher degree; repeated expansion was also reported to increase computation time by a factor proportional to the number of additions. Performance measurements averaged over 1000 initial-design realizations showed that optimization takes longer than unoptimized expansion, and that optimization scales less favorably as dimension increases.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the expansion method is specialized for sampling a uniform hypercube. Extending it to constrained spaces, non-uniform boundaries, or weighted samples is left for future work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The LHS degree measures only one-dimensional bin occupancy, so it does not by itself establish low correlation, good multidimensional projection behavior, or strong performance on a particular response model. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose generalizing the implementation to LHS-like methods for constrained spaces, non-uniform boundaries, and weighted samples. They also plan to apply the software to numerical-relativity surrogate models and stellar-physics simulation interpolation.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Bayesian experimental design with large language models (BED-LLM), a method for choosing questions adaptively in multi-turn information-gathering tasks. It is designed for settings where an agent wants to learn an unknown target, such as an entity in 20 Questions or a user's film preferences. At each turn, the method generates possible questions, estimates how much each is expected to reduce uncertainty about the target, and asks the question with the highest expected information gain (EIG). It builds and updates candidate beliefs by generating diverse hypotheses and filtering out those inconsistent with the interaction history. In the tested tasks, BED-LLM outperformed direct prompting and other adaptive question-selection approaches, including when the questioner and answerer used different models.
narrate.key_results: In 20 Questions, the paper reports that BED-LLM improved success by an average of 37.4 percentage points over direct prompting; its success rate more than doubled in over half of the evaluated setups and did not decrease in any. Across the reported model and dataset combinations, final success rates for BED-LLM ranged from 26% to 95%, compared with 8% to 45% for direct prompting, and BED-LLM was the strongest method in the table. For Qwen2.5-72B on the Animals dataset, BED-LLM took 2 hours, 28 minutes, and 43 seconds, while the data-estimation alternative took 1 day, 17 hours, 13 minutes, and 34 seconds. In preference elicitation, BED-LLM produced higher-rated film recommendations than direct prompting and the entropy-based comparison across the evaluated models, with results measured over 200 user profiles and five question turns.

key_equations.name: Expected information gain
key_equations.explanation: Here, EIG is expected information gain, x is a candidate question, theta is the target, y is the response, p denotes the probability distributions in the model, H is entropy, and the expectation averages over possible responses.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that selecting each question by its immediate information gain is myopic and can be suboptimal compared with planning for the final uncertainty after several turns. They also explain that full Bayesian updating can require too many costly language-model evaluations, and that the preferred model formulation depends on the relative complexity of the target and response spaces.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses language models to generate answers or judge recommendation quality rather than testing the method with actual users or a physical process, so performance in operational experiments is not established. Results also depend on generated candidate questions and hypotheses, filtering thresholds, and limited benchmark sets; the candidate pool may omit useful designs.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest that BED-LLM's model formulation, belief updates, and information-gain estimates could support policy-based experimental-design methods that plan beyond the next question. They also discuss using the data-estimation formulation when responses are more complex than the target, and updating the likelihood with interaction history when the target does not capture all information needed to predict responses.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method in real user studies and controlled engineering experiments, comparing its chosen questions with measured outcomes rather than language-model-generated answers or ratings. Further work could examine constrained or costly questions, broader response formats, and whether sequential use remains effective when candidate designs must meet practical operational restrictions.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a measure-based approach to optimal sensor placement for continuous-time stochastic filtering. It represents the observation budget as a probability measure over time, so discrete measurement schedules and continuously varying sensor strength fit within the same framework. The filtering equations depend on that schedule, and the authors derive utility gradients using a backward adjoint equation. They demonstrate the approach with a logistic-growth parameter-estimation example and a linear Gaussian filtering example. The examples show schedules concentrating observation effort at informative times, although the paper does not report a numerical comparison against competing optimization methods.
narrate.key_results: In the logistic-growth example, projected gradient descent began with a uniform schedule over the time interval from 0 to 6 and used 15 iterations with one Monte Carlo sample per gradient estimate; the schedule concentrated near time 3 and produced greater posterior contraction than the initial uniform schedule. In the linear Gaussian example, a two-dimensional Brownian signal was observed through one component before time 3 and the other afterward, over a time interval from 0 to 6. Over 100 minimization iterations, the optimized schedule concentrated observation effort just after times 0 and 3, and the plotted integrated covariance utility decreased. These are illustrative simulation results; the paper reports no numerical efficiency comparison with greedy, discrete-selection, or other gradient-based design methods.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say that most calculations are formal and that rigorous justification, including well-posedness of the adjoint equation, is omitted. They also report that solving the filtering equation becomes infeasible at high dimensions and note that their simple projected gradient descent does not account for the stochastic nature of the utility.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The demonstrations use only low-dimensional simulated examples, so they do not establish how well the approach performs in real experiments or in larger, more complex filtering problems. The paper also does not benchmark its method against discrete sensor-selection or greedy methods, leaving practical comparative efficiency untested.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring stochastic optimization methods, including simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation, and gradient flows based on Wasserstein or Rao-Fisher geometry. They also identify adjoints for particle filters, the relationship between smooth schedules and discrete measurement locations, adaptive sensor placement, and extension to spatial sensor placement as future directions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test robustness when the assumed signal or observation model is misspecified and assess performance using real experimental data. They could also evaluate schedules under operational constraints such as minimum spacing, sensor availability, and limits on how sharply observation effort can concentrate.

narrate.summary: The paper develops designs for group testing studies that estimate disease prevalence and diagnostic assay sensitivity and specificity when the assay is imperfect and study resources are limited. It uses a pooled-test probability model and constructs designs under several estimation criteria, as well as maximin designs that balance multiple criteria. For large studies, the authors compute approximate designs by convex optimization and verify their properties with optimal-design theory. For smaller studies, they propose rounding procedures to produce implementable exact designs subject to sample-size or budget constraints. In the Chlamydia examples, the designs retain high efficiency, while a numerical downstream example shows that sufficiently inaccurate parameter assumptions can increase the expected number of tests.
narrate.key_results: For the Chlamydia parameter values used in the main examples, maximin designs for two objectives had minimum efficiencies above 0.90, and designs balancing three objectives had minimum efficiencies above 0.81 across the reported settings. The proposed exact designs for individual criteria achieved efficiencies above 0.96 in the reported budget examples; exact multi-objective efficiencies approached their approximate-design benchmarks as sample size or budget increased, with a reported discrepancy of about 0.018 in small cases. Compared with optimizing one criterion at a time, a design can perform poorly on competing criteria: for maximum group size 61 and cost parameter 0.2, the determinant-optimal design had efficiencies of 0.568 under the least-information criterion and 0.536 for the selected sensitivity-specificity combination. The determinant-optimal and prevalence-focused designs reproduce results reported by earlier methods, while the paper adds other criteria and multi-objective designs. In the downstream example with 10,000 subjects, the oracle choice required an expected 5,108.374 tests; severe parameter misspecification increased this by up to 461.348 tests, or 9.031 percent.

key_equations.name: Pooled-test positive probability

key_equations.name: Maximin design
key_equations.explanation: The design weights w over the allowable group sizes in set Delta_M are chosen to maximize the smallest efficiency Eff_j across K objectives.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the approximate-design theory may not apply when sample sizes are small, and that approximate designs may not be implementable as exact designs. They also describe the designs as locally optimal, so their performance depends on the nominal parameter values; the proposed rounding procedures are practical constructions rather than direct proofs of exact-design optimality.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main model and numerical examples do not establish performance when pooled outcomes have dependence, group-specific prevalence, or assay behavior that differs from the assumed model. Evaluation is primarily numerical and centered on specified Chlamydia parameter values, so the paper does not provide prospective validation in an operating screening program.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to multiple assays, more complex cost structures, and closer integration with fully sequential or adaptive testing procedures.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test these designs in field screening studies and assess how sensitive their performance is to dependence among subjects, prevalence heterogeneity, and pooling-related changes in assay accuracy. It could also optimize the first-stage estimation design and downstream testing rule jointly under a single total-resource constraint.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces Stepwise Deep Adaptive Design (Step-DAD), a method for sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED). It is designed for probabilistic models with unknown parameters and aims to maximize expected information gain (EIG) over a full sequence of experiments. The method first trains a policy-based BED (PB-BED) policy before the experiment, then uses observed outcomes to update the posterior and fine-tune the policy at selected points during the experiment. The authors evaluate the method in simulated source-location, temporal-discounting, and economic-preference problems. Across these problems, Step-DAD generally achieves higher information gain than the fully amortized Deep Adaptive Design (DAD) baseline, and can remain more robust when the prior used for training differs from the test-time prior.
narrate.key_results: For source location with 10 experiment steps and refinement at step 6, Step-DAD’s reported lower-bound total EIG was 7.759 ± 0.114, compared with DAD’s upper-bound estimate of 7.089 ± 0.013; these are conservative estimates using different bounds. With 10K DAD training steps followed by 2.5K refinement steps, Step-DAD matched or exceeded the 50K-step DAD baseline for refinement steps later than step 3. For hyperbolic temporal discounting, Step-DAD at step 10 achieved a lower-bound total EIG of 6.711 ± 0.040, versus DAD’s lower-bound 4.778 ± 0.013. For the constant elasticity of substitution problem, the corresponding lower-bound estimates were 13.879 ± 0.352 for Step-DAD and 10.181 ± 0.021 for DAD. In a source-location test with shifted priors, the paper reports that DAD’s information gain fell to essentially zero at larger shifts, while Step-DAD retained positive information gain.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that Step-DAD requires computation during the experiment, which can be difficult when design decisions must be made very quickly. It also requires posterior inference and policy refinement, and the paper’s results show that performance can depend on the available inference and fine-tuning budgets.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on simulated experiments and model-based information-gain estimates, so it does not establish how the method performs with real experimental data or substantial model error beyond the tested prior shifts. The comparisons cover a limited set of benchmark problems, and practical use depends on having enough time and computational resources to obtain a useful posterior and refine the policy between experiment stages.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate Step-DAD in real experiments and under broader forms of model misspecification, including errors in the outcome model and constraints on available designs. Further work could also test refinement schedules and compute budgets in constrained deployments, and develop reusable software or procedures for choosing when to update the policy.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a method for testing whether a new strategy improves outcomes in a randomized online experiment, with particular focus on detecting small average treatment effects. Its weighted two-armed bandit statistic combines a mean component and a volatility component, while a policy chooses subsequent arms based on the statistic’s running value. Because the statistic depends on observation order, the authors also propose calculating it across multiple reordered datasets and combining the resulting p-values. Counterfactual outcomes are estimated with doubly robust methods, using cross-fitting and machine-learning outcome and propensity models. The paper reports theoretical error control and higher power in simulations and analyses of operational data from a ride-sharing company.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with a sample size of 20,000, the paper compares the proposed method with the unweighted bandit statistic, a normal-score doubly robust test, a covariate-adjusted test, and a difference-in-means estimator; it reports controlled type I error rates and generally higher power for the permuted method. In semi-synthetic experiments based on real data, its reported power was 0.758 with one gradient-boosted model and 0.764 with a stacked model, compared with 0.738 and 0.732 for the corresponding unpermuted bandit results; type I error was 0.052 for the permuted method in both cases. On real dataset B, the permuted method’s p-values were 0.044 with either of two individual models and 0.032 with stacking, compared with 0.053 for the covariate-adjusted test. The authors used 25 reorderings and report that using more did not substantially improve power.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method across organizations and outcome types, and assess performance when treatment assignment, allocation ratios, or data order are constrained by operational practice.
