narrate.summary: This paper designs a way to assign treatments under a fixed resource budget while retaining each unit’s intended treatment probability. It applies swap rounding to convert fractional assignment probabilities into binary decisions, with exactly B units treated and the original marginal probabilities preserved. The resulting assignments are negatively correlated, which the authors show can reduce the variance of the inverse propensity weighting (IPW) estimate of the average treatment effect compared with independent assignment. They also describe pairing units with similar covariates before rounding to seek further variance reduction. Simulations and semi-synthetic studies generally support the approach, though which version performs best varies by dataset.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical results show that swap rounding preserves the assignment probabilities and gives an unbiased IPW estimator; under the paper’s assumptions, its variance is no greater than that under independent assignment. The synthetic experiments use sample sizes of 50, 100, 250, 500, 1,000, and 5,000, with 100 scenarios replicated 100 times; the authors report that covariate-matched swap rounding has the lowest empirical variance across the three synthetic settings. The semi-synthetic infant health dataset contains 747 individuals, and the public housing dataset contains 3,163; covariate-matched swap rounding is reported as competitive in the infant health study, while regular swap rounding performs best in the housing study. The paper presents variance plots and comparisons with independent IPW, limited Bernoulli assignment, rerandomization, uniform random assignment, and self-normalized IPW, but does not state exact numerical variance reductions in the text.

narrate.summary: The paper develops optimal experimental designs for drug-combination studies that aim to identify dose combinations producing a specified proportion of the maximum response. It considers nonlinear response-surface models, including an additive model and the Greco model, and defines effective combinations as response contour sets. The proposed design places observations to reduce prediction variance along the contour sets, using a selected L q norm; a Bayesian version averages the criterion over uncertainty in model parameters. The authors derive optimality conditions and an efficiency bound, then evaluate the method using a real oncological data set and simulations. In the reported examples, tailored designs estimate the target contours more precisely than common factorial and ray designs, while Bayesian designs help when interaction effects are uncertain.
narrate.key_results: For the case study’s target levels of 10% and 50%, the tailored design has efficiency 1.00 by definition, compared with 0.60 for the determinant-optimal design, 0.34 for the original design, 0.04 for the factorial design, and 0.06 to 0.07 for the ray designs. For levels of 20% and 80%, the corresponding tailored design has efficiency 1.00; the determinant-optimal and original designs have efficiencies of 0.80 and 0.47. Across two simulation scenarios, the tailored design had the lowest reported contour prediction errors among the compared designs at sample sizes of 27, 36, 45, 90, and 152, based on 1,000 simulation iterations per sample size. In the second robustness setting, the Bayesian design performed nearly as well as the design optimized for the true interaction, while a design based on a misspecified interaction had clearly higher errors.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the norm order must be selected in advance; they compare selected values, including 1 and 2, but do not study higher values or the supremum-norm case. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate constrained designs that respect practical dose grids, allocation limits, and replication requirements, then validate their performance in prospective combination studies. narrate.summary: This paper compares a Taguchi design with an active-learning approach for predicting weld-bead geometry in wire arc additive manufacturing. The inputs are current, weld speed, and contact-tip-to-work distance, and the objective is to predict a combined response based on penetration depth, width, and height. The Taguchi method uses an orthogonal array, while Gaussian process regression starts with Latin hypercube samples and selects additional experiments in regions of high prediction uncertainty. Both approaches are tested against experimental results. The authors report that the regression approach reaches better predictive accuracy with fewer experiments than the Taguchi method.
narrate.key_results: On 15 test cases, the Taguchi model trained on 25 points had a root mean square error of 1.33 and a coefficient of determination of 0.80. The final Gaussian process regression model, trained on 20 points, had a root mean square error of 1.00 and a coefficient of determination of 0.89. The regression model approached the Taguchi model’s performance after 7 experiments and surpassed it after 17; the authors also report that its prediction errors were more symmetrically distributed around zero, while the Taguchi predictions showed systematic underprediction.

key_equations.name: Taguchi main-effects prediction
key_equations.explanation: μpredicted is the predicted response mean, μ is the overall mean, and αᵢ, βⱼ, and γₖ are the effects of current, weld speed, and contact-tip-to-work distance at levels i, j, and k.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that Taguchi’s linear assumptions and lack of uncertainty quantification limit its predictive power in nonlinear, continuous design spaces. They do not identify a limitation of their own study.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The comparison is limited to one wire arc additive manufacturing setup, one electrode-substrate pairing, and a design space with five specified levels for each of three inputs. Evaluation uses 15 test cases from that design space and a single combined response, so the reported results do not establish performance for other materials, continuous input settings, or separate predictions of bead width, height, and penetration depth.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the Gaussian process regression framework to inverse design and using an expected-improvement acquisition function to optimize weld parameters for a target bead geometry. They also suggest applying the approach to materials design and nonlinear process optimization, including powder metallurgy and additive manufacturing.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the approach across additional material pairs and manufacturing setups, with repeated experiments to assess measurement and process variability. Comparing separate bead-geometry objectives and practical process constraints, as well as testing sequential use in production settings, would also clarify its broader usefulness.

narrate.summary: This review surveys designs for computer experiments that aim to spread simulation runs across an input region and improve prediction with surrogate models. It focuses on Gaussian process emulation and explains how geometric coverage, especially fill distance, relates to prediction error. The authors review Latin hypercube designs, distance-based and projection-based criteria, and methods for constrained, mixed-input, and multi-fidelity experiments. They compare several design approaches using simulated test functions and Gaussian process predictions. The main finding is that no design is best in every setting, although some approaches are substantially faster to generate than others.
narrate.key_results: In the Robot Arm simulation, designs were compared at 81, 162, and 256 runs over 50 repetitions; the distance-distributed designs had the lowest root mean squared prediction error at the smaller run size, while uniform projection designs gave the most accurate predictions at larger run sizes. Orthogonal-array-based Latin hypercube designs performed worst in that comparison, and the authors note that available run sizes for these designs are limited. Across four additional test functions with 3, 5, 6, and 9 inputs and run sizes of 50, 100, 200, and 300, no approach consistently led in prediction error; distance-distributed designs generally had the highest errors, though the errors remained reasonably accurate on the reported log scale. For selecting the best design from 100 candidates at 300 runs and 9 inputs, generation took 199.993 seconds for minimum average reciprocal distance designs and 125.012 seconds for uniform projection designs, compared with 4,417.411 seconds for maximin Latin hypercube designs.

key_equations.explanation: The response y_i at input x_i equals the mean mu, the process value Z at that input, and error epsilon_i; Z is a zero-mean Gaussian process with scale tau and kernel K, and epsilon_i is normally distributed with scale sigma.

key_equations.explanation: The fill distance h is the largest, over points x in region Omega, of the Euclidean distance from x to its nearest design point x_i in design X.

key_equations.name: Distance-based design criteria
key_equations.explanation: The maximin design X_mm maximizes the smallest pairwise distance among n design points in Omega, while the minimax design X_mM minimizes the largest distance from any point in Omega to its nearest design point.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that constructing optimal space-filling designs is computationally and mathematically challenging, especially in high dimensions, and that minimax design algorithms have received relatively little attention because of this complexity. They also note that orthogonal-array-based designs are limited to particular run sizes and that no design class is universally optimal.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The prediction comparisons use a small collection of simulated test functions, a univariate response, and a Matern kernel with a fixed smoothness choice, so the reported rankings may not carry over to other response structures or kernels. The generation-time comparisons are tied to one Apple laptop and particular software implementations, and do not establish performance under different hardware or computational budgets.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for more scalable algorithms for large and high-dimensional problems, and for adaptive or sequential sampling strategies. They also propose extending methods to non-Euclidean and mixed input spaces and integrating machine learning to automate design selection and optimization.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could benchmark the reviewed criteria under model misspecification, noisy simulation outputs, and different kernel choices, using both synthetic and real engineering studies. Practical extensions could also evaluate designs under explicit run budgets and feasibility constraints, and provide reproducible software comparisons across hardware.

narrate.summary: This paper evaluates statistical methods for estimating treatment effects in A/B tests, especially business experiments with small samples, repeated observations, confounding, or sparse and heavy-tailed outcomes. It compares regression adjustment, generalized estimating equations, and rank-based tests, and develops a doubly robust generalized U statistic for flexible treatment-effect definitions. The proposed method uses pairwise outcome comparisons, adjustment for treatment assignment and outcome predictions, and joint estimating equations for the treatment effect and nuisance quantities. The authors provide theoretical efficiency results, simulations, and analyses of LinkedIn experiments. Their findings show that methods suited to the outcome distribution and experiment structure can improve power over a basic t-test, but no single method dominates in every setting.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with zero-inflated heavy-tailed outcomes, at sample size 200 and effect size 1, the ZTU power was 0.555 for positive Cauchy data and 0.138 for lognormal data, compared with 0.262 and 0.082 for the Mann–Whitney U test, and 0.048 and 0.011 for the t-test. In the confounding simulations at sample size 200, the DRGU power was 0.610 for lognormal data and 0.660 for Cauchy data; corresponding ordinary least squares power was 0.435 for each, while the unadjusted rank test power was 0.235 and 0.310. In LinkedIn experiments, the ZTU detected a 0.94% conversion-value lift with p-value below 0.001, while the t-test gave p-value 0.249; regression adjustment found a 1.84% lift in conversions per impression with p-value below 0.001, compared with p-value 0.154 for the t-test. For a 28-day campaign experiment, the repeated-measurement GEE analysis had p-value 0.051, compared with 0.184 for the final-day snapshot analysis; the longitudinal doubly robust test estimated a treatment-versus-control win probability of 0.54 with p-value 0.045.

key_equations.name: General treatment-effect definition
key_equations.explanation: The equation defines the treatment effect δ as the expectation E of the function φ applied to the difference between response Y₁ under treatment and response Y₀ under control.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors require the function defining the generalized treatment effect to be monotone and to have a finite second moment for distributional robustness; the identity function does not meet that moment requirement for some heavy-tailed distributions. They also note that ZTU is not always more efficient than the tie-adjusted Mann–Whitney U test: its relative efficiency depends on the direction of the effect and the proportion of positive outcomes.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence for the new DRGU method is based on selected simulated distributions and a small set of business experiments, so its performance across other outcome structures and operational settings is not established here. The paper does not compare alternative randomization or assignment designs; its main contribution is improved analysis of experiments rather than construction of a new experimental design.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate these methods across a wider range of allocation schemes, practical constraints, and outcome distributions, including settings with limited overlap between treatment groups. Prospective validation in additional real experiments and evaluation of sequential or repeated decision-making would help establish how the methods perform in routine quality-engineering use.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces grouped orthogonal arrays (GOAs) for computer experiments in which factors are divided into groups, and the response is assumed to be additive across those groups. The goal is to provide better within-group projections for estimating effects and predicting responses than designs without that group structure. The authors construct designs with strength-three or near strength-three groups, as well as designs whose groups have minimum aberration. Their methods use finite-field constructions, projective geometry, recursive combinations of arrays, and a search algorithm. Simulations show improved main-effect estimation and prediction in the tested settings compared with several conventional designs.
narrate.key_results: The construction results provide strength-three groups for designs with s-cubed and s-to-the-fourth runs for any prime-power number of levels, and recursive constructions allow other run sizes; the paper also gives minimum-aberration group designs. In 1,000 main-effect estimation replications, the 27-run GOA had average errors of 1.223, 6.091, and 12.009 at interaction variances 1, 25, and 100, compared with 1.283, 6.323, and 12.623 for the minimum-aberration design. For 81 runs, the GOA errors were 0.110 at all three interaction variances, compared with 0.495, 2.417, and 4.845 for the minimum-aberration design. In 1,000 prediction replications, the 27-run GOA had root mean squared errors of 3.860, 19.238, and 38.053 at those variance settings, compared with 3.936, 19.542, and 38.664 for the minimum-aberration design; the corresponding 81-run values were 3.882, 19.434, and 38.879 versus 4.020, 20.098, and 40.259.

key_equations.explanation: D is the resulting design, A is a difference scheme, B is an orthogonal array, and the plus-in-circle operator is the Kronecker sum used to combine them.

key_equations.name: Lower bound on three-column strength
key_equations.explanation: p(D) is the proportion of three-column combinations in the resulting design that have strength three, c is the number of columns in the difference scheme, and n is the number of columns in the orthogonal array.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that they leave the theoretical arguments for the main-effect bias properties of their designs for future work. They also note that Latin hypercube designs may be preferable when the underlying functions are highly complex and many levels are needed.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The performance evidence comes from simulations of a particular additive polynomial model and a small set of design sizes and group structures, so it does not establish performance under other response structures or practical constraints. The paper does not validate the designs in real experiments, and its use may require users to accept the selected run sizes and level structure rather than accommodate arbitrary restrictions on settings or randomization.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating strong orthogonal arrays constructed from GOAs, developing GOAs with variable group sizes beyond those obtained by dropping columns, and studying GOAs in analysis of computer experiments. They specifically identify connections to Gaussian processes with blocked additive kernels as a research direction.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the designs with nonadditive responses, model misspecification, and constraints such as restricted factor combinations or split-plot randomization. Sequential or adaptive use of GOAs, as well as validation in industrial experiments and accessible software for generating and analyzing them, would also help establish practical utility.

narrate.summary: This paper proposes a sequential Bayesian experimental design framework for estimating physical model parameters while also learning model discrepancy. It targets the expected information gain for each of these goals, treating low-dimensional physical parameters with standard Bayesian methods and high-dimensional neural-network coefficients with auto-differentiable ensemble Kalman inversion (AD-EKI). The method estimates information gain from the change in an ensemble’s distribution and differentiates through the inversion iterations so gradient-based optimization can select measurement designs. The authors test it in simulations of contaminant source estimation governed by a convection-diffusion equation, including both a misspecified source parameter and a misspecified source function. In these tests, designs chosen for discrepancy calibration improve local model accuracy and support more accurate estimation of the source location than designs that ignore discrepancy.
narrate.key_results: In the parametric-error simulation, six sequential stages corrected the source-strength parameter toward its true value and reduced the source-location estimation error, whereas the uncorrected baseline remained higher and less stable. In the structural-error simulation, a neural network with 37 coefficients was used; the corrected model reduced local error near the current design in every reported stage, although total-domain error did not always fall. For example, at stage 3, local mean squared error fell from 0.0503 without correction to 0.0016 with correction, and local relative error fell from 0.2245 to 0.0340. Design optimization involved 70 updates in the parametric case and stopped after 64 updates in the structural case when it reached a search boundary; the reported structural test used an ensemble size of 40. Computational tests found memory use increased linearly with ensemble size; checkpointing kept memory roughly constant after the first inversion iteration, while computation time increased linearly with iteration count.

key_equations.name: Physics model with learned discrepancy
key_equations.explanation: The state u evolves over time t according to the physics-based model G with parameters theta_G plus the discrepancy neural network NN with coefficients theta_NN.

key_equations.name: Expected information gain criterion
key_equations.explanation: The expected information gain for design d is the expectation over data y of the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the posterior distribution p(theta given y and d) and prior distribution p(theta), for target parameters theta.

key_equations.name: Ensemble Kalman inversion update
key_equations.explanation: The j-th ensemble parameter member theta at iteration n plus one is updated from its value at iteration n using the parameter-output covariance Sigma-theta-g, output covariance Sigma-g-g, observation-noise covariance Gamma, perturbed observation y, and model prediction g for that member.

key_equations.name: Design for discrepancy calibration
key_equations.explanation: The selected design d-star for neural-network discrepancy parameters maximizes the expected ensemble-estimated Kullback–Leibler divergence over the design space D, using data y, network coefficients theta-NN, and the maximum a posteriori physical-parameter estimate theta-G-star.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the ensemble-based divergence relies on a Gaussian approximation and finite ensembles, so performance can degrade for strongly skewed or multimodal posteriors. Small ensembles restrict updates to the subspace covered by the ensemble and can cause biased estimates, underestimated uncertainty, or slow convergence. They also note that ensemble Kalman inversion can become biased or collapse in later iterations, motivating early stopping.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is limited to a simulated contaminant-source problem with a particular convection-diffusion model and a 37-coefficient discrepancy network; it does not establish performance on measured industrial or other real-system data. The comparisons do not broadly benchmark the method against alternative high-dimensional Bayesian design methods, and each design measures only one space-time point under the study’s specified sequential design constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose integrating and evaluating methods such as covariance inflation, localization, dropout, and other covariance-estimation techniques to improve robustness with non-Gaussian posteriors or small ensembles. They also point to potential use of AD-EKI in other bilevel optimization problems, including meta-learning and structure optimization.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the sequential designs in physical experiments, including cases where sensor placement, measurement cost, safety, or sampling schedules constrain feasible designs. Further comparisons could test other discrepancy representations and design criteria, and assess whether the method remains reliable when the physical model or assumed measurement-noise distribution is wrong.

narrate.summary: The paper develops optimal designs for isothermal experiments to estimate microbial growth-model parameters. It uses the Baranyi model for growth over time and the Ratkowsky square-root model to describe how the maximum growth rate depends on temperature, using a study of Pseudomonas growth on button mushrooms as its case study. The authors construct determinant-based and c-optimal designs for experiments with fixed temperatures, then design jointly over time and temperature. They also examine how much final experiment time can be shortened while retaining high design efficiency. Their results show that commonly used schedules are less efficient than the proposed designs, particularly for estimating the temperature-model parameters.
narrate.key_results: For fixed temperatures, the existing schedules had D-efficiencies from 0.80 to 0.86 relative to the proposed D-optimal designs for estimating the primary-model parameters. For estimating the maximum growth rate, the existing schedules had c-efficiencies from 0.42 to 0.47 relative to the c-optimal designs. For joint estimation across time and temperature, the existing schedule had D-efficiency 0.58 and the union of the fixed-temperature optimal designs had D-efficiency 0.65, relative to the joint design; the authors report a 42% reduction in observations compared with the existing schedules. At a minimum efficiency of 99%, the fitted final-time relationships imply time savings of 48.5% to 58.6%. The joint D-optimal design had c-efficiency 0.015 relative to the design specifically optimized for estimating the two secondary-model parameters, indicating that the joint design is poor for that narrower objective.

narrate.limitations_stated: The designs are locally optimal and depend on nominal parameter values. The authors report that the joint design is sensitive to uncertainty in the lag-duration parameter, especially when that parameter is underestimated.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The designs are approximate designs with proportions at support points, so users must translate those proportions into feasible integer replicate counts; the paper does not demonstrate that conversion in a real experiment. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest applying the robust-design methodology they previously developed to reduce efficiency loss when nominal parameter values are uncertain, particularly for the lag-duration parameter.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to implement and validate the proposed schedules in new laboratory experiments, then compare observed parameter uncertainty and prediction accuracy with the existing schedules. Further work could also assess practical integer-run designs and operational constraints, such as limits on available temperatures or the number of independent experimental units.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes an adaptive dose-optimization design for early cancer clinical trials, where the best dose and the patients most likely to benefit may not be known in advance. It first uses the time-to-event continual reassessment method (TITE-CRM) and pharmacokinetic (PK) data to identify doses considered safe, then explores those doses using efficacy outcomes and patient characteristics. Bayesian sparse group selection (BSGS) is used to find characteristics associated with response and with different optimal biological doses (OBDs), while futility assessments can stop enrollment of groups unlikely to benefit. The design combines dose escalation, randomized dose exploration, and later dose optimization. Simulations based on an entrectinib trial found that it often identified target groups and could recommend different doses for groups with different dose-response patterns.
narrate.key_results: In scenarios where one characteristic defined the target population, the design correctly identified it about 90% of the time with a total trial size of 60; with a total size of 80, identification improved by about 3 percentage points. When two characteristics defined the target population, complete identification was 31% at a total size of 60 and 40% at 80, although at least one characteristic was identified 84% of the time at size 60. Across scenarios, the false positive rate (FPR) was at or below 15%; for scenarios with dose heterogeneity, the true positive rate (TPR) was at least 76% at size 60 except when only two doses were safe, where it was 37%. In scenarios with multiple OBDs, the proposed design often selected subgroup-specific doses more accurately than the naive method that assumed homogeneity; for example, in one scenario it selected both subgroup doses correctly over 80% of the time, while the naive method could recommend an unsuitable single dose for much of the target population.

key_equations.explanation: The response probability pi_E at dose level j for patient i depends on dose score p_j, covariate values z_mi, covariate effects gamma_m, plateau parameter alpha_0, dose parameter alpha_1, and the total number M of covariates; theta denotes the model parameters.

key_equations.explanation: The adjusted acceptable set A_d^* contains dose d_j values no greater than the smaller of the toxicity-based estimated maximum tolerated dose MTD_TOX and the PK-based estimated maximum tolerated dose MTD_PK.

key_equations.name: Adaptive randomization probability

key_equations.name: Subgroup-specific OBD criterion
key_equations.explanation: For covariate pattern z, the OBD is the minimum acceptable dose d_j whose posterior probability of reaching at least proportion epsilon of the maximum estimated response across the final acceptable set A_d** exceeds threshold Psi_OBD; pi-hat denotes estimated response and theta-hat the estimated model parameters.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the design does not use a pharmacodynamic biomarker, assumes the PK threshold is known, and assumes toxicity is similar across patients. Its efficacy model assumes a shared plateau limit and does not handle non-monotone, unimodal efficacy curves; the authors recommend using it when monotone or plateau profiles are suspected. They also note that the simulation study did not compare the method with phase I/II designs built for predefined subpopulations.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is simulation-based, using scenarios motivated by one entrectinib trial, rather than validation in a prospective clinical trial or independent dataset. The proposed total trial sizes of 60 and 80 and the covariate patterns simulated may not represent the recruitment feasibility or patient mix of other cancer trials. The method also relies on estimating multiple effects and subgroup-specific dose responses from relatively small samples, so performance under rarer covariate levels or changing enrollment patterns remains uncertain.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify incorporating a pharmacodynamic biomarker and allowing patient characteristics to affect toxicity as possible extensions. They also state that robustness to non-monotone efficacy profiles has not been studied and recommend applying the method when monotone or plateau efficacy is suspected.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective or external-data validation, including assessment of enrollment feasibility and patient safety under real trial operations. Further work could test performance when covariate prevalence changes during enrollment and when practical constraints require balanced allocation across dose and patient groups.

narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for estimating intervention effects that may change with exposure duration in stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trials with multiple interventions. It considers concurrent and factorial designs, and derives how the usual constant-effect estimator behaves when the true effects vary over exposure time. The authors compare a constant-effect model with a flexible fixed-effect model and a more parsimonious random-effect model, using simulations and data from the PONDER trial. Simulations show that assuming constant effects can produce biased estimates and poor confidence-interval coverage when effects change over time. The PONDER analyses found no significant average effect for either intervention, although the models produced estimates with different precision and direction.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 11 periods, large average effects, and a delay lasting half the exposure duration, the constant-effect model had zero coverage for both interventions; the fixed time-varying model had coverage of 94.6% and 94.8%. The flexible fixed-effect model generally had little bias across the tested effect patterns, but produced wider confidence intervals than the constant-effect model when effects were constant. In the design comparison, the concurrent design usually had 5% to 10% greater power than the factorial design; for an average effect of 0.2, it reached about 90% power with 100 individuals per cluster, while 30 per cluster required an effect of about 0.4 for similar power. In the PONDER primary-outcome analysis, constant-effect estimates were 0.22 for Intervention A and 0.30 for Intervention B, while the random-effect estimates were 0.21 and 0.33; all corresponding intervals included no effect, and the fixed time-varying model gave wider intervals and estimates in the opposite direction.

key_equations.name: Exposure-time-varying outcome model
key_equations.explanation: The individual outcome is modeled using the study-period effect, each intervention indicator multiplied by its effect at the current exposure duration, a cluster random intercept, and residual error.

key_equations.name: Exposure-time-averaged treatment effect
key_equations.explanation: The average effect for an intervention is the arithmetic mean of its effects across the exposure periods, with the number of periods determining the averaging denominator.

key_equations.name: Random treatment-effect decomposition
key_equations.explanation: An intervention effect at a particular exposure duration equals its overall mean effect plus a random deviation for that exposure duration.

key_equations.name: Expected constant-effect estimate under varying effects
key_equations.explanation: The expected vector of constant-effect estimates equals a design- and covariance-dependent weighting matrix multiplied by the vector of true exposure-time-specific effects.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors focus mainly on models with a simple cluster-level random intercept, and their development covers continuous outcomes. They note that binary and count outcomes, covariate adjustment, sample-size and power calculations for multiple-intervention designs, and effects that vary by calendar time or by both calendar and exposure time require further work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulations examine a limited set of configurations, including two interventions, five or eleven periods, and selected effect patterns, so the comparative findings may not carry over to other trial sizes, rollout schedules, or intervention combinations. The analyses also rely on assumptions such as additive combined effects in the PONDER example, and the repeated within-cluster-period bootstrap may be demanding to run in practice.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose examining more complex within-cluster correlation structures, binary and count outcomes, covariate adjustment, and sample-size and power methods for multiple-intervention trials. They also identify calendar-time effects and models combining calendar time with exposure time as important extensions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could compare designs under practical rollout constraints, such as limited implementation capacity or unequal cluster sizes, and examine how non-additive intervention interactions affect identification and estimation. Prospective validation in additional real trials and tools that make the models and their uncertainty analyses easier to use would help assess their practical value.

narrate.summary: The paper designs an optimal measurement strategy for estimating the recessed copper-pad depth in a two-dimensional periodic semiconductor interconnect. It combines a diffraction model, a camera-noise model, and prior ranges for the unknown parameters to calculate the Fisher information matrix. The design criterion is to maximize the smaller eigenvalue of the normalized matrix, so that the least-sensitive combination of parameters is measured more precisely. Applying the method to simulated measurements identifies a wavelength of 14.1 nanometers and incidence angles of 15.3 and 17.3 degrees as optimal for the two-parameter case. A separate laboratory measurement using light near 29 nanometers estimates the dishing depth as 1.60 nanometers, with an uncertainty of 0.05 nanometers.
narrate.key_results: In the laboratory experiment, measurements at seven incidence angles used 50 diffraction images per angle; the fitted dishing depth was 1.60 nanometers, with an uncertainty of 0.05 nanometers. A Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis used 500 independent reconstructions and found that dishing-depth uncertainty remained low despite correlations with other fitted parameters. For the simulated two-parameter design, the criterion selected a wavelength of 14.1 nanometers and incidence angles of 15.3 and 17.3 degrees. The paper shows sensitivity varies substantially with wavelength and angle, but does not report a numerical percentage improvement against the laboratory measurement conditions.

They describe extending the design method to more parameters and to additional experimental choices, including polarization, sample orientation, and multiple wavelengths, with the aim of improving sensitivity and throughput. They also identify dose-constrained measurements, including possible applications to soft materials, as a future use.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a laboratory validation of the predicted 14.1-nanometer design, with direct comparison against the existing measurement conditions for both uncertainty and measurement time. Further work could test how robust the selected settings are across broader parameter ranges and realistic deviations from the assumed noise and diffraction models, and could provide a reproducible software implementation for design evaluation.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how many simulations are needed to train neural networks to extract cosmological information from simulated dark matter data. Its main case uses the nonlinear matter power spectrum to estimate five cosmological parameters, with performance compared against a Fisher-information bound. The authors fit a power-law relationship between training-set size and test loss, then test their prediction using simulations sampled with a Sobol sequence. They also examine neural posterior estimation using wavelet scattering statistics. They find that the 2,000-simulation Latin hypercube set is insufficient for information saturation, while performance with the new simulation suite approaches saturation near 4,000 training simulations.
narrate.key_results: The authors generated a 32,768-simulation Big Sobol Sequence suite and used 16,600 simulations in the training, validation, and test analysis. For the power-spectrum task, the test loss scaled approximately as the number of training simulations to the power of negative 0.39 for the Latin hypercube data and negative 0.36 for the Sobol data. The original 2,000-simulation Latin hypercube set did not reach the information bound; the neural summary approached information saturation near 4,000 Sobol simulations, with little improvement beyond that point. For wavelet-based neural posterior estimation, the reported log probability scaled approximately with training-set size to the power of 0.15; posterior constraints improved most clearly for matter density and the amplitude of matter fluctuations.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the Sobol and Latin hypercube sampling designs have different sample efficiencies and produce different constants in the loss scaling, even though they give similar Fisher information for comparable training sizes at the central parameter point. They also explain that test loss is averaged across the prior range, whereas the Fisher information comparison is evaluated at the fiducial point, so the two measures need not agree.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main power-spectrum study is restricted to five cosmological parameters in specified ranges, a particular dark matter simulation setup, and a single summary statistic, so the approximately 4,000-simulation finding may not carry over to other models or experimental conditions. The design comparison is limited to Sobol and Latin hypercube sampling, and the paper does not report uncertainty intervals for the fitted scaling exponents or a replicated comparison across alternative training procedures.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating the theoretical basis of the observed power laws, other parameter-sampling strategies, and additional summary statistics and their combinations. They also plan to study hierarchical training approaches and point to fast-forward models as a way to accelerate simulation production.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare these designs under practical constraints such as parameter-dependent simulation costs, restricted parameter regions, or required marginal coverage, rather than uniform coverage alone. Sequential design strategies that select new simulation points based on current model uncertainty, followed by validation on independent cosmological simulations or observational data, would test how well the reported run-size guidance transfers to practice.

narrate.summary: The paper develops methods for designing and analyzing full factorial experiments with two-level factors and binary outcomes, using randomization-based inference for finite populations. It defines main effects and interactions as contrasts of potential response outcomes, then estimates them from randomized treatment-group proportions. It also gives procedures for confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, power calculations, and sample-size choices, including balanced and optimal allocations. The methods are applied to a randomized email audit experiment that varied signals of race, gender, and income when contacting lawyers. The analysis identifies a positive average effect for the white-race signal without multiplicity adjustment, and shows that substantially larger studies would be needed to detect the reported effects reliably.
narrate.key_results: In the audit experiment, 96 lawyers were randomized equally across 8 treatment combinations, with 12 lawyers per combination. The estimated race effect was 0.1875, with a two-sided p-value of 0.0409; the gender effect and gender-by-income interaction were each 0.1042, while the other reported effects were smaller. With individual error rate control, the normal-approximation calculation required 768 units for at least 80% power to detect all three highlighted effects; experiment-wise error rate control required 1,152 units, and finite-population simulations gave corresponding requirements of 720 and 1,056 units. For the A-optimal allocation, finite-population simulations indicated requirements of 672 and 1,056 units under individual and experiment-wise control, respectively; the paper describes the savings from optimal allocation as modest. The race logarithmic and logit factorial effect estimates were 0.63 and 0.91, respectively.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate these allocation and inference methods when treatment assignment is constrained by cost, availability, or other operational restrictions, and validate their power predictions in additional real audit experiments. narrate.summary: The paper introduces a method called SBI-BOED that combines simulation-based inference (SBI) with Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED). It targets models that can generate simulated observations but may have no usable likelihood or gradients through the simulator, and seeks designs with high expected information gain (EIG) while also training a likelihood approximation for later inference. The method optimizes a conditional normalizing flow and a distribution over candidate designs using a regularized information noise-contrastive estimation (InfoNCE) objective. The authors also use expected predictive information gain (EPIG) to select informative parameter settings for simulation when the experimental design is fixed. Across synthetic and scientific simulator studies, the method often produces better-calibrated or more accurate posterior estimates than comparison methods, even when those methods report higher EIG.
narrate.key_results: On the susceptible-infected-recovered (SIR) task, the paper reports about 5.1 million simulator calls for SBI-BOED versus about 260 million for iDAD, or roughly 50 times fewer; it reports better posterior accuracy by its median-distance measure, while iDAD has higher EIG. For the two-round SIR comparison, SBI-BOED with lambda 0.1 had an EIG of 1.47, a local calibration statistic of 0.03, and median distance of 46.85; iDAD had 2.67, 0.10, and 71.65, respectively. On the three-round bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) task, SBI-BOED had EIG 10.39, local calibration statistic 0.01, and median distance 0.61, compared with 14.23, 0.25, and 0.82 for MINEBED-BO; SBI-BOED also ran in 2,235 ± 9 seconds versus 7,095 ± 2,519 seconds. The authors report that EPIG-based query selection improved calibration over random parameter sampling under the same simulation budget in the Two Moons study, and that sequential SBI refinement improved calibration in the BMP example.

key_equations.name: Design-distribution construction

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that the likelihood-based flow can show mode collapse on Two Moons, which they associate with errors in the approximate marginal likelihood and finite contrastive samples. They also found joint training of likelihood and posterior estimators while optimizing designs unstable, and note that some comparisons use a single inference round rather than refining the inference model after each experiment.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical comparison is narrow: the scientific tasks are SIR and BMP, and the reported table results are averaged over only three seeds. Results are based on simulated data and do not establish performance in physical experiments, where execution costs, feasible design constraints, and randomization requirements may differ. The method also depends on training and evaluating a flow likelihood, so its practicality for high-dimensional observations or simulators with very costly calls remains unclear beyond the tested cases.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest extending the method to more expressive generative models, including diffusion models and flow-matching models. They also propose addressing mode collapse and estimation stability through improved marginal-likelihood approximations and possible pretraining of the likelihood or posterior estimators.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the approach on additional simulator families and real experiments, with explicit evaluation of operational constraints such as restricted design ranges, costs, and run-order randomization. It would also be useful to compare alternative design criteria and assess whether sequential refinement remains effective when observations arrive over multiple practical experimental rounds.

narrate.summary: This paper extends convergence results for Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) from sample means to Z-estimators, which estimate parameters by setting a sample mean of estimating functions to zero. It studies parameter estimation under regularity assumptions, including twice continuous differentiability and finite moments. The authors derive the estimators’ asymptotic covariance and a central limit theorem (CLT), and show theoretically that its covariance is no larger than for independent and identically distributed (IID) sampling in the positive-semidefinite sense. They illustrate the results with maximum-likelihood estimation in a Poisson generalized linear model (GLM). In that example, estimates from LHS generally have lower variance and mean squared error (MSE) than estimates from IID sampling.
narrate.key_results: In a Poisson regression example with nine covariates, the authors compared LHS and IID using 1,000 designs for each sampling method at sample sizes from 40 to 100 in increments of 10. Across the nine parameters, LHS had lower average estimation variance overall, the squared biases showed no significant differences, and the MSE was lower. For a further comparison, the paper reports asymptotic normalized variances of 0.6195, 0.3763, 0.3388, 0.3395, 0.3963, 1.4805, 0.3575, 0.3423, and 0.4328; empirical normalized variances from 1,000 LHS designs approached these values as sample size increased from 50 to 1,000 in increments of 50. Quantile plots for sample sizes 50, 250, and 1,000 showed heavy tails at 50 and closer agreement with normality as sample size increased.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a method that combines sequential Bayesian experimental design with online learning of model discrepancy. At each stage, it selects a measurement design to estimate parameters in a physics-based model, then uses the resulting data to update a neural-network correction. An ensemble-based indicator estimates whether the data are informative enough to justify updating that correction. Simulations of contaminant-source inference show that the approach can reduce parameter bias and improve model predictions while using far fewer forward evaluations than a full Bayesian analysis in the parametric-error comparison.
narrate.key_results: In the parametric-error example, the full Bayesian design evaluated a grid of 51 by 51 by 31 points, requiring 80,631 forward-model evaluations per stage; the hybrid method used a 51 by 51 grid and 2,601 evaluations per stage, while obtaining similar source-location and error-parameter results. For structural error, the neural-network correction improved field agreement: the good design achieved a mean squared error of 0.005 and relative error of 0.297, compared with 0.032 and 0.665 for a poor design and 0.142 and 1.553 for the uncorrected baseline. The ensemble indicator ranked the better correction data above the poorer data in the examples, and using the better data improved subsequent source-location estimates. In the ill-posed example, the method improved source-location inference even though the jointly optimized convection-rate parameter did not converge to its true value.

key_equations.name: Discrepancy update

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that neural-network corrections can compensate for or obscure physics-based terms, making parameters difficult to identify; the paper mitigates this in its main structural-error example through restrictions on what the network learns. Averaging multiple posterior modes can be harmful when the posterior is genuinely multimodal, and the numerical studies use only measurements at the selected design point for model correction. The authors also report less satisfactory performance when relying only on simulated data to estimate design information gain.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is primarily from controlled numerical examples, so the results do not establish performance with noisy measurements, operational constraints, or real engineering systems. The structural-error demonstration uses a small, pre-trained network and a tailored constraint; its performance may not carry over to more general discrepancy patterns or substantially larger models. The method also has to solve both the design problem and repeated network optimization, but the paper does not quantify total runtime or sensitivity to optimization settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using the ensemble-based information-gain approximation to select designs that are directly informative for discrepancy calibration and extending it to non-Gaussian prior and posterior distributions. They also discuss mode-specific networks for multimodal parameter posteriors, post-training decomposition of learned model terms, and further work on estimating design value from simulations alone.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the method in physical experiments and under practical limits such as sensor relocation, measurement cost, and safety constraints. It would also be useful to develop stopping rules and sequential validation procedures that test whether a correction improves predictions beyond the locations used for calibration.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Qualitative factors via Integer Programming (QuIP), a method for designing experiments when an expensive simulator has many categorical inputs. It uses a Gaussian process (GP) with an exchangeable covariance model and addresses both initial design and sequential selection for prediction or optimization. Initial runs are chosen to maximize the minimum Hamming distance between design points, and the resulting optimization is formulated as an assignment problem. For sequential work, the authors reformulate active-learning and upper-confidence-bound criteria as assignment problems that can be solved with an integer-programming solver. In path-planning simulations and a rover trajectory application, QuIP generally performed better than the compared design methods under limited evaluation budgets.
narrate.key_results: For initial designs with 50 runs, 10 to 30 levels, and factor counts from 5 to 25 above the number of levels, QuIP generally produced better maximin designs than differential evolution after a warm-up period of at most 15 seconds; with 30 levels it reached the stated upper bound in every tested case. In the maze experiment, QuIP improved prediction error over random and candidate-set sampling, and found lower-cost paths than random sampling, candidate-set sampling, and the latent-variable GP approach. In the greedy-snake experiment, QuIP found paths with greater reward than the compared methods; for the 10th sequential point, the solver's estimated optimum was close to the oracle optimum, and the stopping rule required the objective gap to be within 10% of the estimate. In rover optimization, all methods began with 30 runs and added 200 sequential points, and QuIP achieved lower current-best path costs than the random, candidate-set, and latent-variable GP comparisons.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The method depends on the exchangeable covariance structure and maximum-likelihood estimation of its parameters, so performance may be weaker when factor effects or interactions do not fit that structure. narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test the method under model misspecification and compare its predictive and optimization performance on real simulator studies with engineering constraints. narrate.summary: The paper designs experiments for estimating direct and spillover treatment effects when outcomes can depend on treatments received by other units and on prior treatments. Its method is for multi-unit experiments over time: at selected decision times, the design chooses between two population treatment probabilities, then independently assigns units to treatment or control and holds assignments fixed until the next decision time. It chooses decision times to minimize the worst-case weighted mean squared risk over bounded potential outcomes. The authors also study Horvitz–Thompson estimators, provide conservative variance estimates, and examine what happens when the carryover order is specified incorrectly. Their theory and numerical studies indicate that the proposed schedules can reduce risk relative to common schedules, while supporting asymptotic inference under the stated assumptions.
narrate.key_results: The authors provide a polynomial-time algorithm with time complexity O(T²) for finding the minimax design. In simulations, the selected minimax designs reduced the combined risk by an average of 19.7% compared with the design that randomizes every time period, and by 3.7% compared with the design using intervals of length p plus one. In simulations with correctly specified or over-specified carryover order, reported coverage probabilities for nominal 95% confidence intervals were generally close to 95%; single-center experiments with short observation periods had poorer coverage. In an analysis using synthetic outcomes fitted to trading data from 10 markets in 2016, the preferred schedule had combined risk 0.368, compared with 1.106 for randomizing every time period and 0.388 for the interval-length comparison design.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that specifying an order p below the true carryover order m introduces non-negligible asymptotic bias, while choosing p larger than m can increase risk by reducing the effective sample size. Their theoretical results rely on assumptions including bounded outcomes, stratified interference through population treatment probabilities, and growth conditions; they also note that short single-center studies can have poor confidence-interval coverage.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The exposure model represents interference through a common population treated probability, so it may not capture network-specific exposure, heterogeneous peer effects, or effects driven by the realized treated proportion. The assignment scheme also assumes common treatment probabilities and independent unit-level assignments, which may not fit operational constraints such as fixed treatment counts or restricted schedules. Numerical comparisons focus on a small set of alternative schedules, and the trading-data application evaluates synthetic outcomes rather than a new randomized field experiment.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring optimal designs through deterministic or stochastic optimization, incorporating time-varying covariates to improve efficiency, and relaxing assumptions related to stratified interference.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to adapt the optimization to practical restrictions such as fixed treatment counts, limited switching, unequal assignment probabilities, or network-based exposures, and assess how those constraints affect risk. The method could also be implemented in publicly available software and validated prospectively in real multi-unit experiments, with sequential procedures for updating the design as outcomes accrue.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a multi-fidelity estimator for expected information gain, the objective used in Bayesian optimal experimental design to choose experiments that are expected to reduce uncertainty about model parameters. The method applies an approximate control variate framework, combining a high-fidelity utility estimate with estimates from cheaper models to reduce variance under a fixed computational budget. It first rewrites the information-gain expectation in terms of model parameters and data noise, so sampling the expectation does not require running each data model. The authors demonstrate the approach on a nonlinear benchmark and on simulated turbulent flow, where a pressure-probe location is selected to learn turbulence-model parameters. The estimates preserve the high-fidelity utility mean, and the examples show substantial variance reductions compared with a single-fidelity nested Monte Carlo estimator.
narrate.key_results: In the nonlinear benchmark, multi-fidelity estimates with inner-loop sample reuse reduced empirical variance by about 17 to 23 times relative to the single-fidelity nested Monte Carlo estimator; optimizing low-fidelity inner-loop sample sizes gave a more modest additional improvement. In the simulated flow study, under the same computational budget, the empirical variance reduction averaged across 875 candidate designs was 61.48 times for the fixed inner-sample setting and 70.19 times for the optimized setting. At the selected best design, the corresponding reductions were 94.24 times and 233.12 times. The authors report that estimated means align with the high-fidelity utility mean; this does not remove the finite inner-sample bias in the underlying nested Monte Carlo utility calculation.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method requires cheaper lower-fidelity models that are sufficiently correlated with the high-fidelity model, and the models must share the same parameterization and random inputs. The paper also notes that finite inner-loop sampling leaves bias relative to the exact information gain, and that using one design-averaged covariance matrix can make the estimator suboptimal at particular designs.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical validation covers only a one-dimensional benchmark and one simulated flow-calibration application, so it does not establish performance across other experimental domains or against a broad range of information-gain estimators. The flow example also depends on a particular set of nested numerical grids and pressure-probe candidate locations, which may not represent practical constraints such as probe access, measurement costs, or physical experiment variability.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying low-fidelity utility models created by changing inner-loop sample sizes and extending the method to models that share only some parameters. They also propose embedding the estimator in the overall design optimization, adapting estimator structure across the design space, and improving pilot sampling and the sharing or prediction of correlation information across designs.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the estimator with physical experiments and quantify how measurement errors or model misspecification affect the chosen design. It would also be useful to incorporate practical constraints on probe placement and experiment execution, and to test sequential design strategies that update the information-gain estimate as data arrive.

narrate.summary: The paper presents raxpy, a Python package for designing, evaluating, and running space-filling experiments on computer models with optional and hierarchical inputs. It uses Python type annotations and code introspection to derive a model's input space, then generates experiment points under a user-specified run budget. The authors introduce design measures for optional and hierarchical dimensions and propose several design-generation methods, including methods that construct designs separately within feasible full-subspaces. They compare these methods with random designs and with versions improved by maximum-projection optimization. In their numerical study, the full-subspace Latin hypercube method with value pools and maximum-projection post-optimization performs especially well on minimum interpoint distance, while the strongest method depends on the metric being considered.
narrate.key_results: The study compares 12 algorithms across four input spaces and three design sizes, using 30 replications per setting; the paper reports 360 designs evaluated. Lower average rank is better: the full-subspace Latin hypercube method with value pools and maximum-projection post-optimization ranks 1.0 for minimum interpoint distance, 2.5 for average single-dimension projection distance, 2.5 for star discrepancy, and 4.25 for weighted discrepancy. For weighted discrepancy, the full-subspace Latin hypercube method without value pools or post-optimization ranks best at 1.58, and the version with value pools ranks 2.67. The authors report that maximum-projection post-optimization generally improves minimum interpoint distance and star discrepancy, but can worsen weighted discrepancy; random, tree-traversal, and whole-projection methods also often miss target point allocations among full-subspaces.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not give a separate limitations statement. They identify space-filling optimization for union parameters and support for list parameters as unexplored, and note that sequential design for optional and hierarchical inputs remains future work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons use constructed input spaces rather than real computer models or industrial experiments, so the paper does not establish how the designs affect practical model learning or prediction. The comparisons focus on a selected set of space-filling measures and a Latin hypercube implementation based on centered-discrepancy optimization; the paper does not report computational cost or how performance scales for larger spaces.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying space-filling optimization for union parameters, exploring list parameters, and developing sequential exploratory experiments for optional and hierarchical inputs. They also plan to refine raxpy with the open-source community and suggest that its annotations could support optimization experiments.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could test the package on real simulation and engineering studies, measuring whether its designs improve surrogate prediction or engineering decisions as well as geometric space filling. Further work could examine practical constraints such as unequal run costs, infeasible combinations, and user-defined allocation targets, and assess run time as the number and depth of input dimensions grow.

narrate.summary: This software paper introduces MOODE, an R package for finding designs for quantitative-factor experiments. The package targets response-surface experiments where researchers want to estimate a chosen polynomial model, detect lack of fit, and reduce estimation bias if additional polynomial effects are present. It combines estimation, lack-of-fit, and robustness criteria using user-selected weights, and searches for designs with point-exchange or coordinate-exchange algorithms. Its examples show that compound criteria can produce compromises among competing objectives. In the reported comparisons, compound designs often retain useful estimation and lack-of-fit performance while providing replicated runs for estimating experimental error.
narrate.key_results: For a three-factor experiment with 36 runs, the compound design using weights 0.4 for inference, 0.2 for lack-of-fit detection, and 0.4 for robustness had reported efficiencies of 94.20%, 89.30%, and 99.50% for those objectives, respectively; it had 17 pure-error degrees of freedom and 9 lack-of-fit degrees of freedom. The three designs optimized for just one objective each performed poorly on at least one of the other objectives. In comparisons of 12-run designs for 3 to 9 two-level factors, compound designs achieved at least 50% efficiency for inference and typically did better, while retaining four pure-error degrees of freedom when possible. For four factors and 12 runs, the compound design used 8 distinct treatments, compared with 5 for the inference-optimal design and 12 for the mean-squared-error-optimal design.

key_equations.name: Weighted compound design criterion

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the exchange algorithms are heuristics and are not guaranteed to reach an optimum, so they recommend multiple starts and often substantially more than the default number. They also note that candidate-list construction and design-region choice are not covered in detail, and that some example designs might improve with more random starts.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons cover two case studies and selected polynomial models, weights, factor levels, and run sizes; they do not establish how the package performs across a broad range of real experiments. The examples do not assess sensitivity to misspecified prior assumptions for potential effects, practical restrictions on treatment combinations, or operating time as problem size grows.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors plan to add blocking factors. They also identify alternative optimization algorithms, including nature-inspired heuristics, and hybrid nonlinear model classes as possible extensions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the criteria under alternative error and prior assumptions and with practical constraints on feasible treatments and randomization. Evaluation on real experimental data, alongside studies of runtime and sequential design updates, would help establish the package’s practical scope.

narrate.summary: The paper develops collaborative designs for multiple controlled experiments that share the same subjects and have subject covariates. Its objective is to improve the precision of each experiment’s treatment-effect estimates by modeling the shared subject-specific random effect and maximizing a D-optimality criterion. The authors propose a randomized greedy method that solves a sequence of semi-definite programs and a faster method that solves one semi-definite program and uses random orthogonal vectors to create allocations. The design seeks to balance covariates within experiments while making allocations orthogonal across experiments. Simulations show that the proposed methods outperform covariate-agnostic allocation methods when the number of covariates is large.
narrate.key_results: The simulation used 96 subjects, 4 or 8 experiments, and either 10 or 70 covariates; the subject-specific random-effect standard deviation was 0.25 or 2, and each experimental-error variance was 1. Each randomized method was replicated 100 times per covariate matrix, and optimization times were capped at 50 seconds. With 70 covariates, the proposed methods generally had higher D-efficiency and lower treatment-effect variances than fully random allocation and Plackett-Burman designs. The greedy method using deterministic binary programming performed best in the comparisons and nearly reached the Hadamard-based D-efficiency upper bound with 10 covariates, but it does not randomize assignments. With few covariates, covariate-agnostic methods could outperform the single-design randomized method.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could assess robustness when the random-effect model or variance assumptions are inaccurate, and evaluate designs under operational constraints such as limited treatment capacity or restricted assignments. The methods could also be validated in real experiments and packaged in accessible software that compares randomized and deterministic allocation options.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a way to construct augmented row-column designs for unreplicated trials, particularly trials in plant breeding where each test line has only one plot. It considers a square field with controls appearing once in every row and column, and constructs the control positions by converting an equireplicate incomplete-block design into a square array. The authors evaluate designs by the average variances of test-line and control-to-test-line comparisons, under a fixed-effects model with independent normal errors. They show that the construction works for cyclic and non-cyclic auxiliary designs, and that minimizing the auxiliary design’s average variance also minimizes the two principal comparison metrics. Their examples identify practical designs with control proportions in a range they recommend, and show that some non-cyclic designs can improve on cyclic alternatives.

The paper examines 147 cyclic designs with array sizes from 10 to 30 and control counts from 3 to 9, reporting that for a fixed array size the test-line comparison variance decreases as more controls are used. narrate.summary: This paper develops a method for optimal experimental design when measurement choices vary continuously and the model is nonlinear. Its goal is to select measurement times or locations that improve estimation of unknown model parameters. The method represents the design as a probability distribution and evolves sampled design points using a particle approximation to Wasserstein gradient flow. It couples this design update with parameter estimation, either by repeatedly solving the estimation problem or by using an implicit-function-based update. Simulations with the Lorenz 63 system and a steady-state Schrödinger model show that the method finds informative designs and improves parameter reconstruction in the tested settings.
narrate.key_results: For the Lorenz 63 model, the D-optimal design recovered 9 of the 14 benchmark-important observation points, while the A-optimal design recovered 7 of 10. In a Lorenz reconstruction comparison using 63 measurements for each strategy, strategic sampling converged faster and reached better final parameter-error and loss values than uniform sampling. The authors estimate a cost of O(dNT′) per outer iteration for the accurate-inner-loop method and O(d³ + d²N) for the streamlined method; these are complexity estimates, not measured run times. In the Schrödinger simulations, the designs concentrated measurements near the source-detector diagonal; A-optimal sampling also favored locations where the true potential was larger, while D-optimal sampling showed no similarly favored locations along the diagonal. The reported particle counts include 10,000 for uniform-start Schrödinger tests and 1,000 for warm-start tests.

key_equations.name: Information matrix

narrate.summary: This paper reviews exact optimal designs for spherical harmonic regression on the unit sphere in three dimensions. The model represents a response measured in a direction as a sum of real spherical harmonics up to a chosen order, with the goal of estimating its regression parameters precisely. The paper shows theoretically that equally weighted spherical t-designs with strength at least twice the model order attain the same optimality as the uniform distribution over the sphere for the criteria considered. It surveys available designs and their construction, and uses stereographic diagrams to illustrate their symmetry. Its examples focus on model orders from 1 through 7 and compare design sizes with previously published exact designs.
narrate.key_results: The paper establishes that spherical t-designs with strength t at least 2d give optimal exact designs for the stated parameter-estimation criteria. For model orders 1 through 7, the smallest listed Hardin and Sloane designs have 4, 12, 24, 36, 60, 84, and 108 points, respectively; the corresponding designs from Dette and colleagues have 6, 20, 42, 81, 143, 221, and 345 points. The paper therefore recommends the Hardin and Sloane designs over those compared designs for their lower run counts and, where possible, manageable numbers of polar angles. For orders above 7, it reports that available designs are limited in variety, but their minimum point counts are close to twice the number of model parameters.

key_equations.explanation: The integral of polynomial f over the unit sphere S² under uniform measure σ equals its average over the finite point set Y, for every spherical polynomial f of degree at most t.

key_equations.explanation: For the uniform design ξ*, the information matrix M is the identity matrix I of size equal to the number of regression parameters, (d+1) squared.

narrate.limitations_stated: The paper notes that numerical construction of spherical t-designs can be difficult because optimization on the sphere has many local minima with different characteristics. For model orders above 7, it says only a small number of sources and designs are available for a given strength.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The examples compare design sizes using published catalogues rather than evaluating estimation precision or prediction on simulated or real responses. The recommendation also assumes the spherical harmonic model and spherical measurement domain are appropriate, and does not assess practical constraints that could prevent runs at the specified directions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The paper suggests that available designs for hyperspherical regression in four dimensions could be assessed in the same way as the three-dimensional designs, including whether their minimum run counts are adequate. narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate these designs under realistic restrictions on allowable measurement directions, replication, and run costs, and to compare their resulting parameter uncertainty with alternative feasible designs. The paper could also motivate software that makes the catalogued points, design selection, and stereographic visualizations easier for practitioners to use.
