narrate.summary: The paper presents a practical method and open-source software for choosing seismometer locations to improve estimates of earthquake locations at volcanoes. It uses Bayesian experimental design to maximize expected information gain about source location, with travel-time, amplitude, and seismic-array measurements considered together. The design is built from a prior distribution of likely source locations, a forward model and data likelihood, and a genetic algorithm that searches locations allowed by terrain and other constraints. The authors demonstrate the workflow using simulated events at Etna and also examine layered and three-dimensional velocity models. They find that optimized layouts can reduce expected location uncertainty compared with random layouts, and that the software can produce an initial design quickly.
narrate.key_results: For the Etna example with three nodal stations and one array, the reported design has an expected information gain of 5.7 nats and an approximate posterior standard deviation of 545 meters. With a population of 64 candidate designs, the genetic algorithm needed about 200 generations to converge, with only slight improvements through about 600 generations; the authors report that this example can be computed in minutes using the DN method, compared with tens of minutes for the nested Monte Carlo method using the same number of samples. Across designs with up to 10 receivers, optimized layouts had the lowest expected uncertainty; Sobol space-filling layouts performed better than uniformly random layouts and approached the optimized results, while optimized designs could match the mean Sobol uncertainty using one fewer receiver when more than two receivers were used. In the velocity-model comparison, the homogeneous, layered, and heterogeneous designs scored 5.08, 5.10, and 5.26 nats, respectively, with approximate standard deviations of 667, 662, and 628 meters when evaluated using the heterogeneous model.

key_equations.name: Expected information gain (EIG) criterion
key_equations.explanation: EIG is expected information gain; ξ is the design; E is the expectation over the prior distribution p(m); m is the source-location model; I is Shannon information; d is the data; and p is a probability distribution.

key_equations.name: Optimal design selection
key_equations.explanation: ξ* is the selected optimal design; arg max means the choice that maximizes the quantity; ξ is a candidate design; Ξ is the set of possible designs; and EIG is expected information gain.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify simplifying assumptions: a homogeneous velocity model in the basic workflow, Gaussian data likelihoods, and independent errors across data. They note that these assumptions can affect design quality and can be relaxed with additional scenario-specific information, but that more complex velocity models increase computation. The paper does not model full waveforms or optimize the full source solution including moment tensor, and the authors say an efficient extension to the latter remains unclear.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main worked comparison uses simulated events and one volcano, Etna, so the reported gains do not establish performance in real deployments or across diverse volcanoes. The layouts also depend on the specified prior, velocity and noise assumptions, and encoded placement constraints; the paper does not quantify how errors in those inputs or field logistics would change the selected locations.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify extending the methods and software to optimize networks for the full source solution, including moment tensor, as a possible direction, while noting that an efficient implementation is not yet clear. They also describe the methods as adaptable to more complex constraints and data types when scenario-specific information is available.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation against actual seismic deployments and observed event locations across several volcanoes, including tests of how misspecified priors and noise assumptions affect performance. The method could also be developed for sequential redesign as monitoring data update the source-location prior, and for explicit field-cost or access constraints tested with practitioners.

narrate.summary: The paper describes fdesigns, an R package for finding Bayesian optimal experimental designs when controllable factors vary over time within a run. It covers functional linear models and functional generalized linear models, including binomial responses with a logit link and Poisson responses with a log link. The method restricts otherwise infinite-dimensional functions using basis expansions, principally B-splines, and optimizes the resulting basis coefficients with coordinate exchange. For linear models it offers Bayesian A- and D-optimality, with roughness penalties available to encourage smooth parameter functions. For generalized models it uses prior information and either quadrature or Monte Carlo approximation to form pseudo-Bayesian criteria. The examples demonstrate varied designs for profile and scalar factors, but are demonstrations rather than comparisons against competing methods.
narrate.key_results: The package implements the coordinate exchange algorithm, supports repeated searches from multiple starting designs, and uses C++ components for computational work. In the four-run functional linear example, the Bayesian D-optimal design had an objective value of 0.4051947 and required 4 iterations. The 12-run linear example with two profile factors and an interaction reported an A-optimal objective value of 13.33739, 12 iterations, and 10 seconds; the bioreactor example produced four distinct feed-volume profiles in a 12-run design. The 12-run logistic example reported a pseudo-Bayesian D-optimal objective value of 847.976, 31 iterations, and 1 second, while the 12-run Poisson example reported a pseudo-Bayesian A-optimal objective value of 2.212573, 4 iterations, and 34 seconds. These objective values come from different models and criteria and are not presented as directly comparable performance measures.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say the examples are intentionally relatively simple because complex models with multiple profile factors can require greater computational resources. They also note that the current generalized-model implementation supports only the binomial family with a logit link and the Poisson family with a log link.
narrate.limitations_unstated: Coordinate exchange is a local search, so repeated starting designs can improve the chance of a good solution but do not establish that the global optimum has been found. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors plan to extend the package to more model types and additional design criteria, including criteria tailored to profile factors, to broaden its applicability.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Useful next steps would include methods for enforcing practical trajectory constraints and evaluating robustness to model misspecification and prior choices. The package could also be assessed through comparisons with alternative search methods and validation in real experiments, and extended to update designs sequentially as observations arrive.

narrate.summary: This tutorial presents a framework for planning experiments with generative agent-based modeling (GABM) using Concordia. It is intended for researchers, particularly in the social sciences, who want to simulate complex interactions without having to build a full simulation framework themselves. The authors organize the process into conceptualization, tool selection, agent and environment design, and execution and simulation. They illustrate these steps with a fictional social media scenario involving five agents and the spread of information. The paper offers practical guidance and validation suggestions, rather than a quantitative comparison of experimental designs.
narrate.key_results: The paper provides a four-stage workflow for building and running Concordia simulations, including guidance on defining research questions, selecting a language model, specifying agents and environments, and recording simulation interactions. Its demonstration uses five agents on the fictional ConnectNet platform, with agent attributes, goals, and memories used to shape their behavior. The paper reports example interactions but gives no numerical performance, estimation, or prediction results and does not compare design efficiency or run sizes against alternative designs.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The demonstration is limited to five agents in a fictional social media environment, so it does not establish that the approach works similarly in larger or real-world settings. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose an interactive web platform where users can create and customize agents, adjust their behaviors, and visualize agent information. They also suggest simulations comparing agents with similar or contrasting personalities or political ideologies.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could compare language models and simulation settings using the same benchmark scenarios, and validate simulated behavior against observations from human experiments. It could also develop repeatable procedures for setting run counts, tracking uncertainty across runs, and reporting model and configuration details.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces an information-matching method for optimal experimental design and active learning. It is intended for models where the goal is precise downstream predictions, even when many model parameters are poorly identifiable. The method compares the information supplied by candidate training data with the information required to meet a specified prediction uncertainty, then uses a convex optimization problem to select and weight data. The authors demonstrate the method in simulated power-system sensor placement, underwater source localization, and interatomic-potential development. Their examples show that small selected data sets can meet the specified prediction-precision targets.
narrate.key_results: For the IEEE 14-bus power-system example, the method selected buses 2, 6, and 9 for full observability, consistent with prior studies; for the IEEE 39-bus example, its full-network placements were also reported as broadly consistent with earlier findings. In the main underwater-acoustics case, selected receivers were 5% of candidate locations, and across the tested sediment and frequency scenarios no more than 8% were needed to meet the source-location targets of plus or minus 2.5 meters vertically and plus or minus 100 meters horizontally. For the molybdenum disulfide potential, 7 of 2,000 candidate configurations met a target uncertainty set at 10% of predictions from the full-data-trained potential. For silicon, designs used at most 5 of 400 candidate configurations; the reported uncertainties for lattice constant, cohesive energy, and three elastic constants were each below their stated target uncertainties. The paper does not provide a quantitative head-to-head performance comparison with conventional parameter-focused design criteria; it contrasts their objectives conceptually.

key_equations.name: Information required for target prediction precision
key_equations.explanation: The required information matrix J is formed from the prediction Jacobian J_g, its transpose, and the inverse of the target covariance matrix Σ.

key_equations.name: Information-matching design criterion
key_equations.explanation: The method minimizes the sum of absolute design weights w, requires every candidate weight w_m to be nonnegative, and requires the weighted information from M candidate data to be at least the required information matrix J in the positive-semidefinite ordering.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the optimization can be infeasible if the candidate set lacks data informative about parameters relevant to the predictions. The information matrix is local and can vary with parameter values; initial parameter choices can also change selected data, weights, and estimates, although the target uncertainty is met when the problem is feasible.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The prediction guarantee relies on local information matrices and a linearized uncertainty argument, so it may not hold accurately for strongly nonlinear behavior or substantial model misspecification. The demonstrations use a limited set of simulated scientific examples and do not establish real-world acquisition costs or compare performance quantitatively against competing design algorithms.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to larger models and machine-learning applications, including machine-learned interatomic potentials. They also propose deeper theoretical analysis of the optimization's limiting behavior to better understand robustness and broaden applicability.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the selected designs in physical experiments and compare their prediction accuracy, total acquisition cost, and robustness with established design methods. Further work could incorporate practical constraints such as limited sensor locations, variable measurement costs, and sequential decisions after new observations arrive.

narrate.summary: The paper presents CDsampling, an R package for choosing constrained samples in paid research studies and clinical trials. It finds allocations for generalized linear models (GLMs), including linear and logistic regression, and multinomial logistic models (MLMs), with the goal of improving parameter estimation by maximizing the determinant of the information matrix. Its construction uses a lift-one algorithm that optimizes allocation proportions one at a time within user-specified constraints, then converts the proportions to integer sample counts. The package also provides expected weighted designs that use parameter priors and uniform allocations for settings with limited model information. In the paper’s simulation example, the D-optimal approaches had lower estimation errors than simple random and constrained uniform sampling, though the full-data estimates had the lowest errors.
narrate.key_results: For the simulated trial example, 200 people were sampled from 500 available volunteers across six gender-and-age groups. The local D-optimal exact allocation was 50, 40, 10, 100, 0, and 0; the expected weighted allocation was 48, 40, 10, 43, 19, and 40. Across 100 simulation runs, both D-optimal methods had slightly higher root mean square errors (RMSEs) than using all 500 people, but lower errors than simple random sampling without replacement (SRSWOR) and constrained uniform sampling; constrained uniform sampling also performed better than SRSWOR. In the trauma-data example, the package allocated a sample of 600 from 802 patients across eight treatment-and-severity groups, with counts of 155, 0, 0, 100, 168, 0, 0, and 177. The paper reports no numerical RMSE values or broad benchmark timings, so the comparison is qualitative rather than a quantified efficiency ranking.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how to estimate the global average treatment effect (GATE) in A/B testing when one unit’s outcome can depend on other units’ treatment through a network. Rather than proposing a new treatment assignment rule, it uses data from existing ramp-up experiments that tested different treatment proportions. The method stacks those stages’ data to train a regression model, then predicts average outcomes under global treatment and global control. The authors derive bias and variance results for ordinary least squares under a general linear interference model and also evaluate graph neural network estimators in simulations. Their main finding is that variation in treatment proportions can reduce bias and improve estimation, while repeating experiments at one fixed proportion mainly reduces variability rather than bias.
narrate.key_results: Under the paper’s regular-interference assumptions, the one-stage linear regression estimator has bias of constant order and variance of order one over the number of units, so bias is the dominant error as the network grows. In the two-hop simulation, merging four stages reduced the graph neural network estimator’s MSE from 1.963 to 0.025 under unit-level randomization and from 0.904 to 0.008 under cluster-level randomization, compared with the single-stage baseline. Merging five stages gave MSE values of 0.026 and 0.010, respectively, so adding a stage did not always improve on four stages. Repeating the 50 percent treatment stage did not reduce bias: under unit-level randomization, MSE rose from 1.968 for one round to 2.214 for five rounds, despite lower standard deviation.

key_equations.explanation: Here Y(z) is the vector of potential outcomes under treatment vector z, beta zero and beta one are baseline and direct-effect coefficients, 1 is the all-ones vector, B is the interference matrix, and epsilon is random noise.

key_equations.name: Global average treatment effect
key_equations.explanation: Here tau is the GATE, beta one is the direct-effect coefficient, n is the number of units, 1 is the all-ones vector, and B is the interference matrix; the superscript T denotes transpose.

key_equations.explanation: Here tau-hat is the estimated GATE, f is the fitted prediction function, n is the number of units, 1 and 0 are the all-treated and all-control vectors, and A is the network adjacency matrix.

key_equations.name: Leading bias for merged stages
key_equations.explanation: This is the leading bias expression for the merged-stage linear regression estimator: tau-hat is the estimate, T is the number of stages, c sub t is the treatment proportion in stage t, B sub ij is an element of the interference matrix, n is the number of units, and O(1/n) is the smaller-order remainder.

narrate.limitations_stated: The theoretical results concern static GATE and assume potential-outcome parameters remain fixed across stages; they exclude cross-round spillovers. The authors note that a traffic cap can leave substantial bias, and their results for nonlinear interference and changing graphs are simulation evidence rather than general theoretical guarantees.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulations use a small number of network datasets and specified synthetic outcome models, so the reported improvements may not transfer to other networks, outcome processes, or real platform data. The evidence for the more flexible estimator also comes from one lightweight graph neural network setup and 100 Monte Carlo repetitions; performance with other model choices and operational constraints is not established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify extending the analysis to carryover effects and adaptive rollout decisions as important future work. They also recommend that stage selection account for exposure diversity as well as sample size, subject to operational risk and traffic constraints.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the approach using real platform outcomes and additional networks, while testing sensitivity to heterogeneous treatment effects, misspecified network structure, and other prediction models. Further work could develop practical stage-selection procedures that incorporate traffic, clustering, and business constraints, then validate them in sequential experiments.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a deterministic rounding method for experimental design using interlacing polynomials. It addresses D-design, A-design, and E-design, where the goal is to select a fixed-size multiset of vectors that optimizes a matrix-based measure of information. The method first solves a convex relaxation, then uses a polynomial family built from repeated random sampling to choose vectors one at a time. For E-design, the authors derive a new guarantee that also applies when the selection budget is close to the vector dimension. The framework also recovers established guarantees for D-design and A-design and extends to a generalized ratio objective.
narrate.key_results: For E-design, the deterministic algorithm has approximation factor equal to one divided by the square of one minus the square root of the dimension-minus-one divided by the budget. It is a near-one approximation when the budget is sufficiently large relative to the dimension and the inverse square of the desired accuracy; when the budget equals the dimension, its factor is the dimension squared, and when the budget is twice the dimension, the factor is constant. For D-design, the factor is the budget times the d-th root of the ratio of the budget-minus-dimension factorial to the budget factorial; this is at most the budget divided by the budget-minus-dimension-plus-one, and at budget equal to dimension it is at most e. For A-design, the factor is the budget divided by the budget-minus-dimension-plus-one. For all three objectives, the rounding stage takes order k times m times d raised to the matrix-multiplication exponent plus one; the generalized ratio objective also receives a stated approximation guarantee and the same rounding runtime.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not know how to extend the interlacing-polynomial method to selection without repetitions, because they do not yet know how to define suitable probability distributions and expected polynomials. They also identify an open gap for E-design when the budget equals the dimension: their factor is the dimension squared, while the known integrality gap of the relaxation is only the dimension.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The guarantees depend on the stated matrix objectives and on the fractional convex relaxation; the paper does not evaluate how sensitive the method is to departures from those assumptions in real experiments. The reported runtime covers the rounding stage, while the paper does not quantify the practical cost of solving the convex relaxation or demonstrate performance on a real data set.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying whether the method can be adapted to selection without repetitions. They also identify closing the gap between the dimension-squared E-design guarantee and the dimension-sized relaxation integrality gap at budget equal to dimension as an open question.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate implementations on real experimental-design problems and report end-to-end runtime, including the convex optimization step. Further work could also test the method under practical constraints on which candidates may be selected and examine whether related guarantees hold for other design objectives.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a method for designing excitation signals to support identification of nonlinear dynamic processes. It uses an iterative approach inspired by receding horizon control, optimizing a finite segment of the signal at each time step. The design aims to cover the model's input space by reducing weighted nearest-neighbor distances to reference points. Increasing the weights for a selected region concentrates more generated points there; the figure illustrates weight values of 1, 5, and 20. The plotted excitation signals contain 300 data points. Results are qualitative: the paper reports no numerical efficiency, prediction-accuracy, or estimation-accuracy measures and does not compare the method quantitatively with other design methods.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a randomized method for choosing a smaller set of experiments while retaining the local parameter sensitivity of the full dataset. It targets parameter estimation in inverse problems, with the Fisher information matrix used to measure sensitivity. The method uses matrix sketching to derive a sensitivity-informed probability distribution over pairs of experimental designs, then uses ensemble sampling and early stopping to select designs. The authors test it on simulated potential reconstruction for the Schrödinger equation, using measurement locations and, in one experiment, source settings as design choices. In those tests, small selected designs can have better measured information-matrix conditioning than the full-data design.
narrate.key_results: In the fixed-source experiment, the full design used 841 sensor locations and had a minimum eigenvalue of 0.8 and an inverse condition number of 8.18 × 10^-4. With 18 locations, early-stopped Ensemble Kalman Sampler selection raised these measures to 1.77 and 1.91 × 10^-3, while Consensus-Based Sampler selection yielded 1.17 and 1.24 × 10^-3. Starting from a poorly placed design, the corresponding results were 2.06 and 2.25 × 10^-3 for the Ensemble Kalman Sampler, and 1.41 and 1.56 × 10^-3 for the Consensus-Based Sampler. In the experiment where source settings were also design choices, the inverse condition number improved from 2.25 × 10^-4 for the uniform initial design to 1.83 × 10^-3 and 1.68 × 10^-3 for the two samplers; from a concentrated normal initial design, it improved from 3.02 × 10^-9 to 1.68 × 10^-3 and 8.75 × 10^-4, respectively.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that ensemble sampling methods lack non-asymptotic convergence guarantees, especially for non-Gaussian target distributions. The sensitivity-based sampling distribution depends on the local parameter value and quantities that may be unknown, and useful design selection therefore requires a linearization near the true parameter or dynamic estimation of the target distribution.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation is limited to simulated Schrödinger potential reconstruction, so the reported conditioning improvements do not establish improved parameter estimates or reduced costs in real experiments. The method may also require calculating sensitivities across many candidate designs, and the paper does not quantify whether that computation offsets the savings from collecting and processing fewer observations.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying how this qualitative design approach relates to Bayesian optimal design. They also identify sequential design that alternates design selection and parameter inference, and applications to least-squares inversion using Gaussian processes or neural networks, as directions for further work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare the method against established optimal-design procedures using both estimation accuracy and total computational and experimental cost, including settings with practical placement, budget, or run-order constraints. Testing sequential updates on real experiments and providing publicly accessible implementation software would also help establish its practical reliability.

narrate.summary: Backfill and Adaptive Randomization for Dose Optimization (BARD) is a two-stage clinical trial design for selecting an optimal dose by balancing efficacy and toxicity. In stage 1, a dose-escalation design identifies safe doses, and additional patients may be treated at eligible doses through backfilling. In stage 2, patients are assigned to selected doses using covariate-adaptive randomization, which accounts for the stage 1 patients and aims to balance prognostic factors across dose groups. The combined data from both stages are used to select the optimal dose by an efficacy comparison or a utility-based approach, subject to safety and efficacy requirements. Simulations found that BARD reduced sample size and trial duration while generally improving dose-selection accuracy and covariate balance compared with designs that used simple randomization and did not combine stage 1 data.
narrate.key_results: Across 8 simulated scenarios, the BARD design using Bayesian optimal interval escalation reduced average total sample size by 10 to 15 patients and trial duration by 6 to 8 months compared with its simple-randomization counterpart. Its average correct-selection rate was higher by 1.74 percentage points for the efficacy-based approach and 1.45 percentage points for the utility-based approach. The version using Bayesian logistic regression reduced sample size by 12 to 15 patients and duration by 6 to 8 months compared with its simple-randomization counterpart, and it generally improved correct selection and covariate balance. For the interval-escalation version, the imbalance in the two covariates used for adaptive randomization was often about one-third of that under simple randomization, and was close to the benchmark using Pocock-Simon randomization. The simulations included 30,000 trials per evaluation, with 5 dose levels, a maximum of 30 stage 1 escalation patients, and a target of 40 total patients across the two stage 2 dose groups.

key_equations.explanation: Here, p_hat_low and p_hat_high are the estimated efficacy rates at the lower and higher selected doses, and delta is the prespecified noninferiority or indifference margin.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their simulations did not include interim toxicity or futility monitoring, which could further reduce sample size. They also focus on single-agent dose-finding trials and identify extension of BARD to combination trials as future research. They note that backfilling may be inefficient when efficacy outcomes take too long to observe.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is based on simulated scenarios rather than results from real trials, and the main comparison uses particular escalation methods, dose configurations, enrollment assumptions, and outcome-generation settings. The evaluated stage 2 examples randomize between two doses and balance selected categorical prognostic factors, so performance with more dose arms, more complex covariates, or other practical constraints is not established here.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify extending BARD to combination trials, where the optimal biological dose is selected from a dose matrix, as future research. They also note that interim toxicity and futility monitoring could be incorporated to potentially reduce the sample size.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the design with real trial data or prospective applications, and examine whether its performance holds under different endpoint delays, enrollment patterns, and patient populations. It would also be useful to assess practical constraints such as dose availability and covariate imbalance when there are more than two randomized doses.

narrate.summary: This paper presents an active experimental design method for calibrating a robot arm’s kinematic parameters. It uses a Gaussian process (GP) to model position and orientation errors over end-effector poses, with a geometry-aware kernel for the combined rotation and position space. The method selects the next pose using an upper confidence bound (UCB) rule, then estimates corrections to Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) parameters from the collected measurements. The authors test the method in simulation and on a seven-degrees-of-freedom (DOF) arm in the Ocean Worlds Lander Autonomy Testbed (OWLAT) at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). They report better simulation performance and data efficiency than random sampling, and demonstrate successful calibration using 20 pose measurements on the testbed.
narrate.key_results: In simulation, the proposed method is reported to provide better calibration performance and data efficiency than random sampling; the comparison uses 20 iterations, but the paper does not report a numerical efficiency ratio or calibration-error value. In the OWLAT experiment, the method successfully overcame injected encoder biases using 20 pose measurements. The system ran on an Intel NUC with eight cores and less than 8 GB of memory.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose improving the smoothness of the objective function and considering learning methods for rotations to address its discontinuities.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further studies could evaluate repeated calibrations across different arms and naturally occurring parameter errors, while quantifying final pose accuracy and variability. Another useful direction is to incorporate measurement noise and practical constraints, such as collision avoidance and camera visibility, directly into the pose-selection rule and test whether the method can be used sequentially during field operation.

narrate.summary: The paper applies Response Surface Methodology (RSM) to optimize a simulated, single-family tropical social-housing model in San Pedro Sula, Honduras. Its objective is to reduce Indoor Overheating Hours (IOH) while increasing Useful Daylight Illuminance (UDI), combining the two goals in an overall desirability score. The authors first screen eight facade-specific window-to-wall ratio (WWR) and roof-overhang factors with a fractional factorial design, then use sequential first- and second-order response surface designs to optimize the selected factors. The final settings use a 3.78-meter roof overhang on the south and west, 3.76% west WWR, and 29.34% south WWR. The authors report that the method found a balanced solution using relatively few simulations and assessed uncertainty in the optimized settings with bootstrap resampling.
narrate.key_results: The 64-run fractional factorial screening design reduced the initial 256 full-factorial combinations to one quarter of that number and identified four influential factors, which the authors combined into three optimization factors. The sequential optimization used 74 additional design runs; together, screening and optimization required 138 design settings, corresponding to 276 thermal and daylight simulation runs completed in about 30 hours and 8 minutes. The final additional simulation reported an overall desirability of 0.6247, IOH of 8.33%, and UDI of 79.67%; the quadratic response model explained about 92% of the variation in desirability. The reported 95% bootstrap confidence intervals were 3.47–3.94 meters for the roof overhang, 1.54–5.59% for west WWR, and 26.19–31.78% for south WWR; the paper compares the run count with a full factorial design but does not report a direct controlled comparison against another optimization method.

They also suggest investigating additional measures, including roof improvements and east-facade solar protection.

narrate.summary: This tutorial explains how experimental designs for causal inference can be formulated as optimization problems. It focuses on estimating treatment effects and, in its discussion of optimal experimental design, on estimating model parameters. The author organizes design choices into robust, stochastic, and deterministic optimization, depending on what is known about potential outcomes. Examples include balanced treatment-control assignment, covariate-based stratification and matching, regression-based assignment, and synthetic controls. The paper’s main message is that the appropriate design framework depends on the experimenter’s knowledge of outcome uncertainty; under the stated assumptions, several familiar designs have optimality guarantees.
narrate.key_results: The tutorial reports that, under permutation-invariant uncertainty and an even sample size, a balanced completely randomized design assigning half the units to each group is minimax optimal when using the difference-in-means estimator. With bounded potential outcomes and independent Bernoulli assignments, assigning each unit to treatment with probability one half is minimax optimal for the inverse-probability-weighted estimator. For covariate-based stratification with an even sample size, equal treatment probabilities, and independent complete randomization within strata, pairing units after sorting their baseline outcomes from high to low is optimal. The paper also describes a pi-squared-approximation result for an algorithm that solves the regression-based treatment-effect variance design problem; the tutorial presents theoretical results rather than empirical comparisons or data-based efficiency rankings.

narrate.limitations_stated: The author explicitly limits the tutorial’s scope: it adopts the potential-outcomes approach and does not cover structural causal models, and it discusses optimal experimental design and optimal Bayesian design only where they overlap with causal experimental design. The paper also identifies its assumptions, including non-interference, homogeneous units in the classical setting, and random assignment, and surveys research directions arising when these assumptions fail.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The optimality results depend on restrictive conditions such as permutation-invariant uncertainty, bounded outcome ranges, even sample sizes, or a specified linear model; their guarantees may not carry over when those conditions are imperfect in practice. The tutorial is theoretical and does not empirically validate the designs across industrial experiments or compare their practical performance under common run-size, cost, and operational constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The author recommends choosing among robust, stochastic, and deterministic optimization according to the experimenter’s degree of knowledge about potential outcomes. The conclusion also notes that the tutorial creates potential research opportunities, but does not lay out a specific research program.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to benchmark the three frameworks on real experiments, including how their efficiency changes when outcome models or prior distributions are misspecified. Further work could also develop and validate designs that accommodate practical restrictions such as fixed treatment counts, unequal unit costs, and operational constraints.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how to choose microstructural volume elements for physics simulations so that fewer simulations can produce a more accurate micromechanical surrogate. The tested model predicts full-field stress responses for three-dimensional microstructures under an elastic material model. The authors compare three ways of describing microstructures, including a new self-supervised feature method, and three space-filling design criteria. The self-supervised method learns features by bringing cropped examples from the same microstructure together in a feature space and separating examples from different microstructures. Across the study, selected designs often improve prediction over random selection, although performance depends on the feature representation, design criterion, and training-set size.
narrate.key_results: The study generated 6,825 candidate microstructures and compared designs using 10 designs and 10 surrogate-model runs per feature and design combination. The largest reported improvement was 8.8% in validation performance for the variational-autoencoder and maximum-projection combination when using 25% of the candidate data. Data twinning provided a nearly constant improvement of about 5%, while conditional maximin with contrastive features was described as the most robust option as the training set grew. At 10% of the data, about 600 simulations, results were variable and several designs did not significantly outperform random selection; some maximum-projection results also deteriorated at 50% of the data, about 3,413 simulations.

narrate.summary: The paper constructs orthogonal arrays, balanced tables used in the design of experiments, for arbitrary numbers of levels and other parameters. Its objective is to give explicit arrays with few rows, approaching the lower bound established by Rao. The construction uses linear codes over finite fields; it maps code values to the required levels and corrects exceptional values by making repeated rows. Algebraic geometry codes yield the main construction, while Reed–Solomon codes provide a simpler alternative. The authors prove that the construction is deterministic and near-optimal in size for all parameters, and also show how the approach gives t-independent hash families.
narrate.key_results: For arbitrary parameters, the main construction has at most (c mn/t) to the power 35t rows and can be produced deterministically in time polynomial in the array size and its number of columns. The authors describe this as near-optimal relative to Rao’s lower bound, which grows at least as (c mn/t) to the power ct for a universal positive constant c. Their Reed–Solomon construction has at most n to the power t times (c(n+m)) to the power 5t rows, but is not near-optimal for all parameter regimes. For hash functions with arbitrary domain and codomain sizes, the paper reports representation space proportional to t log(mn), evaluation time proportional to t, and expected construction time proportional to t plus (n+m) to any positive epsilon; under the generalized Riemann hypothesis, construction time improves to t plus a polylogarithmic term.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential framework that combines symbolic regression (SR) with model-based design of experiments (MBDoE) to discover process mechanisms and improve process flow diagrams (PFDs). It targets formulated-product manufacturing, using a simulated cream-like process with product states, operating conditions, and a key performance indicator (KPI). The method searches for interpretable rate equations constrained by prior physical knowledge, then selects experiments that distinguish candidate models, improve the process, or balance both goals. The authors tested the framework using in-silico experiments from a constructed process model. In these simulations, the framework recovered the underlying mechanisms in a small number of iterations and reduced batch time while meeting the specified product target.
narrate.key_results: In the knowledge-discovery case with expressions rebuilt from scratch, prediction error fell from 3.87% to 0.14% by the third MBDoE iteration; when expressions were carried forward, it fell from 3.90% to 0.30% by the fourth iteration. Carrying expressions forward performed better overall than rebuilding them, even though the from-scratch search was given ten times longer per iteration. Without the physical structure constraint, prediction error fell from 25.6% to 1.98% and then plateaued, showing poorer performance than the constrained searches. In the combined discovery and optimization case, the ground-truth model was recovered by iteration 7; the final simulated batch time was 59 minutes rather than the initial 100 minutes, and the final KPI was 6.79 against a target of 7 with a stated tolerance of plus or minus 3%.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces PDXpower, an R package for estimating power and sample size in pre-clinical patient-derived xenograft experiments. For uncensored outcomes, the package uses a mixed-effects analysis of variance model; for right-censored time-to-event outcomes, it uses a Cox frailty model. It simulates data and tests treatment effects across candidate numbers of PDX lines and animals per line per treatment group. The examples show that increasing either sample-size component increases estimated power and that users can select among line-and-animal combinations to meet a target power.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 2,000 replicates, PDXpower’s two model-based tests had estimated Type I error rates close to the nominal 5% across the tested combinations of 3 to 10 PDX lines and 3 to 8 animals per line per treatment group. With preliminary data, the reported approximately 80% power combinations were (3, 4), (4, 3), or (6, 2) for the uncensored example, and (3, 8), (4, 6), (5, 5), (6, 4), or (7, 3) for the censored example. The authors report that 500 simulations took around 0.5 minutes for the uncensored example and about 20 minutes for the censored example on their stated computer; the paper does not report a benchmark comparison against other software.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Active In-context Prompt Design (AIPD), a method for choosing which initially unlabeled training examples to label and place in prompts for large language models (LLMs). Its goal is to reduce uncertainty in predictions across a set of test examples while using a limited labeling budget. The G-Optimal design (GO) algorithm selects examples using posterior variance in a linear-model approximation, while Simulation-Based Active Learning (SAL) estimates uncertainty reduction by simulating the model's outputs. The authors analyze these methods under linear-model assumptions and evaluate them on benchmark, language, and pattern-recognition tasks. They report that GO and SAL outperform comparison methods on a majority of tasks, but neither is best on every task.
narrate.key_results: Experiments used a labeling budget of 5 examples and 20 test examples, and each experiment was averaged over 10 trials. Across the reported classification, regression, natural-language, and pattern-recognition tasks, the authors say GO and SAL are best-performing methods on a majority, rather than all, of the datasets. For example, on the Falcon-40B rotation task, SAL's reported error was 0.01 ± 0.01, compared with GO's 0.80 ± 0.40; on the add-subtract pattern task, SAL's error was 0.02 ± 0.01, compared with GO's 0.20 ± 0.40. The paper gives computational costs of O(Kd²nT) for GO and O(nKmT) for SAL, but does not report a direct runtime comparison; in experiments, SAL was approximated using one simulation and a GO-based shortlist of five candidates. The theoretical analysis gives a near-optimal O(1/T) decrease in posterior variance under stated structural assumptions, and establishes equivalence between SAL and GO in the linear-model setting when the simulation count is sufficiently large.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test these selection rules with larger and more varied real-world datasets, higher labeling budgets, and human labeling workflows, while assessing whether selected examples fit within practical prompt-length and cost limits. narrate.summary: The paper develops a general framework for rerandomization in two-group randomized experiments, where treatment assignments are repeated until covariate imbalance meets a specified threshold. It studies balance scores defined by a quadratic form and explains how the choice of weighting matrix affects covariate balance and precision when estimating the average treatment effect. The framework covers established approaches such as Mahalanobis and principal-component rerandomization, and also examines Euclidean rerandomization. The authors derive theoretical results, evaluate methods in simulations, and apply them to a mentoring experiment dataset. They find that Euclidean rerandomization is a robust default when the relationship between covariates and outcomes is unknown.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 500 units per dataset, 10,000 datasets per setting, and an acceptance probability of 0.01, the authors vary the number of covariates from 5 to 250 and examine several covariate eigenvalue patterns and outcome relationships. Mahalanobis rerandomization performs best among the non-oracle methods when outcome relationships emphasize lower principal components, while Euclidean rerandomization is strongest when principal components are equally weighted and remains competitive when higher components matter. In the mentoring application, based on 308 adolescents and 21 covariates, the variance relative to complete randomization is 0.565 for Euclidean, 0.576 for squared Euclidean, 0.585 for the Kaiser principal-component rule, 0.608 for the weighted-eigenvalue rule, and 0.611 for Mahalanobis rerandomization. The theoretical results identify the outcome-informed oracle matrix as optimal for treatment-effect variance and establish Euclidean rerandomization as minimax optimal when that outcome relationship is unknown.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a way to learn combined metrics for randomized A/B tests, with the goal of making tests more powerful and reducing their cost. It focuses on software platforms where the North Star business outcome, such as retention or revenue, may be delayed or insensitive, while short-term engagement signals are available sooner. The method learns linear combinations of those signals from logged experiments and optimizes p-value-based objectives to improve agreement with vetted outcomes while limiting wrong-direction conclusions. The authors also add spherical regularization to improve the convergence of gradient-based training. On historical data from two large social platforms, the learned metrics improve statistical power and can reach comparable significance with substantially fewer samples than the North Star metric alone.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation uses 153 historical A/B experiments in total, including 58 conclusive experiments, and more than 25,000 A/A pairs from ShareChat and Moj; each platform had over 160 million monthly active users. On ShareChat, at a significance level of 0.05, the paper reports a 67% power increase using learned metrics alone and a 133% increase when adding a learned metric to the North Star and top proxy; across the reported settings, it also reports improvements of up to 78% over the North Star alone and up to 210% when used alongside it. The authors report that ShareChat can attain the North Star’s statistical confidence with up to eight times fewer samples, while the Moj results show a twelvefold reduction. Spherical regularization reduced training iterations to convergence by up to 40%; the authors also report that optimizing log p-values improved median sensitivity relative to the compared learned-metric approaches.

narrate.summary: This paper presents a method for Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) in nonlinear inverse problems where posterior distributions and design utilities are difficult to compute. It constructs a transport-map surrogate for the joint distribution of designs, observations, and unknown parameters, using functional tensor trains (FTTs) and layered deep inverse Rosenblatt transport (DIRT). Samples from the surrogate are used to estimate expected utility for criteria including posterior variance reduction and information gain. The authors also extend the method to sequential optimal experimental design (SOED), reusing transport maps from earlier stages to precondition later calculations. Simulations show that the method can identify informative batch and sequential designs while reducing the repeated forward-model work required by direct sampling approaches.
narrate.key_results: For a nonlinear one-design example, constructing the transport map required 12,960 forward-model evaluations; under the same evaluation budget, nested Monte Carlo used 255 samples per objective evaluation, and its optimized designs were more spread out, while the transport-map method generally found the optimum at design value 1 (though it selected a local kink in 6 of 50 runs). For the two-design version, map construction required 84,448 evaluations, and 46 of 50 transport-map optimizations found designs near the two global optima; the other four converged to local optima. In the disease-model simulation, estimated posterior-to-prior Kullback-Leibler divergence was about 5.1 for uniform observation times, 6.3 for one-at-a-time greedy design, and 6.8 for planning two times at a time. In the subsurface example, the sequential D-optimal joint-density construction cost decreased from 4,339 finite-element solves at stage 1 to 1,898 at stage 5, and the optimal designs recovered the simulated diffusivity channel better than random designs in the reported comparisons.

key_equations.name: Transport-map approximation

key_equations.name: A- and D-optimal utilities

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the method is generally impractical for very high- or infinite-dimensional parameter problems and works best with moderate numbers of inference parameters and experiments. narrate.limitations_unstated: The reported evidence comes from simulated examples and a small set of model types, so it does not establish performance on real experiments or across a broad range of design constraints. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify theoretical analysis of approximation errors and rank bounds for the tensor-train surrogates as an important next step. They also point to a priori dimensionality reduction as a way to extend the approach to higher-dimensional problems.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method with real experimental data, model misspecification, and more varied noise structures, and compare it against a broader set of design algorithms under equal computational budgets. It would also be useful to develop approaches that account directly for practical constraints such as discrete candidate settings, costs, or safety limits, and to evaluate alternatives to the paper’s greedy sequential planning.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces BRAIN, a rerandomization method for assigning treatment and control in randomized experiments while improving covariate balance. It formulates balance as an optimization problem that minimizes the Mahalanobis distance subject to the required group sizes. The method starts from a random assignment, accepts swaps that improve balance, and makes random swaps when local search finds no improvement; it stops once the balance threshold is met. The authors adapt the approach to sequential, stratified, and cluster randomized experiments. They report that BRAIN generates balanced assignments much faster than existing rerandomization methods while retaining the statistical benefits of rerandomization.
narrate.key_results: In a simple experiment with 500 units, 250 covariates, and an acceptance probability of 10^-4, BRAIN generated 1,000 acceptable assignments in 1.3 seconds, compared with 2,878.8 seconds for pair-switching rerandomization; acceptance-rejection sampling was omitted from that setting because of its computational burden. In structured experiments with 1,000 units, BRAIN took 5.8 seconds in the sequential setting, 3.0 seconds in the stratified setting, and 3.9 seconds in the cluster setting; acceptance-rejection sampling took 3,288.5, 3,386.8, and 3,116.2 seconds, respectively. In the clinical-trial example, generating 10,000 acceptable assignments took 12 seconds with BRAIN, about 2.3 minutes with acceptance-rejection sampling, and more than half an hour with pair-switching rerandomization. The simulations found that BRAIN’s treatment-effect estimates, testing, and confidence intervals had broadly similar statistical performance to other rerandomization methods and improved precision compared with complete randomization; the paper proves unbiasedness for equal-sized treatment groups and a variance-reduction bound under stated assumptions.

key_equations.explanation: W is the current assignment, W* is the assignment after a proposed treated-control swap, M is the balance distance, and a is the acceptable-distance threshold; if no improving swap is found among L examined pairs, the method makes S random swaps before continuing.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not address experiments with tiers of covariates, which require simultaneous balance across tiers. They also state that it is unclear whether other integer-programming techniques, such as branch and bound, could produce better rerandomization methods.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method is a heuristic search, and the paper gives no bound on how long it may take to reach a very strict balance threshold or guarantee that it will do so quickly. Its variance guarantee relies on stated modeling conditions, including equal group sizes, and the empirical evidence comes mainly from simulations plus one clinical-trial dataset rather than a broad range of real experiments.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending BRAIN to tiered covariates using multi-objective optimization. They also identify adapting other integer-programming techniques, including branch and bound, as a direction for future research.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method under unequal group sizes and model departures from the assumptions used for its variance guarantee. It could also evaluate how well the search handles practical allocation constraints and compare its balance and runtime in a wider range of real experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper compares how greediness affects algorithms for constructing exact optimal experimental designs. It considers a second-order response-surface model with continuous factors and compares coordinate exchange (CEXCH), implemented as either coordinate-by-coordinate or whole-row optimization, with particle swarm optimization (PSO). The study assesses designs using D-optimality for parameter estimation and I-optimality for prediction, across 21 established design scenarios. The exchange methods showed essentially the same performance despite their different levels of greediness. PSO performed better for some D-optimal scenarios and had a smaller, scenario-dependent advantage for finding I-optimal designs.
narrate.key_results: The authors ran each exchange method 10,000 independent times per scenario and compared them with results from 140 previously reported PSO runs. The coordinate-by-coordinate and row-wise exchange methods had essentially no difference in either the probability of finding a design at least 95% efficient or the probability of finding the best-known design. For D-optimal designs, PSO more often found highly efficient and best-known designs when there were 1 or 2 factors; its advantage was smaller for 3 factors. For I-optimal designs, the methods had similar probabilities of reaching at least 95% efficiency, while PSO's advantage in finding the best-known design varied by scenario.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say the apparent lack of a greediness effect between the two exchange methods should be investigated further. They also note that the relative difficulty of the I- and D-criteria, and the possibility that the I-criterion is less affected by local optima, warrant further investigation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The comparison uses 10,000 exchange runs but only 140 PSO runs drawn from previously published work, so the estimates have different amounts of sampling evidence and may not reflect a controlled, equal-budget comparison. The study covers only second-order response-surface models with up to 3 factors and uses previously reported best-known designs as its benchmarks, rather than proving those designs are globally optimal.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose expanding the model set to include first-order, interaction, linear, and nonlinear models, and studying larger experiments with more factors. They also propose including A- and G-optimality and additional exchange methods and metaheuristics, including genetic algorithms and simulated annealing.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to compare the methods under matched computational budgets and report both run time and design quality. The methods could also be tested with practical factor constraints and in real experiments, and adapted for sequential use as data become available.

narrate.summary: This paper gives a computational classification of binary orthogonal arrays (OAs) with 2048 rows, 14 columns, and strength 7. The goal is to find all such arrays up to equivalence, rather than to choose one design by an experimental optimality criterion. The author treats these arrays as completely regular codes and builds them recursively from smaller local configurations. Exact-cover search, integer linear programming (ILP), and isomorphism rejection are used to construct and distinguish the cases. The classification finds 30,848 equivalence classes and also identifies one equivalence class of almost-OA with strength 8.
narrate.key_results: The paper reports 30,848 equivalence classes of OA(2048, 14, 2, 7), of which 8 are square-free and 14,960 are punctured 1-perfect codes. It reports 541,012,580,165,257,200 distinct arrays in total, including 267,743,838,601,839,600 punctured 1-perfect codes. The derived classification contains 202,917 equivalence classes of OA(1024, 13, 2, 6). The computational work included around 1,300 central processing unit (CPU) days for filtering continuable local codes and 124 CPU days for one equivalence-rejection step.

narrate.summary: The paper studies quasi-Hermitian varieties in a three-dimensional projective space over a finite field of even order. It shows that all varieties in the studied Buekenhout-Metz family are projectively equivalent and determines their stabilizing collineation group. Using these varieties, the authors construct a simple orthogonal array intended for settings where balanced combinations can help reduce the number of experiments. The array has q to the fifth rows, q to the fourth columns, q levels per column, and strength two. The construction is established theoretically; the paper does not report an applied experiment or a comparison of practical design performance.
narrate.key_results: For even prime powers q greater than 2, the authors construct a simple orthogonal array with q to the fifth rows, q to the fourth columns, q levels, and strength two. Its index is q cubed, so every pair of levels occurs equally often in every pair of columns. The paper also proves that all the studied varieties are projectively equivalent and gives the order of their full stabilizer as q to the sixth times q minus 1. The results are theoretical; the paper reports no efficiency ranking against other experimental designs.

The result is proved theoretically, without empirical validation or comparisons of run-size savings against alternative arrays or experimental designs.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors state that their long-term aim is to characterize the Buekenhout-Metz quasi-Hermitian varieties among all possible quasi-Hermitian varieties in spaces of the same dimension and order.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to investigate constructions for higher-strength arrays or for constraints commonly imposed on experimental factors, and to compare their run requirements with existing designs. Practical validation could also test whether these arrays are usable in real experiments and whether the mathematical construction can be implemented efficiently.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a way to choose how much randomness to retain when rerandomizing assignments in small, two-group experiments. Its objective is to improve covariate balance and treatment-effect precision while preserving useful exact randomization tests and intervals. The authors construct candidate assignments using a covariate-balance threshold, then use prior information about covariates and plausible outcome relationships to simulate expected p-values across thresholds. They select the threshold that minimizes the expected p-value, and provide an open-source software package to implement rerandomization and explore thresholds. The central finding is that very strict balance can leave too few acceptable assignments for informative inference, so a carefully chosen intermediate level can be preferable to either unrestricted or deterministic assignment.
narrate.key_results: The paper shows that the minimum attainable p-value is the reciprocal of the number of acceptable assignments; with only one acceptable assignment, exact tests cannot reject a null hypothesis. In simulations with 6, 12, and 18 units, the prior-based threshold-selection procedure had lower relative root mean squared error than uniform selection of the threshold, although it tended to select probabilities somewhat below the simulated optimum. In the agricultural-data semi-synthetic example, the expected-p-value-minimizing acceptance probability was 0.008, corresponding to about 128 acceptable assignments out of 184,756; the expected p-value was 0.027 with rerandomization versus 0.10 without it. In that example, treatment-effect estimates deviated from the true effect by 14% or more without rerandomization and by less than 5% with the selected procedure.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors focus on Fisherian permutation-based inference, and their simulations assume constant, additive treatment effects, excluding treatment-effect heterogeneity and covariate-treatment interactions. They also state that very low acceptance thresholds can be computationally intensive for experiments with many units.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence uses a linear outcome model with Gaussian covariates and errors and examines only 6, 12, and 18 units, so performance in other data structures and experiment sizes is not established. The agricultural illustration is semi-synthetic and estimates its outcome model from the full experiment, so it does not provide validation in a prospective experiment using only information available before assignment.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify rerandomization under heterogeneous treatment effects as an area for continued work and say that the point at which interval widths begin increasing needs further theoretical study. They also propose further computational work on adaptively building acceptable assignment sets to improve balance while retaining exact or conditional randomization tests.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful extension would assess threshold selection for multi-arm experiments, unequal allocation, and practical restrictions such as blocks or clusters. Prospective evaluations could also compare the selected thresholds with simpler prespecified rules using realized balance, treatment-effect precision, and interval coverage.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a design-based way to approximate Shapley values, which allocate a coalition’s total value among its players and are used in applications such as sensitivity analysis and model explanation. Rather than sampling permutations independently, it uses order-of-addition designs: component orthogonal arrays when the number of players permits them, and Latin squares as an alternative. The estimator averages each player’s marginal contribution over the selected permutations; the designs balance player positions and, for component orthogonal arrays, pairs of players across positions. The authors prove that the estimates are unbiased and that they exactly recover the true values in certain cases. Simulations and network data analyses generally show improved accuracy over simple random sampling, with the component orthogonal array performing best when it is practical to use.
narrate.key_results: In the airport game with 101 players, the paper reports simulations with 1,000 realizations and sample sizes from 10,100 to 101,000 permutations. The component orthogonal array method had the lowest reported processor time: simple random sampling took 1.14 to 1.39 times as long, the Latin-square method took 1.29 to 1.37 times as long, and structured random sampling took 5.23 to 5.54 times as long. For the 9/11 network with 69 members, across 300 replications and sample sizes from 4,968 to 24,840, all methods identified the top 10 members correctly; the component orthogonal array method had the lowest error for identifying the top 20. For the C. elegans network with 279 neurons, the Latin-square method had lower top-five identification error and squared loss than simple random sampling in 90 replications; the authors report that the smallest component orthogonal array analysis would take about two days.

key_equations.name: Component orthogonal array estimate
key_equations.explanation: The estimated Shapley value for player j is the average of that player’s marginal contributions over the sampled arrays; d is the number of players, n is the number of arrays, i indexes an array, D_i is the set of permutations in that array, pi is a permutation, and c with subscripts is the marginal contribution.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that a component orthogonal array can be constructed directly only when the number of players is a prime power. They propose adding null players to reach a prime-power total, and use Latin squares when component orthogonal arrays are unavailable or too costly; they also note that some value functions are difficult to calculate exactly and may require Monte Carlo estimation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The accuracy advantage depends on the chosen value function producing marginal contributions that benefit from the balance in these particular permutation designs; the paper does not establish that the designs outperform random sampling for every game or model. The comparisons cover a limited set of examples and datasets, and the large design size can itself be impractical, as illustrated by the reported two-day calculation for the 279-player case.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could compare these designs under additional value functions and constraints that arise in actual experiments, including limits on which component orders are feasible. Sequential or adaptive versions could also be evaluated to determine when to stop sampling, alongside broader validation on real applications and accessible software for constructing and using the designs.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how to allocate a fixed sampling budget when choosing the better of two alternatives with unknown Bernoulli rewards. Its objective is to minimize the probability of selecting the wrong alternative. The authors define a class of consistent and stable adaptive procedures and use information-theoretic lower bounds to analyze their performance. They prove that uniform sampling cannot be uniformly improved upon for the two-arm problem: an adaptive method that is at least as good in every instance cannot be strictly better in any instance. For three or more arms, they derive an exact asymptotic error rate for Successive Rejects and show that uniform sampling can outperform it on some instances.
narrate.key_results: For two arms, the asymptotic ratio of the budget to the logarithm of the inverse error probability under uniform sampling is the reciprocal of the exponent at an equal allocation; every algorithm that is at least as good as uniform sampling on all instances has the same asymptotic performance. The paper also proves that this equal-allocation performance is a lower bound for consistent and stable algorithms. For the three-arm instance with means 0.5, 0.3, and 0.3, the reported asymptotic ratio is approximately 71.1 for Successive Rejects and 70.3587 for uniform sampling, so uniform sampling has the better error rate there. In a simulation on a two-arm instance with means 0.0005 and 0.0001, the authors used 40,000 trials per setting and budgets from 6,000 to 40,000; the thresholded adaptive design performed similarly to or worse than uniform sampling, while an oracle allocation performed better.

key_equations.name: Uniform-sampling asymptotic performance
key_equations.explanation: Here T is the fixed sample budget, p with subscripts µ and T is the probability of selecting the wrong arm, µ is the vector of arm means, and g is the static-design error exponent evaluated at an equal allocation.

key_equations.name: Exact asymptotic performance of Successive Rejects
key_equations.explanation: Here T is the sample budget, p with subscripts µ and T is the error probability, K is the number of arms, j is a candidate-set size, the overlined log K is the paper's phase-allocation constant, and Gamma-j is the paper's minimum divergence quantity for candidate-set size j at means µ.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that they obtain a complete picture only for two-arm A/B testing with Bernoulli rewards; the minimal error probability is not known even for Gaussian rewards with unknown variances or for rewards in a one-parameter exponential family. They also state that extending the results to more than two arms is challenging and that they have not found an adaptive algorithm that beats uniform sampling on every instance.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main optimality results are asymptotic, so they do not establish which procedure is best at the finite budgets typically available in an experiment. The simulations cover a single two-arm instance and one family of threshold settings, while the multiar m comparison is primarily theoretical; the conclusions therefore have limited direct empirical validation across different effect sizes, reward models, and operational constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors conjecture that uniform sampling remains universally optimal for two-arm problems in a one-parameter exponential family. They also report that they are working on extending the notion of stable algorithms to problems with more than two arms and comparing those algorithms with uniform sampling.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the conclusions with real experiments and with practical constraints such as unequal sampling costs, delayed outcomes, or limits on allocation changes. It would also be useful to compare finite-budget procedures across a broader set of Bernoulli instances and to examine whether the results extend to sequential stopping or other reward models.

narrate.summary: Bayesian experimental design (BED) chooses experimental conditions to improve inference about unknown parameters. This paper develops methods to optimize expected information gain (EIG) by estimating its gradient with respect to the design variables. The first method, unbiased estimation of the EIG gradient with Markov chain Monte Carlo (UEEG-MCMC), uses posterior samples; the second, biased estimation of the EIG gradient with atomic priors (BEEG-AP), reuses a batch of parameter samples to reduce simulation cost. The authors derive a posterior-based gradient representation and analyze how sample reuse relates to nested Monte Carlo. Their results find BEEG-AP more efficient for small EIG problems, while UEEG-MCMC is more robust across EIG levels.
narrate.key_results: The analysis shows that the sample-reuse estimate is a lower bound on EIG that increases with sample size, and under stated likelihood bounds its mean squared error converges at rate O(1/M). The authors also show that keeping a fixed-size sample-reuse calculation within a given error of the true EIG can require a sample count that grows exponentially with EIG. In the toy, pharmacokinetic, and STAT5 simulations, BEEG-AP generally performed well in small-EIG settings, while UEEG-MCMC performed best in the tested large-EIG settings; the adaptive contrastive method failed in some high-dependence settings. The reported optimization simulation budgets were 2 × 10^4 for the toy model, 2 × 10^6 for the pharmacokinetic model, and 5 × 10^5 for the STAT5 model; comparisons also included prior contrastive estimation and gradient-based Bayesian experimental design.

key_equations.name: Expected information gain objective
key_equations.explanation: U is expected information gain, I is mutual information, theta is the unknown parameter, y is the observation, and lambda is the experimental design.

key_equations.name: Posterior expected gradient
key_equations.explanation: The gradient is taken with respect to lambda; the expectation is over prior parameter theta, model noise epsilon, and posterior parameter theta-prime given observation y and design lambda; l is the likelihood and q is the posterior distribution.

key_equations.name: Atomic-prior gradient estimate
key_equations.explanation: The approximate gradient averages likelihood-weighted likelihood gradients over M generated observations and M reused parameter samples; y_i is an observation, theta_j and theta_k are parameter samples, lambda is the design, and i, j, and k index samples.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that finite-length Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling does not produce exact posterior samples and therefore introduces bias into the UEEG-MCMC gradient estimate. They also show that BEEG-AP can perform poorly when the true EIG is large, because reducing its estimation error can require a rapidly growing simulation budget.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluations use simulated examples and a small set of models, so they do not establish performance in real experiments or across a broad range of design constraints. Both approaches also depend on differentiable sampling paths and likelihood calculations, while the posterior-sampling cost and convergence of the Markov chains may be substantial in difficult parameter spaces.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the methods on real experimental data and under practical constraints such as discrete or costly-to-change settings and limits on the number of runs. Further work could also examine sequential design, alternative inference objectives, and ways to reduce or diagnose posterior-sampling error in the Markov chain method.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a design method for universal kriging, where a correlated spatial response is modeled with a linear mean and spatial errors, to improve simultaneous predictions at a finite set of unsampled locations. Its objective is to minimize the generalized variance (GV), the determinant of the covariance matrix of the prediction errors, so that the joint uncertainty of predictions is reduced. The authors derive formulas for updating prediction weights and prediction-error covariances when new design points are added. These updates lead to an incremental construction that selects an added batch by maximizing the determinant of its prediction-error covariance matrix. In the reported examples, incremental designs approach GV-optimality efficiently, and the method is applied to temperature prediction across Upper Austrian municipalities.
narrate.key_results: In simulations across 54 Matérn covariance parameter combinations, the average relative efficiency of 9-point GV-optimal designs under the G-optimality criterion was 0.9707 for a linear trend and 0.9928 for a quadratic trend. Single-step incremental designs had mean GV efficiencies of 0.9911 for the reported quadratic-trend setup and 0.9881 for the linear-trend setup; their median efficiencies were 100%. In the search comparison, finding a GV-optimal design took an average of 3.34 seconds, compared with 64.2 seconds for a V-optimal design and 1.41 hours for a G-optimal design. In the Upper Austria example, a 32-station GV-optimal network achieved the same GV criterion value as the existing 36-station network while predicting at 406 rather than 402 locations; 7 selected locations already had stations, and 7 others were within 5 km of an existing station.
