key_equations.explanation: Here j and x select the variable and value to intervene on, the starred pair is the chosen intervention, G ranges over candidate graphs in the set of graphs, P(G) is the current graph probability, X_{-j} denotes all variables except the intervened variable, and the expectation and posterior are evaluated under the intervention.

key_equations.name: Monte Carlo estimate of the intervention objective
key_equations.explanation: Here G ranges over candidate graphs, P(G) is the current probability of a graph, M is the number of sampled outcomes, m indexes those samples, x_{-j}^{(m)} is the mth simulated outcome for the variables not intervened on, and the log posterior probabilities estimate the expected objective for intervening on variable j at value x.

key_equations.name: Upper confidence bound used in Bayesian optimization
key_equations.explanation: Here x_{t+1} is the next candidate intervention value, t indexes optimization steps, mu_t(x) and sigma_t(x) are the predictive mean and standard deviation of the objective model at x, and beta controls the tradeoff between exploring uncertain values and exploiting values with high predicted objective.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the number of candidate acyclic graphs grows super-exponentially, so the approach in its current form is intended for settings with only a few variables. They also identify challenges with flexible root-variable distributions, updating Gaussian process hyperparameters, and the computational burden of the Monte Carlo and Bayesian optimization loop; they note that Gaussian process computation scales cubically with the number of observations.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence is limited to a bivariate illustration, and the reported high-confidence result uses randomly selected interventions rather than the proposed Bayesian optimization procedure. The method also assumes acyclicity, causal sufficiency, additive noise, and the ability to perform single-variable interventions at selected values; its performance under violations of these assumptions or practical intervention constraints is not evaluated.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest using Dirichlet process mixtures for more flexible root-variable distributions and considering adaptive or fully Bayesian treatment of Gaussian process hyperparameters. For larger graph spaces, they propose approximate graph inference; they also suggest combining the method with constraint-based causal discovery or regression followed by independence testing.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to compare the optimized intervention policy with random and established design strategies across broader simulated settings, including cases with model misspecification and constrained intervention values. Further work could incorporate intervention costs and feasibility constraints, then validate the resulting sequential design in real experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes supervised randomization to collect experimental data for customer-level treatment effect models while reducing the cost of random targeting. It is designed for marketing experiments in which an existing scoring model can identify customers who are more likely to benefit from treatment. The design uses the score to assign different treatment probabilities to different customers, while retaining random assignment and recording each probability. The authors describe inverse probability weighting and doubly robust estimation to correct for the resulting selection bias. In a simulation based on bank telemarketing data, supervised randomization improved campaign returns during the experiment, while downstream treatment effect models remained competitive with models trained on fully randomized data.
narrate.key_results: In the simulation, targeting 50% of customers under supervised randomization produced a 14.3% conversion rate, compared with 13.5% under equal-probability full randomization; this matched the 14.3% rate from full randomization with a 66% treatment probability while targeting fewer customers. For 40,000 prospective customers, the authors report experimental campaign cost savings of 7.1% to 9.4% compared with full randomization and 2.9% to 8.2% compared with imbalanced full randomization. Treatment effect estimates remained unbiased after correction, though their variance increased; doubly robust estimates had significantly lower variance than inverse probability weighted estimates. For the causal forest, mean absolute error increased from 0.0276 under full randomization to 0.0295 under supervised randomization, and the Qini coefficient decreased from 0.0056 to 0.0047. The reported campaign profit decrease for models trained on supervised-randomization data was about 0% to 1.3%, depending on the model and profit setting.

key_equations.name: Score-based treatment probability
key_equations.explanation: M is the mapping from model score to treatment probability, s_i is the score of customer i, and e_i is that customer's treatment probability.

narrate.limitations_stated: The evaluation is an offline simulation, and the authors state that further evaluation in real-world experiments is necessary to establish net cost savings in practice. They also note that supervised randomization increases uncertainty in treatment effect estimates and can reduce downstream model performance.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The results rely on one public bank marketing dataset with simulated treatment effects and potential outcomes, so they do not establish performance across other industries, outcomes, or real campaign mechanisms. narrate.summary: This paper develops flexible sliced Latin hypercube designs for computer experiments, where slices may have arbitrary run sizes rather than equal sizes. The designs preserve Latin hypercube structure both overall and within every slice, supporting experiments that are run in batches or at multiple levels of fidelity. The construction assigns lattice positions to slices and adds random jitter; an optimization procedure then improves space filling using a criterion that combines the whole design with its slices. The authors use the sliced enhanced stochastic evolutionary algorithm for optimization and propose a faster two-part algorithm for larger designs. Their simulations show improved criterion values over random designs and lower computation times for the two-part method, though the sliced evolutionary method often gives better criterion values.
narrate.key_results: For a design with slices of 4, 8, and 12 runs and 2 factors, the paper's text reports that optimization reduced the combined space-filling measurement from 14.4740 to 5.7958; the figure labels instead report 14.4223 and 5.6844. In 100,000 randomly generated designs of that size, the best reported criterion value was 6.8387, higher than the text's optimized value. For designs with 15- and 30-run slices, the average criterion was 8.3100 for the sliced enhanced stochastic evolutionary algorithm, compared with 9.1712 for the two-part algorithm; their average times were 406 seconds and 18 seconds. For designs with 5, 10, 15, and 30 runs across four slices and 6 factors, the corresponding average criterion values were 2.0823 and 2.2424, while average times were 1110 seconds and 71 seconds. narrate.summary: This paper presents a hands-on classroom exercise for teaching split-plot design of experiments using a boomerang tin toy. The example is intended to show how to run an experiment when one factor is hard to change while other factors can be randomized more readily. The authors vary screw weight, rubber-band tension, whether the rubber band is twisted, and ramp position, and measure forward and backward travel distances. They describe how to plan a screening design, assess degrees of freedom, and analyze the data using a model that accounts for whole-plot and run-level errors. Their 24-run example illustrates both factor screening and simultaneous optimization of the two distances, and the authors judge the toy suitable for a class exercise.
narrate.key_results: The example used 24 experimental units arranged as 6 whole plots with 4 runs in each; the authors recommend at least 6 whole plots to provide at least 4 degrees of freedom for whole-plot error. For forward distance, the model had an R-squared of 0.89 and a root mean square error of 60.3 cm; all four main effects were statistically significant, while none of the interactions were. For backward distance, the model had an R-squared of 0.52 and a root mean square error of 53.9 cm; screw weight was the only significant factor. The authors used D-optimality to generate the design but did not compare it with other designs; their prediction profiler favored the heavier screw weight for increasing both responses.

narrate.summary: This paper designs multidimensional diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) acquisitions for estimating tissue parameters in the Standard Model (SM). The authors seek b-tensor measurement sets that provide precise parameter estimates, using a D-optimal criterion based on the determinant of an averaged Fisher information matrix (FIM). They optimize information about the diffusion and second cumulant tensors as a surrogate for optimizing the full SM, averaging over a plausible tissue-parameter space. They test two design constraint schemes for 60 measurements, with tensor orientations fixed and different freedoms for tensor shape and size. The resulting designs use linear tensor encoding (LTE) and planar tensor encoding (PTE), and simulations show lower estimation errors than a balanced LTE/PTE comparison protocol.
narrate.key_results: The optimized designs used only LTE and PTE, with LTE making up about 75% to 85% of measurements; the designs also grouped measurements at two diffusion weightings. For the comparison, the authors simulated 10,000 voxels with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 100 and compared the more flexible design against a balanced LTE/PTE acquisition. The optimized design improved estimation accuracy by 14% for the diffusion and second cumulant tensors and by 7% for the double-Watson Standard Model. The design used 60 b-tensor measurements, while the paper does not report a run-size comparison across alternative measurement counts.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors use the fourth-order cumulant expansion rather than the analytical SM signal to compute information, and regard it as a reasonable surrogate only over the stated diffusion-weighting range. narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on simulated signals and does not establish performance on acquired clinical data or in the presence of experimental deviations from the assumed tissue model. narrate.summary: This paper develops a sequential design method for predator-prey functional-response experiments. It considers Holling type II and type III models, with prey consumption represented by either a binomial or beta-binomial distribution. At each step, the method selects the initial prey density for the next experiment using the current parameter and model information, then updates that information after observing consumption. narrate.key_results: The main simulation compared four candidate models across 40 true model-and-parameter settings, with 30 independent runs for each design method and 25 observations per run. Across all four true models, sequential designs outperformed static and random designs for parameter estimation, and the authors report the same overall advantage for model discrimination. For the combined parameter-estimation and model-discrimination objective, sequential designs outperformed static designs on both components; the total-entropy design was only marginally less effective than the single-purpose designs in the additional utility comparison. narrate.summary: The paper develops methods for placing sensors in Bayesian linear inverse problems governed by partial differential equations. Its goal is to reduce uncertainty in the estimated parameters using an A-optimal design criterion, which measures the reduction in average posterior variance. The authors use randomized subspace iteration to approximate the objective and its gradient by exploiting low-rank structure, and construct sparse, nearly binary sensor selections with a reweighted penalty solved through majorization-minimization. They also introduce a modified A-optimal criterion intended to reduce computational work. In a simulated contaminant-source identification study, the methods produced sparse sensor layouts, and the modified criterion yielded designs with similar posterior variance to those from the standard criterion at lower computational cost.
narrate.key_results: The numerical study used 109 candidate sensor locations and measurements at three observation times, for 327 total observations. With 127 columns in the randomized approximation, the reported design objective, active-sensor count, and number of optimization subproblem solves matched the results obtained with larger approximations; at the reported penalty setting, the design used 30 sensors. A design with 18 sensors was also shown, and at 207 columns the reported A-optimal criterion approximation accuracy was on the order of 10^-7. Across the tested designs, those computed by the proposed method had lower exact A-optimal values than the random designs compared against them; designs from the modified criterion had similar posterior variance to standard A-optimal designs while requiring one fewer group of PDE solves per evaluation.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a way to choose a rerandomization threshold for a non-sequential treatment-control experiment. It targets estimation of the treatment effect with a covariate-adjusted linear regression estimator, seeking protection against high estimation error caused by unobserved factors. The method starts with a large set of balanced random assignments, orders them by observed-covariate imbalance, and evaluates progressively larger sets using a tail quantile of the estimator’s mean squared error. The threshold is chosen where this tail criterion is minimized, balancing covariate balance against retaining enough randomness. Simulations and a bootstrap study based on an education experiment show that the resulting designs can improve tail error over unrestricted balanced randomization, while very restrictive deterministic assignment can have a much worse tail.
narrate.key_results: In a simulation with 100 subjects, 10 covariates, and 25,000 candidate assignments, the selected thresholds across six residual-distribution procedures ranged from 0.232 to 0.289; the three proposed designs retained 5,881, 5,601, and 6,901 assignments. In a separate simulation, the proposed designs had the lowest 95th-percentile error among the compared strategies, and their performance was similar to selecting the least imbalanced 0.5% of assignments. In the education-data bootstrap study, the two practical proposed procedures reduced mean squared error relative to balanced complete randomization by 4.6% and 6.2%, and reduced the 95th-percentile error by 5.7% and 4.9%. The deterministic design had slightly lower mean error in that study, but its 95th-percentile error was almost 300% larger than that of the proposed designs.

narrate.summary: This paper presents the abtest package for Bayesian analysis of an A/B (A-versus-B) test with binary outcomes. The method models the two groups’ success rates with binomial distributions and compares hypotheses of no effect, a positive effect, a negative effect, or any difference. It uses normal priors on the grand mean of log odds and the log odds ratio, and lets users encode expert expectations by eliciting prior distributions from quantities such as absolute risk. The package calculates hypothesis probabilities and Bayes factors, estimates effect sizes, and tracks evidence as observations accumulate. The authors demonstrate the method with a fictitious business example and a reanalysis of a medical trial; they do not construct or optimize an experimental design.
narrate.key_results: A simulation comparison covered all combinations of group sizes from 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 observations, with success counts drawn from four specified fractions of each group size; Laplace approximations and bridge sampling gave highly similar log Bayes factors, including at the smallest sample sizes. In the medical trial reanalysis, the placebo group had 1,459 live births among 2,013 participants and the progesterone group had 1,513 among 2,025; the Bayes factor favoring a positive effect over no effect was 0.4866, and the posterior probability of no effect was 0.7954 under the package’s default prior probabilities. narrate.summary: This paper studies whether methods for identifying mean-changing effects remain reliable when an unreplicated two-level factorial experiment also has effects that change response variance. The authors simulate four-factor experiments with one or two variance-changing effects and compare the Box–Meyer, Lenth, Berk–Picard, and Loughin–Noble methods. The simulated variance follows a multiplicative model, which can correlate estimated location effects even though the methods do not account for that correlation. The first three methods generally retain control of false detections, while the Loughin–Noble method can lose that control as variance effects become large. The paper also finds that variance effects can change the chance of detecting pairs of location effects together, depending on their relationship and signs.
narrate.key_results: The study used 1,825 simulated data sets per setting in a four-factor, two-level experiment, and calibrated methods to an individual error rate near 0.05. With no active location or variance effects, the individual error rates were 0.051 for Lenth, 0.051 for Box–Meyer, 0.050 for Berk–Picard, and 0.049 for Loughin–Noble; their experimentwise error rates were 0.414, 0.474, 0.459, and 0.274, respectively. The individual error rates of the first three methods stayed near their nominal level across the simulated variance-effect sizes, whereas the Loughin–Noble rate rose above 0.1 for the largest sizes, with the increase more pronounced when two variance effects were present. The Loughin–Noble method’s average power also increased with variance-effect size, alongside its elevated error rates; the other methods showed little power increase, and Box–Meyer sometimes had a small power advantage. Joint power for two location effects could rise or fall substantially when the variance effect induced correlation between their estimates, depending on whether the signs aligned.

narrate.summary: This paper designs an online learning method for publishers choosing the order and prices at which they offer ad slots to ad networks. narrate.summary: The paper develops a computational method for Bayesian experimental design with nonlinear models, especially when an experiment should teach us about selected parameters rather than every model parameter. Its objective is the expected information gain (EIG) in those parameters, averaged over possible experimental outcomes. The method, called layered multiple importance sampling (LMIS), reuses samples and model evaluations from earlier steps to build better importance-sampling distributions for estimating posterior normalizing constants. The authors assess it in linear Gaussian examples and in a nonlinear Mössbauer spectroscopy example. They find that LMIS estimates the design objective more accurately than prior-based sampling at the same computational effort.
narrate.key_results: In the four- and eight-dimensional linear Gaussian examples, LMIS reduced estimation error by several orders of magnitude compared with prior-based sampling; with 1,000,000 model evaluations, its mean squared error (MSE) was comparable to the method using exact posterior distributions as the sampling distributions. In the Mössbauer example, LMIS reduced MSE by up to two orders of magnitude relative to prior-based sampling. For the three-velocity designs studied, the reported optimum for learning the peak center was minus 1.3, zero, and 1.3, while the optimum for learning the offset was minus 2, zero, and 2. The authors’ theoretical analysis gives an MSE rate proportional to computational work to the power of minus two-thirds under an asymptotically adjusted inner-to-outer sample ratio, compared with minus one-half for a fixed ratio; they caution that the adjusted ratio may not help at finite budgets when bias dominates.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors demonstrate the method on problems of moderate dimension. They report that performance can deteriorate for outcomes in the tails of the prior, where fewer previous samples are available for reuse, and that conditional biasing distributions can be sensitive to errors in estimated posterior covariance at small sample sizes.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is based on simulated examples, including a single nonlinear spectroscopy model, rather than validation in a real experiment. The method also requires many likelihood or model evaluations and a sequential sample-reuse procedure, while the paper does not demonstrate an end-to-end optimization workflow under practical experimental constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using surrogate models to construct biasing distributions more cheaply, and combining surrogates or marginal-likelihood approximations with LMIS through control variates or multilevel Monte Carlo while preserving consistency. They also suggest using Laplace approximations when posterior gradients are available, pairing LMIS with stochastic design-optimization methods, and applying focused design to parameters representing model discrepancy.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test LMIS on real experiments and on higher-dimensional nonlinear models, measuring both computational cost and the quality of the selected design. It would also be useful to assess the method when run sizes, allowable settings, or randomization are constrained, and to compare alternative parameterizations and criteria for selecting or pruning reusable samples.

narrate.summary: This paper develops theoretical bounds for Bayesian hypothesis testing in two-group A/B testing of binomial outcomes, such as conversion rates. It compares a zero-effect hypothesis, in which both groups have the same success probability, with an alternative in which their probabilities differ. The derivation bounds the most favorable evidence for the zero-effect hypothesis using the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the observed proportions, then relates that divergence to Welch's test statistic. The resulting Bayesian and frequentist sample-size rules are reported to be close up to a constant factor. The paper does not construct an experimental layout or analyze real experimental data.
narrate.key_results: For two groups with r trials each, the paper gives a Bayesian sample rule of r much greater than 1 divided by twice the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the group success probabilities. Its frequentist comparison is r much greater than twice the sum of the groups' binomial variances divided by the squared difference in success probabilities. The authors say these rules are close up to a constant factor, and that smaller effects or higher variance require more samples. The numerical comparison illustrates a 10% relative uplift and multiplies both rules by 2; the paper also notes that Bayesian evidence against the null corresponds to p-values much lower than 0.05.

narrate.summary: The paper develops treatment-assignment designs for two-treatment A/B testing on social networks, where connected users may have correlated continuous responses. It models this correlation with a conditional autoregressive (CAR) model and seeks to estimate the treatment effect precisely using a D-optimal design criterion. The authors formulate the exact design problem and a modified version as mixed integer programming (MIP) problems. The modified formulation avoids needing a known correlation parameter and is designed to be faster to solve, though it does not guarantee the exact D-optimal design. Simulations and studies using real network structures show that the modified method often improves estimation precision over random assignment, especially when network correlation is not small.
narrate.key_results: For a simulated network of 50 nodes with density 0.1, D-efficiency for the random design fell from 0.98 at correlation 0 to 0.76 at correlation 0.3; the exact and modified designs had values from 1.00 to 0.90 across those settings. For the same network, at correlation 0.3 the reported empirical variance was 0.0037 for the modified design with alpha 0.6, compared with 0.0046 for random assignment with the CAR model. The exact MIP reached a 10.0863% optimality gap after the 24-hour time limit in one reported comparison, while modified-design runs on networks of 50 nodes took 13.26 to 24.80 seconds across the tested alpha values. On five Facebook ego networks, the modified design usually had lower empirical variance than random assignment at correlations 0.2 and 0.3, but its advantage was not substantial at 0.1. For networks of approximately 1,000, 1,500, and 2,000 nodes assembled from disjoint clusters, the modified design had the smallest median variance among the compared methods, and the reported rank-sum tests found that its median was significantly lower than random assignment in all three cases.

narrate.summary: This paper studies space-filling designs generated by determinantal point processes and asks whether they remain regular when some coordinates are removed. The design objective is to retain repulsive point patterns in every coordinate projection, supporting experiments whose active factors may change. In the reported regularity comparisons at dimensions 6, 10, and 100, the Dirichlet designs were generally more repulsive and lost less repulsion under projection than the Gaussian designs; the L1-exponential designs were less favorable than the Gaussian designs. For numerical integration, the authors compared Poisson, Gaussian, and Dirichlet designs at intensities 200, 400, 600, 800, and 1000, using 10,000 replications in dimension 6 and test functions of dimensions 1 through 6. The empirical variance was lower than the Poisson reference for both determinantal designs, and the Dirichlet design had lower variance than the Gaussian design across the reported cases.

narrate.summary: This paper develops optimal allocation designs for two-treatment-group random coefficient regression (RCR) models. It considers both estimation of the population mean difference between treatments and prediction of each individual’s treatment response difference. The model assumes a diagonal covariance matrix for individual random effects and the same number of observations per individual in both groups. The results show that the preferred allocation can depart substantially from equal group sizes when the random-effect dispersions differ.
narrate.key_results: For estimating the population treatment difference, the paper gives a closed-form optimal allocation based on the observational error variances and random-effect dispersions. narrate.summary: The paper develops multilevel nonregular fractional factorial designs for screening and estimating effects of quantitative factors. narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential surrogate-based optimization (SSBO) method for expensive, continuous black-box optimization problems with constraints. It uses radial basis function (RBF) models and alternates among genetic algorithm (GA) searches for promising optima, Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) to find under-sampled regions, and sequential quadratic programming (SQP) for local refinement in a reduced interval. The initial design uses LHS with a sample count of twice the number of design variables plus one. Samples that are too close to existing samples are discarded to avoid costly evaluations with little additional information. In the reported examples, the method generally found better or more consistent solutions with substantially fewer expensive function evaluations than the comparison methods.
narrate.key_results: For the one-dimensional function with alpha equal to 512, SSBO had a reported global convergence probability of 100%, a mean objective value of -8.8988, a standard deviation of 4.1299 × 10^-6, and 61.2 evaluations; the genetic algorithm had 82% global convergence and 3450 evaluations, while sequential quadratic programming had 16% and 28.5 evaluations. In the two-dimensional problem, averaged over 50 simulations, SSBO used 17 evaluations and had a mean objective value of 5.1768 with standard deviation 0.00572, compared with 23 evaluations for sequential quadratic programming and 3152 for the genetic algorithm. For the welded-plate problem, SSBO used 54 evaluations and obtained mean cost 2.6332, compared with 215 evaluations and mean 2.6143 for sequential quadratic programming and 48191 evaluations and mean 5.3000 for the genetic algorithm. In the wing example, SSBO obtained objective value 6.0411 using 153 evaluations and 10.36 hours, compared with 3020 evaluations and 54.37 hours for sequential quadratic programming and 50000 evaluations and 901.24 hours for the genetic algorithm.

narrate.summary: The paper designs battery experiments to estimate parameters of the Single Particle Model with electrolyte dynamics (SPMe), a reduced electrochemical model intended for battery control and state estimation. The objective is to make the parameter estimates more accurate by minimizing their estimated uncertainty. The method calculates how voltage outputs respond to the parameters, then optimizes the applied current using an A-optimal criterion that minimizes the trace of the estimated parameter covariance matrix. To reduce the computation required for long experiments, it designs an input in segments and combines them into a complete experiment. Simulations show that this approach estimates parameters faster than constant-current and multistep discharge procedures, and improves voltage prediction when the more detailed Pseudo-Two-Dimensional (P2D) model is treated as the simulated battery.
narrate.key_results: With the SPMe as the simulated plant, the optimized input produced low parameter-estimate error after the first 1,000-second experiment, while the standard approaches took longer to converge. After the first experiment, the reported parameter variances for the optimized design were between 0.00005 and 0.006; those for constant-current discharge ranged from 0.01 to 14.88, and those for multistep discharge ranged from 0.0166 to 0.8118. After 10 experiments, the sensitivity condition number was 577 for the optimized design, compared with 31,963 for constant-current discharge and 260 for multistep discharge; the corresponding collinearity indices were 152, 7,548, and 110. For a 200-second design problem, splitting the input into 4 segments reduced reported computation time from 68.51 seconds to 18.30 seconds, with the scaled covariance trace changing from 0.020 to 0.025. In the P2D simulation, the optimized design gave the best voltage-prediction result on the validation profile and produced physically meaningful parameter estimates sooner than the two standard approaches.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces sequential randomized trials as a design for learning how to sequence, time, and personalize interventions in scaled digital learning environments. In this design, learners are randomly assigned to intervention options at multiple points, allowing researchers to compare treatment sequences and estimate effects at particular times. The authors demonstrate the design in a four-week massive open online course, where learners were assigned weekly email reminders with different problem content and framing, or no email. The trial included 8,681 learners in India and the United States. The findings suggest that email effects differed across learner groups and weeks, but many comparisons were uncertain, so the study provides exploratory evidence rather than a confirmed best intervention.
narrate.key_results: The Problem-based Email Reminder Coursera Study included 8,681 unique learners: 3,455 in India and 5,226 in the United States; 22,073 emails were sent. In India, emails in weeks two and three generally had positive effects on returning to the course, and no-problem emails were as effective as or more effective than problem emails; week two appeared to be a useful time to send reminders. For learners in the United States, effects were mostly not statistically significant, except for a cultural-problem email in week three, and some estimates suggested emails could reduce return activity. Email open rates were 41.7% for United States learners and 27.0% for Indian learners, with a reported p-value below 0.001, despite the greater apparent email benefit among Indian learners. Most sequence comparisons had overlapping confidence intervals, so the authors describe the differences as suggestive rather than significant; compared with assigning each learner once to a fixed condition, repeated randomization allowed comparisons of many more treatment sequences and time-specific effects.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that sequential randomized trials do not adapt randomization during the trial to favor treatments that appear effective, so a different or combined adaptive design may be preferable when the goal is also to benefit current participants. They note that about 10% of learners took the course more than once and were included in multiple trial iterations, and that the study was exploratory rather than confirmatory. They also note that the large number of possible treatment sequences makes sample-size and power planning important, and that their comparison with single randomization used only one example design.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The experiment was conducted in one course and included only learners identified as being in India or the United States, so its findings may not generalize to other courses, populations, or intervention types. The main outcome was course activity measured by clicks or return activity, which does not establish improved learning, completion, or longer-term retention. The weekly assignment probabilities spread participants across many possible sequences, limiting the precision of estimates for individual sequences.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using the exploratory findings to narrow the treatment options, running a second sequential randomized trial with fewer treatments, and then comparing a promising adaptive email sequence with no email in a confirmatory single-randomization trial. They also propose analyses using course completion and assignment performance, examining email length, and testing learner demographics as moderators. They describe combining sequential randomization with adaptive designs and using different randomization timing or trigger-based assignment as further possibilities.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the selected email strategy in other courses and learner populations, while measuring learning and completion outcomes in addition to clicks. Researchers could also evaluate alternative assignment probabilities and practical delivery constraints, then validate whether the resulting personalization rules work when used prospectively.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a Bayesian experimental design method for implicit models, where the likelihood is intractable but data can be simulated. Its objective is to choose designs that maximize expected information gain about model parameters. The method uses Likelihood-Free Inference by Ratio Estimation (LFIRE) to estimate density ratios and approximate mutual information from simulated data. It uses Bayesian optimisation (BO) to search for high-utility designs with fewer evaluations than grid search, including in higher-dimensional design problems. Tests on two simulated epidemiological models show that the approach identifies informative measurement times and produces parameter estimates with credible intervals containing the generating values in the reported examples.
narrate.key_results: For the Death Model, Bayesian optimisation using LFIRE selected a measurement time of 1.06 with utility 1.359; grid search using LFIRE selected 1.10 with utility 1.350, while analytic grid search selected 1.40 with utility 1.347. For an eight-dimensional Death Model design, the authors report reaching an optimum after around 20 utility evaluations, compared with 76,904,685 evaluations for a four-dimensional grid with 40 points per dimension. In the one-dimensional SIR Model, grid search and Bayesian optimisation selected times of 0.40 and 0.44, respectively; for the eight-measurement design, utility was 1.08 at equally spaced times and 1.10 at the optimized times, with convergence in around 15 evaluations. For that eight-measurement SIR design, posterior mean estimates were 0.13 for the infection rate and 0.05 for the recovery rate, and the reported 95% credibility intervals were 0.02 to 0.18 and 0.02 to 0.07, respectively; both intervals contained the generating values.

narrate.summary: This paper designs follow-up experiments that add runs and factors to an existing balanced design, for settings where important factors may have been omitted at the first stage. narrate.summary: The paper develops a theory for statistical inference after covariate-adaptive randomization (CAR) in two-treatment experiments analyzed with a linear model. It studies what happens when the analysis model includes only some of the covariates used during treatment assignment. The authors relate the distribution of the treatment-effect test statistic to the remaining imbalance in omitted covariates and propose using an estimated asymptotic distribution to correct conservative tests. They apply the theory to complete randomization (CR), rerandomization (RR), pairwise sequential randomization (PSR), and Atkinson’s double-adaptive biased coin design (DA-BCD). Their results show that better covariate balance can make conventional treatment tests more conservative, while the proposed correction can restore type I error control and improve power.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 500 units, the conventional treatment test was conservative under RR, DA-BCD, and PSR when the analysis omitted covariates; with a treatment difference of 0.3, for example, the type I error for working model W1 was 0.011 under RR, 0.007 under DA-BCD, and 0.002 under PSR. The corrected tests generally brought simulated type I errors close to the 5% target; the reported corrected values in that comparison ranged from 0.045 to 0.060. In the synthetic clinical-trial example with 850 units and 10,000 repetitions, PSR with no covariates in the analysis had power 0.858 with the corrected test, compared with 0.803 with the conventional test; its corrected power matched the value using all covariates. The paper’s theoretical and numerical comparisons indicate that PSR can yield the strongest corrected treatment tests when some covariates are omitted, while CR tests remain valid without correction but can lose power.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their main framework assumes linear models with continuous outcomes. They note that correction for the logistic-regression extension is difficult because the relevant imbalance distribution is generally unknown, and leave its properties and the alternative distribution for future study.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main theory assumes independent, identically distributed units, independent covariates, and errors independent of the covariates; performance under correlated covariates or other departures is not established here. The numerical evidence is mainly based on specified simulation settings and a synthetic dataset based on a clinical trial, so it does not establish performance across a broad range of real experiments or finite-sample conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to other nonlinear models, including generalized linear models and survival analyses, and to unequal allocation or multiple treatments. They also suggest studying efficiency for nonlinear models and unbalanced designs, and identifying randomization procedures with a known, low-variance imbalance distribution for the logistic setting.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the correction under correlated covariates, unequal variances, and model misspecification, and assess how accurately its estimated critical values perform at smaller sample sizes. Studies using real experiments could also compare the proposed correction with randomization tests under practical allocation constraints.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces a gradient-descent method for constructing D-optimal experimental designs for least-squares polynomial approximation. For a chosen polynomial basis and degree, the method forms a model matrix by evaluating basis functions at candidate input points and optimizes the determinant of the model matrix cross-product. Its block-coordinate procedure updates one design point at a time, selecting the point with the largest gradient norm and using an inverse-matrix update to reduce computation. The authors compare its predictions with Latin hypercube sampling, Sobol’ sequence sampling, and Maxvol sampling on three two-dimensional test functions and a seven-dimensional piston simulation function. The reported results show that the proposed method performs similarly to Maxvol and generally better than the space-filling comparison methods in these tests, while also having low estimated Lebesgue-constant growth.
narrate.key_results: For the two-dimensional tests, the authors report that the proposed gradient-descent design and Maxvol generally have similar approximation accuracy and outperform Latin hypercube and Sobol’ sequence sampling; oversampling mainly improves the latter two methods. For the seven-dimensional piston function with 1,750 polynomial terms and 1,750 samples, the reported median relative errors are 0.0702 for gradient descent, 0.0928 for Maxvol, 0.3963 for Latin hypercube sampling, and 0.5161 for Sobol’ sequence sampling; with 1,790 samples, the corresponding gradient-descent and Maxvol errors are 0.0477 and 0.0400. In one dimension, the estimated Lebesgue-constant growth for D-optimal designs is comparable to that for Chebyshev roots and slower than for Latin hypercube or Sobol’ sampling; for two-dimensional designs of 10 to 70 points, it is also much lower than the estimates for those space-filling methods. The block-coordinate inverse update requires order of the square of the number of basis terms per update, compared with order of the cube for recomputing the full inverse.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a simulation-based design approach for planning instrumentation at prescribed burns, especially those planned for the Fire and Smoke Model Evaluation Experiment (FASMEE). It uses the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled with the SFIRE fire model (WRF-SFIRE) to simulate burns under historical weather conditions selected as typical of each site. Repeated Latin hypercube sampling (rLHS) and variance decomposition are then used to identify locations where measurements are expected to vary with model parameters. The simulations also inform recommendations on burn duration, sensor height and placement, and the documentation of ignition and fire heat flux. The authors report that the approach can highlight locations and parameters relevant to measurement planning, while emphasizing that its results are guidance rather than deterministic predictions.
narrate.key_results: The typical-day analysis selected historical burn dates using the smallest Mahalanobis distance from the weather-state mean; these dates were used to drive simulations at Fishlake, North Kaibab, and Fort Stewart. The Fishlake sensitivity study varied 7 model parameters and used 200 repetitions across 5 sampling intervals, for 1,000 simulations; the reported computations took about a week. The fire heat-flux multiplier contributed up to 50% of the variance in vertical velocity, smoke concentration, and plume-top height, while heat extinction depth contributed up to 40%. At some locations, simulated vertical-velocity variance reached 3 square meters per second squared, corresponding to deviations of about 1.7 meters per second; the paper recommends burn durations of at least a couple of hours to capture plume evolution. The paper does not rank this design against competing design methods; it compares simulated burn scenarios, including baseline and doubled-heat cases, and examines results across selected typical days.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say that results based on typical historical days cannot provide deterministic forecasts because actual burn-day weather may differ. They also describe the sensor-placement sensitivity study as a pilot, note limits in the model’s representation of plume and near-surface flow, and report that insufficient grid resolution can underestimate local updrafts.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The sensitivity-based sensor-placement analysis is demonstrated for the Fishlake case rather than across all three sites, so its transfer to other terrain, fuels, and ignition patterns is not established by these results. The analysis uses first-order parameter effects, so it may not fully characterize interactions among parameters when selecting sensors.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest exploring an alternative typical-day method that randomly selects states from multivariate bins of frequently occurring conditions, while noting that robust bin sizes would need to be chosen. They also propose considering additional model parameters and repetitions, and suggest running simulations, potentially with a shortened sensitivity study, shortly before a burn.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the proposed placements against measurements from completed burns and assess whether the identified high-variance regions actually improve parameter estimates. The authors could also extend the design to explicitly account for practical sensor constraints and parameter interactions, then compare those designs with the variance-based placement strategy used here.

narrate.summary: The paper develops designs for experiments in which a treatment is an ordering of a fixed number of components, with the goal of estimating how the order of each component pair affects the response. Its model extends the pairwise-order model by allowing the effect of a pair to decrease with the distance between the components in the order. The authors use approximate design theory to prove that the uniform design is optimal for a broad class of criteria, and derive the moment matrix and its eigenvalues to assess other designs. They also give constructions for smaller exact designs, including designs that can be arranged in blocks. The constructed designs match the uniform design's moment matrix under the usual pairwise-order model and show high reported efficiencies under the tapered models examined.
narrate.key_results: The uniform design is proved optimal for determinant, inverse-trace, smallest-eigenvalue, maximum-prediction-variance, and moment-matrix-trace criteria. For the earlier 12-run design with five components, reported determinant and inverse-trace efficiencies under the two tapered models are 0.985 and 0.972, and 0.989 and 0.980; for the 24-run designs with six components, the best reported values are 0.992 and 0.984, and 0.994 and 0.988. The authors' fractional designs for four through ten components have both reported efficiencies over 0.99 under both tapered models, and their blocked versions also exceed 0.99 for up to ten components. For eight components, a 168-run design has the uniform moment matrix under the usual model; a reduced 84-run design has reported determinant and inverse-trace efficiencies of 0.986 and 0.973 under that model, 0.973 and 0.946 under one tapered model, and 0.972 and 0.945 under the other.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The model represents pairwise order effects, but does not include higher-order interactions among three or more components; the paper therefore does not establish performance when such effects matter. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing smaller efficient designs, including through incomplete block designs and partial permutations, and report that step-down and exchange algorithms may help. They also call for more work on design algorithms for larger numbers of components and discuss using approximate theory when response variances differ by treatment.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the proposed designs in real chemical or process experiments and compare their predictions with those from alternative models that include higher-order order effects. Further work could also adapt the constructions to practical restrictions such as unavailable orders, run costs, or restricted randomization, and provide accessible software for generating and evaluating designs.

narrate.summary: The paper develops iterative algorithms for finding continuous experimental designs for linear regression models. Its objectives are D-optimality (determinant-based) and A-optimality (average-variance-based), both aimed at estimating model parameters precisely. The algorithms update the design density directly over the continuous design space rather than first discretizing that space. The authors prove monotonic convergence and convergence to an optimal design for the D-optimal algorithm under a stated boundedness condition, while they support the A-optimal algorithm with numerical results and conjecture monotonic convergence. Four numerical settings illustrate the designs and compare their support points and weights with theoretical values and results from a randomized exchange method.
narrate.key_results: The paper reports that its algorithms converged in all four numerical settings, but it gives no numerical runtime or speedup measurements. In the quadratic model on a disk, the theoretical D-optimal allocation places 1/6 of the weight at the center and 5/6 uniformly on the boundary. For the quadratic model on a square, the reported design has 9 support points; the proposed D-optimal weights closely match the theoretical weights, such as 0.1457 versus 0.1457 at each corner. For the quadratic model on a three-dimensional cube, the proposed method identifies 27 support points, and its reported D-optimal weights are close to theoretical values; the comparison also shows that randomized exchange weights can vary across points and runs.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that they do not have a theoretical convergence justification for the A-optimal algorithm and only conjecture that it converges monotonically, based on simulations. Their D-optimal convergence result assumes that the log determinant of the integral of the regressor outer product over the design space is bounded.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation covers four polynomial-regression settings and comparisons with randomized exchange, so it does not establish performance across a broad range of models, design spaces, or competing algorithms. The paper gives no reported runtime, stopping rule, or assessment of how to turn a continuous design into a feasible finite-run experiment subject to operational constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors note that the basic ideas may extend beyond the two criteria studied and to higher-dimensional continuous design spaces. They do not specify a concrete follow-up study.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could establish convergence conditions for the A-optimal update and compare computational cost and accuracy against more methods over varied models and design spaces. It could also study finite-run implementations under process constraints and validate the resulting designs in real continuous-process experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops optimal test designs for estimating a person's ability in the generalized partial credit model, assuming item thresholds and discrimination parameters are already known. It first derives the design maximizing Fisher information for a known ability, then considers Bayesian criteria that average performance over a weight distribution for ability. The locally optimal probability pattern puts equal probability on the first and last response categories and zero probability on intermediate categories, making the model equivalent to the two-parameter logistic model. Because that pattern cannot be attained with finite thresholds when there are more than two categories, the authors also examine Bayesian optimality and its dependence on the weight distribution. Their examples show that the one-point design can be Bayesian optimal for fixed discrimination and sufficiently concentrated symmetric weights, but not in all cases when discrimination and threshold can both vary.
narrate.key_results: For a fixed number of more than two response categories, the locally optimal design does not exist at finite thresholds; it can only be approached as the thresholds move toward limiting values. In an illustrative four-category item comparison, the information of the limiting optimal design was about 2.86 times higher at medium ability and about 3.75 times higher at low or high ability than for the example item. With discrimination fixed at one, the reported critical scales for the expected-log-information and negative-expected-inverse-information criteria were, respectively, 2.5757 divided by J and 2.1773 divided by J for uniform weights, 1.683 divided by J and 1.177 divided by J for normal weights, and 1 divided by J and 0.603 divided by J for logistic weights. Numerical sensitivity checks for three-category items suggest that the necessary conditions are sufficient for both criteria under uniform and normal weights, and for the expected-log-information criterion under logistic weights; for the other logistic criterion, the necessary condition appears not to be sufficient. In numerical examples for the dichotomous model with both threshold and discrimination varying, the optimal one-point designs were not Bayesian optimal for the uniform, normal, or logistic weight distributions examined.

They also identify unresolved cases, including asymmetric ability weights, optimal sampling designs, and Bayesian designs for alternative ordinal models.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The conclusions rely on the specified generalized partial credit model, known item parameters, and an asymptotically efficient estimator; they do not establish performance when those assumptions fail. Numerical sensitivity investigations are limited to items with up to three response categories, and the paper offers no validation using data from actual tests.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying designs under asymmetric ability weight distributions and deriving optimal sampling designs for the generalized partial credit model. They also call for further design work on alternative ordinal models, including Bayesian designs for the graded response model and designs for the sequential model.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to compare the theoretical designs with constrained designs whose thresholds and discrimination levels are feasible in real test development. Future studies could also test robustness to item-parameter uncertainty and model misspecification using real assessment data.

narrate.summary: The paper develops approximation algorithms for choosing a fixed number of experiments to estimate an unknown parameter vector in a linear model with Gaussian measurement errors. It considers the determinant-based design objective, which corresponds to reducing the volume of the confidence ellipsoid for the estimation error. The algorithms first solve a continuous convex relaxation and then use randomized selection based on the relaxed weights, with separate methods for designs that allow repeated experiments and those that do not. The authors also derive deterministic versions of the randomized methods. Their main finding is that constant-factor guarantees hold for both variants, and stronger guarantees are available when the number of selected experiments is sufficiently large relative to the parameter dimension.
narrate.key_results: For designs with and without repetitions, the proposed methods guarantee an objective value of at least one divided by Euler's number times the optimum; deterministic implementations retain the same guarantees. Without repetitions, the asymptotic sampling method guarantees a factor of one minus the target tolerance when the run size is at least four times the parameter dimension divided by the tolerance, plus twelve times the inverse squared tolerance times the logarithm of its inverse. With repetitions, the corresponding guarantee holds when the run size is at least the parameter dimension minus one divided by the target tolerance. These are theoretical results, not empirical comparisons; the paper reports randomized implementations with running times of order n squared or linear in n for the main methods, and more costly deterministic implementations.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating more sophisticated relaxation schemes to improve the approximation analyses and proving whether the bounds are tight. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate these guarantees in real experiments and test sensitivity to departures from the assumed linear Gaussian model. It could also adapt the selection procedures to practical constraints such as costs or restricted candidate sets, and investigate sequential selection when experiments can be added over time.

narrate.summary: This paper develops approximation algorithms for selecting a fixed number of measurement vectors to minimize average estimation variance, the A-optimal design objective. It studies designs both with and without repeated selections, using a convex relaxation to obtain fractional selection weights. The authors introduce proportional volume sampling, which weights candidate sets using a hard-core probability measure and the determinant of their information matrix. They show how approximate independence properties of the measure yield approximation guarantees and give efficient randomized and deterministic implementations for the proposed sampling methods. Theoretical results establish improved guarantees in several run-size regimes, as well as limits on the relaxation and a hardness result when the number selected equals the vector dimension.

narrate.summary: The paper develops ascent with quadratic assistance (AQuA), a method for converting approximate designs into high-quality exact designs for linear regression and related design problems. It targets several information objectives, including D-optimality, A-optimality, and I-optimality, and permits linear constraints on the design. The method approximates the criterion quadratically near an optimal or estimated approximate information matrix, then optimizes that approximation over integer-valued run counts. A low-rank property enables a mixed-integer conic quadratic formulation that avoids storing a large quadratic matrix. In the reported examples, this formulation produced designs with efficiency close to competing methods and substantially reduced computation time in large or constrained problems.
narrate.key_results: For the constrained three-component mixture model with 861 candidate points, the D-optimal exact design had efficiency 0.98374 and took 8.56 seconds with the proposed conic formulation, compared with efficiencies 0.98377 and 0.98373 and times of 616.91 and 625.53 seconds for the mixed-integer second-order cone and direct integer quadratic approaches. For the same model under I-optimality, the conic formulation achieved efficiency 0.99647 in 4.54 seconds, compared with 0.99627 in 602.96 seconds for the mixed-integer second-order cone approach and 0.98928 in 636.16 seconds for the direct integer quadratic approach. The authors report that the conic reformulation can reduce computation time by as much as two orders of magnitude while producing designs of similar efficiency. In a wine-review data example with 111,534 records, the method selected 42 records under a USD 1,000 price limit and a minimum average quality of 90 points; each of five random starts converged to the same solution in as few as four steps, with each step taking less than four seconds.

narrate.summary: This paper develops space-filling designs for computer experiments that aim to identify control settings robust to variation in noise factors. It models the response with a Gaussian process and focuses on accurately estimating control-by-noise interactions, which matter for finding robust settings. The proposed design starts with a cross array, then jitters its points using a maximum projection criterion to improve coverage while preserving the interaction-estimation structure. For normally distributed noise, a double transformation based on a beta distribution with shape parameters of two-thirds spreads design points more than a direct probability transformation. Simulated and manufacturing examples show improved identification of robust settings and clearer estimation of an important interaction, though the reported prediction improvements are mixed.
narrate.key_results: In the simulation study, the authors tested 200 cases and used 100 test samples per case to compare designs with 54 runs. Applying the double transformation improved prediction performance for both the maximum-projection Latin hypercube and the jittered cross array; for estimating the robust setting, the double-transformed jittered cross array performed best among the compared designs. In the manufacturing packing-line example, the new design and the existing design each used 91 runs, and their prediction errors were reported as close. The new double-transformed jittered cross array estimated the most significant control-by-noise interaction more accurately than the transformed maximum-projection Latin hypercube; the paper reports no numerical prediction-error or interaction-error values.

The demonstrated examples also require 54 or 91 runs, which may be costly for some computer models.

narrate.summary: The paper develops Bayesian D-optimal designs for pharmaceutical dose-response studies that compare multiple dosing-frequency groups while allowing some model parameters to be shared. The objective is to estimate all parameters accurately while accounting for uncertainty in their values and choosing doses and sample allocation across groups. The authors derive analytical characterizations of saturated designs, which use the minimum number of dose levels needed to estimate the parameters. They treat shared location parameters separately from shared location and scale parameters, and give results for Emax, exponential, and linear-in-log dose-response models. In a numerical example, the saturated design has estimation efficiency close to that of an unrestricted Bayesian design and the locally optimal benchmark across the parameter combinations examined.
narrate.key_results: For models with a common location parameter, the authors show that the group with the smallest error variance is used to estimate that common parameter, and derive saturated designs from the optimal designs for the individual models. For two models with common location and scale parameters, they characterize the saturated designs by cases determined by the ratio of group variances and functions of the prior distributions. In the example with two Emax groups and 25 parameter combinations, the saturated design's efficiencies range from 94.25% to 99.81% relative to the locally D-optimal design; the unrestricted Bayesian design's efficiencies range from 96.59% to 99.94%. The saturated design uses four dose levels in total in the example, compared with five for the unrestricted candidate design, while retaining efficiency close to that candidate.

narrate.summary: The paper develops optimal experimental design methods for linear inverse problems with constraints on the unknown state, using tomographic image reconstruction as its main application. It aims to reduce measurement costs while limiting reconstruction error. One design approach uses a fine grid of candidate measurement settings and a sparsity penalty; another directly optimizes the locations of a fixed number of measurements. The methods use Bayes risk when distributional information is available and empirical Bayes risk when training examples are used instead. The authors derive efficient calculations for the unconstrained case and use interior point methods and implicit differentiation to optimize designs with inequality constraints.
narrate.key_results: In simulations using four image datasets, each with 20 training images, adding non-negativity or box constraints generally produced lower reconstruction error and required fewer projections than unconstrained or equality-constrained designs. For rectangles, the non-negativity and box-constrained designs selected projections at 0 and 90 degrees; for pentagons, their selected angles were 25, 64, 99, 136, and 171 degrees, and 27, 62, 99, 134, and 171 degrees, respectively. In the fixed-size design comparison, the authors optimized two projection angles and found that box constraints gave the lowest errors overall across the tested datasets. The paper also shows that increasing the sparsity penalty reduces the number of selected projections, with constrained designs often achieving lower error even with fewer projections; it does not report a single numerical efficiency gain across all cases.

narrate.summary: This review examines how to choose simulation or experiment inputs for fitting polynomial chaos expansions (PCEs) by least-squares approximation (LSA). It covers standard random sampling, space-filling designs, quadrature-based sampling, and optimal design of experiments (ODE), including designs aimed at estimating coefficients or improving predictions. The authors propose alphabetic-coherence-optimal sampling, which selects runs using D-, A-, or E-optimal criteria from a candidate set generated by coherence-optimal sampling. They compare methods in three numerical examples: manufactured expansions, a nonlinear oscillator, and lithium-ion battery life prediction. The proposed hybrid approach generally gives the most accurate results, particularly for high-order expansions and when the number of runs is close to the number of coefficients.
narrate.key_results: The numerical comparison averages results over 60 independent replications for the manufactured-function example. For a ninth-order oscillator expansion with 220 coefficients, the authors compare 242, 440, and 660 runs; alphabetic-coherence-optimal designs have smaller prediction errors than the other compared methods, especially at 242 runs, and D- and A-optimal variants perform slightly better than the E-optimal variant. In the battery example, a third-order expansion uses 121 runs and its predicted remaining useful life distributions coincide with Monte Carlo results based on 20 × 10^6 solution runs. The authors report that standard Monte Carlo and Latin hypercube sampling can be adequate for low-order expansions when runs number about three to four times the coefficient count, but may perform poorly for high-order expansions even with that oversampling.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that current algorithms for alphabetic-optimal design become computationally expensive for large numbers of polynomial coefficients, limiting their use to relatively low-order or low-dimensional expansions. narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical comparison covers three numerical examples and a selected subset of the reviewed sampling methods, so it does not establish that the reported ranking holds across other models or practical constraints. The hybrid designs also require generating a candidate set and carrying out an optimization procedure, adding design-generation work that may matter when model evaluations are inexpensive or operational constraints restrict allowable runs.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify developing scalable optimization techniques for alphabetic-optimal designs as an open research problem. They also mention multi-element generalized polynomial chaos as a possible way to address increasing error over time in the oscillator example, while leaving its discussion outside the paper’s scope.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the hybrid method on real experiments and on constrained run plans, such as designs with bounds, discrete factors, or restricted combinations of settings. It could also evaluate adaptive or sequential use in which new runs are selected using observed model outputs, and provide software that makes the design construction practical at larger coefficient counts.

narrate.summary: The paper develops design guidelines for stochastic kriging, a method for predicting the mean response of a noisy computer simulation. It separates prediction inaccuracy into nominal error, numeric error, parameter estimation error, and numeric error in parameter estimation. The authors derive bounds that connect each source of error to design features, including how well distinct sites cover the input space, how far apart they are, and how many runs are replicated at each site. The guidelines also address non-stationary response patterns, changing noise levels, and regression functions. The main finding is that designs should balance space coverage with replication, with more replication favored when noise is large relative to process variation. ࠀ
narrate.key_results: In simulations with a fixed total of 72 runs, the preferred balance shifted toward more replication as noise increased and toward more distinct, space-filling sites as noise decreased. For example, at noise variance 0.5, the MaxPro design with four replications had average maximum squared prediction error 0.192; at noise variance 0.01, its lowest reported error was 0.010 with one replication. In the input-varying noise study, with 18 distinct sites, parameter-estimation-guided allocation had error 0.113 when replications varied by location, compared with 0.141 with constant replication; the corresponding values were 0.125 versus 0.170 with 24 sites and 0.125 versus 0.190 with 36 sites. The study used 300 simulated Gaussian-process draws for its prediction-error comparisons, and the authors report that the proposed bounds gave useful guidance for choosing replication levels.

They also note that characterizing non-stationarity across the input space and optimizing designs under complex criteria can be challenging.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons use simulated Gaussian-process responses in a small number of two-dimensional settings, so they do not establish how well the guidelines transfer to high-dimensional or real simulation studies. The bounds and example allocations also depend on assumed covariance and noise structures; the paper does not test how sensitive the recommendations are when those structures or their parameter values are wrong.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest using localized residual resampling when the Gaussian noise model fits poorly, and adapting the non-stationary model to represent changes in process variability. They also suggest using the numeric-error bounds to identify and remove design points that cause ill-conditioning, and using projected space-filling designs when some inputs are inactive.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the design guidelines in real engineering simulations and across higher-dimensional problems, including sensitivity to misspecified covariance and noise models. Further work could develop software that automates the replication and site-selection trade-off, and assess sequential updates as simulation results arrive.

narrate.summary: This software paper presents acebayes, an R package for finding Bayesian optimal experimental designs. The package applies approximate coordinate exchange (ACE) to maximize expected utility for goals including parameter estimation, model selection, and prediction. It builds a Gaussian process (GP) approximation to expected utility for one design coordinate at a time, then searches for a promising value of that coordinate while holding the others fixed. The package supports user-defined utility functions as well as tailored functions for generalized linear and nonlinear models. Its examples show that the approach can improve design objectives in problems with more design coordinates than methods discussed as existing in the paper.
narrate.key_results: For the compartmental pharmacokinetic example, the final design had 13 unique sampling times rather than 18, and its reported relative D-efficiency was 103.0255 percent compared with the Phase I design. In the logistic-regression example, the normal-based parameter-estimation design had mean approximate utility of -8.056569, compared with -10.61123 for the pseudo-Bayesian A-optimal design; the reported relative A-efficiency between the selected and first-run designs was 118.4983 percent. For chemical model selection, the estimated probability of selecting the data-generating model rose from about 81 percent for the starting design to about 88 percent for the optimized design. In the prediction example, approximate utility increased from 92.41169 to 95.86214 while total placement cost fell from 6.653732 to 3.081133; these are illustrative examples rather than a broad comparative benchmark.

key_equations.name: Expected utility objective
key_equations.explanation: U(d) is the expected utility of design d, E denotes expectation over unknown quantities and responses, and u is the utility.

key_equations.name: Coordinate update
key_equations.explanation: x_ij* is the selected value for coordinate ij, x is a candidate coordinate value, and Uhat_ij is the GP-based approximation to expected utility for that coordinate.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that ACE is heuristic and can be sensitive to the starting design, so it should be repeated from multiple starts to reduce the risk of ending at a local optimum. They also note that complex problems can require substantial computing resources, and that the examples are deliberately simple with small designs.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The examples provide demonstrations of the package, not systematic validation across real industrial experiments or a wide range of competing methods. narrate.summary: This paper studies an extensible randomized design for numerical integration, formed by mapping scrambled van der Corput sequence points through a Hilbert space-filling curve. The objective is to estimate integrals over a multidimensional unit cube and to establish when the standardized estimation error is asymptotically normal. The authors show that the method acts as a stratified design, with one random point in each curve-defined region. They prove normality for continuously differentiable functions and for certain discontinuous functions, under stated conditions. For smooth nonconstant functions, the variance rate matches the previously established upper-bound rate.
narrate.key_results: For smooth nonconstant functions, the paper establishes a variance lower bound of order n to the power negative one minus two divided by d, matching the upper-bound rate reported from earlier work. Empirical variances decayed at rate n to the power negative two for d equal to 2 and n to the power negative five-fourths for d equal to 8; the comparison Monte Carlo variance was 1 divided by n. The numerical study used 1,000 independent replications and sample size 16,384 for its standardized-error density comparisons; the Hilbert-curve method appeared nearly normal for the tested smooth, piecewise-smooth, and indicator functions. Comparisons also showed nearly normal errors for nested-uniform scrambled Sobol points in the reported cases, whereas linearly scrambled Sobol errors were notably nonnormal, especially at d equal to 2.

narrate.summary: This paper develops algebraic tests for deciding whether a qualitative fractional factorial design can be made regular by permuting factor levels. It studies symmetric orthogonal arrays with a prime number of levels, rather than optimizing a response model or a design criterion. One approach represents level permutations with polynomials and uses polynomial algebra to test whether two fractions are equivalent. A second approach represents strength-two arrays with Latin squares and checks whether suitable level permutations make the square rank one. Examples show that the methods can identify arrays equivalent to regular fractions and rule out arrays that cannot be made regular.
narrate.key_results: For five-level, three-factor arrays with 25 runs, the paper examines three examples: one is regular, a second can be transformed into a regular array by level permutations, and a third cannot. In the five-level permutation search, the authors reduce the candidates on the third factor from 120 permutations to six relevant ones. A polynomial-algebra calculation for one example took 29 seconds and produced a Gröbner basis with 91 elements; the calculation recovered permutations establishing equivalence to a regular fraction. The authors also give a seven-level strength-two array constructed to remain nonregular under level permutations.
